teile.einleitung: Postmen and postwomen bring letters, newspapers and parcels right to the front door. In Switzerland they are often called “Pöstler” or “Pöstlerin”, and they are out and about in every neighbourhood almost every day.
wichtigste: In Switzerland the postman is often called a “Pöstler”.
The postman puts the letters into the letter box.
For the post to arrive correctly, the names of the residents must be on the letter box.
The colour of Swiss Post is yellow.
Many postmen ride an electric scooter through the neighbourhoods.
On Sundays there is normally no letter delivery.
Before delivery, the letters are sorted in the letter centre.

abschnitte.text: The postman or postwoman **delivers** post to households and businesses. In the morning they collect their sorted letters, newspapers and parcels and then go on their fixed round. They put the letters into the **letter boxes** and take larger items to the door. For everything to arrive correctly, the names of the residents must be clearly readable on the letter box. Many postmen know their neighbourhood and the people in it very well.

abschnitte.titel: Out and about in the neighbourhood
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland many postmen ride a yellow three-wheeled **electric scooter**, which has a lot of room for post. In towns some go on foot or by bike, and in the countryside also by car. The yellow colour shows at once that someone is from **Swiss Post**. Postmen are out in wind, rain and snow. That is why they wear weatherproof clothing.

If nobody is at home and a parcel does not fit into the letter box, the postman leaves a **collection notice** inside. With it you can collect the item later at the post office or another pick-up point. Registered letters must be signed for by the recipient. Today you can also track parcels online using a **tracking number**.

Before a letter reaches the postman, it is sorted by machines in a large **letter centre**. The machines read the address and the postcode automatically. From there the post goes by lorry or train to the delivery offices. The postmen then put the items in the order of their round. In Switzerland there is no normal letter delivery on Sundays.

In the past the **postman** carried a heavy leather bag over his shoulder and walked many kilometres. In Switzerland **mail coaches** carried letters and travellers over the Alpine passes. The postilion blew the post horn to announce their arrival. This is where the three-note horn of the PostBus comes from, which you can still hear on mountain roads today. Since 1849 the post in Switzerland has been a matter for the federal government.

begriffe.erklaerung: The Swiss word for a postman or postwoman.
Bringing post to the recipient.
A slip of paper that says where you can collect an item.
A large building in which letters are sorted by machine.

gewusst: On their round a postman often covers many kilometres and stops hundreds of times.
The three-note horn of the PostBus comes from a melody by Gioachino Rossini.
In remote mountain valleys the post used to be brought even by mules.

teile.einleitung: A kite is a light flying object made of a frame and fabric or paper that flies in the wind on a string. Many children fly kites in autumn. Kites are an ancient toy, but they are also used for sport, science and festivals.
wichtigste: A kite needs wind to rise.
You hold it on a string.
Kites were invented a very long time ago in China.
A long tail makes a simple kite fly steadily.
You can build a simple kite yourself from wooden sticks and paper.
A stunt kite has two strings and can be steered.
In kitesurfing, a kite pulls a person on a board across the water.

abschnitte.text: A kite consists of a light **frame** made of wood, bamboo or plastic rods. Paper, plastic film or fabric is stretched over it; this is the **cover**. You hold the kite in the wind on a string. Because it hangs on the string, it cannot simply fly away. Modern kites are mostly made of nylon fabric with carbon fibre rods.

The kite stands at an angle in the wind. The air flows against the cover and pushes the kite upwards, creating **lift**. The string holds it in place; otherwise it would simply be blown away. On simple kites, a long **tail** makes sure it flies steadily and does not spin. Without wind a kite falls down, and in a storm it can tear.

Kites were invented a very long time ago in **China**, probably more than 2,000 years ago. There they were used for festivals, but also to send messages. Kites later reached Europe by way of Asia. In 1752 the American scientist **Benjamin Franklin** flew a kite into a thunderstorm to show that lightning is electrical. This experiment was very dangerous and must never be copied.

The classic **single-line kite** has the shape of a diamond and a single string. A **stunt kite** has two strings with which you can steer it and fly tricks. Box kites are three-dimensional and fly very steadily. Huge kites in the shape of animals can be seen at kite festivals, for example in Asia or on North Sea beaches.

In **kitesurfing**, a large stunt kite pulls a person on a board across the water. In Switzerland you can watch this, for example, on Lake Silvaplana in the Engadine, where a strong wind often blows. In winter there is also snowkiting, where you are pulled on skis or a snowboard. Kite sportspeople can even make high jumps with their kites.

You can build a simple kite yourself from two **wooden sticks** and paper. You tie the sticks together into a cross and stretch a string all the way round. Then you glue paper over it and attach a tail made of paper bows. Here people like to fly kites in autumn, because it is often windy then. You should always stay far away from power lines, roads and airfields.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force that pushes an object upwards in the air.
Kite with two strings that you can steer.
The fabric, paper or plastic film over the frame.
Water sport in which a kite pulls a person on a board.

gewusst: In China kites were built more than 2,000 years ago.
The Wright brothers first tested their ideas for the aeroplane on large kites.
On Lake Silvaplana in the Engadine, people often kite thanks to the regular Maloja wind.

teile.einleitung: An antenna is a component that turns electrical signals into radio waves or catches radio waves and turns them back into electrical signals. Without antennas there would be no radio, no television, no mobile phones and no Wi-Fi. Antennas come in all sizes, from the tiny part in a smartphone to the huge transmitter tower.
wichtigste: A transmitting antenna turns electrical signals into radio waves.
A receiving antenna catches radio waves and turns them back into electrical signals.
Around 1887 Heinrich Hertz was the first to demonstrate electromagnetic waves in an experiment.
In 1901 Guglielmo Marconi was the first to send a radio signal across the Atlantic.
The higher the frequency, the smaller the antenna usually is.
Satellite dishes receive signals from satellites.
At about 250 metres, the St Chrischona television tower is the tallest free-standing structure in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: In a **transmitting antenna** an alternating current flows that swings back and forth very fast. This creates electromagnetic waves that spread at the speed of light. When these waves hit a **receiving antenna**, they produce a tiny current there. A receiver amplifies it and turns it back into sound, pictures or data.

The right size for an antenna depends on the **wavelength**. You calculate it by dividing the speed of light by the frequency: at 100 megahertz, a typical FM radio frequency, that is 3 metres. A simple rod antenna, the **dipole**, is often half as long as the wavelength. That is why antennas for high frequencies, as in mobile phones or Wi-Fi, are very small.

Around 1887 in Karlsruhe the German physicist **Heinrich Hertz** demonstrated that electromagnetic waves really exist. The unit of frequency, the hertz, is named after him. The Italian Guglielmo Marconi developed radio technology from this and in 1901 sent a radio signal from England to Newfoundland across the Atlantic. For this he received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1909, together with Ferdinand Braun.

The **Yagi antenna**, with several parallel rods, used to be seen on many rooftops for television reception; it was developed in Japan in the 1920s. The **satellite dish** looks like a bowl and focuses weak signals from satellites at one point. Huge dishes serve as radio telescopes that receive signals from space. Smartphones contain several tiny antennas for mobile networks, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and GPS.

Because of its many mountains and valleys, Switzerland needs especially many transmitters. At about 250 metres, the **St Chrischona television tower** near Bettingen in the canton of Basel-City is the tallest free-standing structure in the country. Other important transmitters stand on mountain peaks such as the Säntis or the Uetliberg. On top of that there are thousands of mobile phone antennas on roofs and masts.

Antennas connect the whole world without cables. Planes, ships and emergency services communicate by radio, and GPS receivers work out their position using signals from satellites. Space probes far out in the solar system send their data to Earth via large antennas. Garage door openers, radio car keys and baby monitors also work with antennas.

begriffe.erklaerung: An invisible electromagnetic wave that carries information through the air.
How many times a wave oscillates per second, measured in hertz.
The distance from one wave crest to the next.
A simple antenna made of two rods that together are usually half a wavelength long.
A bowl-shaped antenna that focuses signals at one point.

gewusst: Our body can also affect a signal like an antenna, which is why radio reception sometimes gets better when you touch the antenna.
The Voyager space probes are more than 20 billion kilometres away and are still received by huge antennas on Earth.
Heinrich Hertz is said to have remarked that his discovery had no practical use.

teile.einleitung: 5G is the fifth generation of mobile communications, the technology with which mobile phones and other devices exchange data wirelessly. The G stands for generation. 5G is meant to be faster than 4G, to connect many more devices at the same time and to transmit data with very little delay.
wichtigste: 5G stands for the fifth generation of mobile communications.
5G transmits data with electromagnetic radio waves.
A low latency means that data arrives with very little delay.
With beamforming, antennas send signals to individual devices in a targeted way.
Very high frequencies, millimetre waves, are strongly weakened by obstacles and only reach a short distance.
Switzerland auctioned the first 5G frequencies in 2019.
In Switzerland the limits for mobile phone radiation are set by the NISV.

abschnitte.text: Each generation brought new possibilities. The first networks transmitted calls in analogue form; in Switzerland the mobile network was called **Natel** from 1978. With 2G came digital calls and text messages, with 3G mobile internet, and with 4G fast surfing and video streaming. 5G was introduced in many countries from 2019, including Switzerland.

5G uses **electromagnetic radio waves**, like radio, Wi-Fi and earlier mobile networks. Depending on the frequency range, the waves have different lengths: lower frequencies reach far and get into buildings well. Very high frequencies, **millimetre waves**, can transmit huge amounts of data but are strongly weakened by walls, trees and even rain. That is why many small antennas close together are needed for them.

Modern 5G antennas consist of many small antenna elements. With the technique of **beamforming** they focus the radio waves and direct them at individual devices, rather like a torch instead of a light bulb. In this way the signal reaches the phone better and the surroundings are exposed to less radiation. In addition, several devices can be served at the same time by different beams.

In good conditions 5G can transmit several gigabits per second, considerably more than 4G. The **latency**, that is the delay, is meant to be only a few milliseconds. This is important for uses where every millisecond counts, for example remote-controlled machines or connected vehicles. In addition, very many devices can be connected at the same time in a small space, for example in a full football stadium.

The **Internet of Things** means that many devices and sensors are connected to the internet. These can be electricity meters, parking sensors, machines in factories or measuring devices in fields. 5G is meant to make such networks possible because it can handle many connections at the same time. This is creating new uses in farming, transport and industry.

In February 2019 Switzerland auctioned the first frequencies for 5G to the providers Swisscom, Sunrise and Salt. The first 5G antennas went into operation that same year. The **NISV**, the Ordinance on Protection against Non-Ionising Radiation, sets out how strongly antennas may radiate. The Swiss limits in places such as homes and schools are stricter than in many other countries, and 5G has been much debated in public.

begriffe.erklaerung: A new stage of a technology that replaces the previous one.
The time data needs to get from the sender to the receiver.
A technique with which antennas send radio waves in a particular direction.
Says how many times a wave oscillates per second, measured in hertz.
The Swiss ordinance that sets limits for radiation from antennas and power lines.

gewusst: The Swiss mobile network used to be called Natel, and many people in Switzerland still call their mobile phone that today.
Millimetre waves are called this because their wavelength is only a few millimetres.
Research is already being done on the next generation, 6G.

teile.einleitung: Empa is the Swiss Federal Laboratories for Materials Science and Technology. It examines materials such as concrete, metals, plastics and textiles and develops new materials and technologies. It belongs to the ETH Domain and has sites in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.
wichtigste: Empa stands for Eidgenössische Materialprüfungs- und Forschungsanstalt, the Federal Materials Testing and Research Institute.
Its forerunner was founded in Zurich in 1880 as an institute for testing building materials.
Empa works in Dübendorf, St Gallen and Thun.
It belongs to the ETH Domain.
In 1891 the young testing institute under Ludwig von Tetmajer investigated the collapse of the railway bridge near Münchenstein.
Its main areas include nanostructured materials and technologies.
On the “move” platform in Dübendorf, mobility without fossil fuels has been tested since 2015.
In 2022 Tanja Zimmermann became the first woman to head Empa.

abschnitte.text: Empa is a research institute of the Swiss Confederation. It tests how strong, durable or safe materials are and looks for new, better materials. It works closely with companies, universities and authorities. It belongs to the **ETH Domain**, together with ETH Zurich, EPFL and other research institutes.

In 1880 an **institute for testing building materials** was set up in Zurich, the forerunner of Empa. At that time many bridges and railway lines were being built, and people wanted to be sure that iron and cement would hold. In 1891 a railway bridge collapsed under a train near **Münchenstein** in the canton of Basel-Landschaft. Under **Ludwig von Tetmajer**, the testing institute investigated the collapse, which greatly increased its importance.

The largest site is in **Dübendorf** near Zurich. In **St Gallen**, Empa researches among other things textiles and materials for medicine and health. In **Thun** the work is, for example, on surfaces and joining techniques. Experts from physics, chemistry, engineering and biology work together there.

One focus is **nanostructured materials**, that is, substances with tiny structures a thousand times thinner than a hair. Other topics are energy, sustainable building, the environment and health. Empa also measures air pollutants and studies how materials age. In this way it helps to make products safer and more environmentally friendly.

In Dübendorf, Empa has test facilities where new ideas are tried out under real conditions. On the **move** platform, opened in 2015, mobility without fossil fuels is tested, for example with hydrogen or electricity. In the **NEST** research building, new building and energy technologies are tested directly in lived-in flats and offices. In this way research results reach everyday life faster.

begriffe.erklaerung: Examining how strong, durable and safe a material is.
Group made up of the two Swiss Federal Institutes of Technology and several federal research institutes.
Material with tiny structures in the range of millionths of a millimetre.
Fuels made from oil, natural gas or coal.

gewusst: The Münchenstein bridge collapse of 1891 is considered one of the worst railway accidents in Switzerland.
In the NEST research building, individual living units can be swapped like drawers.
Among other things, Empa tests whether protective clothing really protects against heat or cold.

teile.einleitung: CSEM is a Swiss research and development centre for microtechnology, electronics and solar energy with its headquarters in Neuchâtel. The name stands for Centre Suisse d'Electronique et de Microtechnique. Here tiny components, smart sensors and new technologies are created that later end up in watches, medical devices or solar panels.
wichtigste: CSEM stands for Centre Suisse d'Electronique et de Microtechnique.
The headquarters is in Neuchâtel.
CSEM was created in 1984 by the merger of several research institutes.
A predecessor organisation, the Centre Electronique Horloger, built one of the first quartz wristwatches, “Beta 1”, in 1967.
At its Alpnach site CSEM does research mainly on microrobotics.
In 2007 the Neuchâtel Observatory with its time and frequency laboratory was integrated into CSEM.
According to its own figures, CSEM has produced more than 50 spin-offs in about 40 years (as of 2026).

abschnitte.text: CSEM is a private, non-profit research centre that works closely with industry. It takes ideas from science far enough for companies to make products out of them. This is called **technology transfer**. CSEM is also supported by the federal government and by cantons. Its strength is **microtechnology**, the technology of very small components.

The history of CSEM begins in the watchmaking region around Neuchâtel and the Jura. In 1962 Swiss watch companies founded the **Centre Electronique Horloger** to research electronic watches. There, in 1967, the prototype “Beta 1” was created, one of the first **quartz wristwatches** in the world. In 1984 several research institutes joined together to form CSEM.

CSEM works on sensors, microelectronics, precision mechanics, robotics and digital technology. One important field is **photovoltaics**, that is, solar cells that turn light into electricity. In 2001 CSEM presented a **3D time-of-flight camera**, which measures distances from the time light takes to travel. Such cameras recognise shapes in space, rather like bats do with sound.

The headquarters is in Neuchâtel on Lake Neuchâtel. There are also other sites in different parts of the country. In **Alpnach** in the canton of Obwalden the focus is on microrobotics. In 2007 the long-established **Neuchâtel Observatory** joined, which used to supply the exact time for the watch industry.

According to its own figures, more than 50 young companies, so-called **spin-offs**, have come out of CSEM (as of 2026). They bring inventions from the laboratory straight to the market. In this way CSEM strengthens the Swiss economy, especially smaller companies without a large research department of their own. That is why many everyday products contain Swiss microtechnology without anyone noticing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology with tiny components, often smaller than a millimetre.
A new company founded out of a research institute.
A watch in which a vibrating quartz crystal sets the beat very precisely.
Technology with which solar cells turn sunlight directly into electricity.

gewusst: In 1967 the quartz watch “Beta 1” from Neuchâtel was among the very first quartz wristwatches of all.
The Neuchâtel Observatory used to supply the exact time that watchmakers set their watches by.
A time-of-flight camera measures how long light takes to travel to an object and back and calculates the distance from that.

teile.einleitung: A building site is the place where a house, a road, a bridge or another structure is built. Many experts and big machines work together there, and safety is the top priority.
wichtigste: An architect draws the plans for a new house.
In Switzerland wooden poles in a field show how big a planned house will be.
For a house with a cellar, a foundation pit is dug first.
The bricklayer builds the walls from bricks or blocks.
Building workers wear safety helmets, bright orange vests and safety shoes.
When the roof frame of a new house is up, people in Switzerland celebrate the “Aufrichte”, the topping-out.

abschnitte.text: Before building starts, an **architect** draws the plans for the new building. Engineers calculate how thick walls, ceilings and supports must be. Then planning permission from the municipality is needed. In Switzerland a **profile frame** (Baugespann) is put up for this: wooden poles in the field show all the neighbours how big and how tall the house will be, so that they can raise any concerns.

abschnitte.titel: From a hole to a house
abschnitte.text: If the house is to have a cellar, a **foundation pit** is dug first. Then the foundations and the base slab are poured in concrete. After that the walls and ceilings go up, floor by floor, often with the help of a crane. Finally come the roof, the windows, the pipes and cables and the interior fittings.

Many different experts work on a building site. The **bricklayer** builds walls from bricks or makes formwork for concrete. Carpenters put up the wooden roof frame, electricians lay cables and plumbers lay water pipes. The foreman directs the workers on site, and the site manager makes sure everything goes according to plan.

Building sites can be dangerous, so strict rules apply. A **safety helmet** protects against falling objects, and bright orange vests make sure that the workers can be seen clearly. **Safety shoes** have a steel cap that protects the toes. In Switzerland Suva, the accident insurance fund, makes sure the rules are followed, and children are not allowed on building sites.

When the roof frame of a new house is up, people in Switzerland celebrate the **“Aufrichte”**. Often a decorated little fir tree is put on the ridge of the roof. The owners invite the workers for food and drink and thank them for their work. This custom is known in many countries, in English as a topping-out ceremony.

begriffe.erklaerung: Wooden poles that show the size and shape of a planned building (Baugespann).
The big hole dug for the cellar and foundations.
The lowest, load-bearing part of a building in the ground.
The head worker who directs the workers on the building site.
A celebration when the roof frame of a new building is up, called “Aufrichte” in Switzerland.

gewusst: The profile frame with its poles is a typically Swiss arrangement that does not exist in many other countries.
On big building sites in Switzerland, Roman walls or old graves are sometimes discovered during excavation; then the archaeologists come first.
Concrete is often delivered to the building site in truck mixers whose drum keeps turning so that the concrete does not harden.

teile.einleitung: A lift, called an elevator in American English, carries people and loads straight up and down. Without lifts there would be no skyscrapers, and many buildings would be out of reach for people in wheelchairs.
wichtigste: A lift carries people up and down.
In Switzerland, as in Britain, people usually say lift.
In many lifts the car hangs on strong steel cables.
A counterweight balances the weight of the car.
In a fire you use the stairs instead of the lift.
If the lift gets stuck, you press the alarm button.
A sensor on the door stops anyone from getting trapped.

abschnitte.text: The **car** travels in a vertical shaft on guide rails. In a **cable lift** it hangs on several strong steel cables. These run over a drive pulley turned by an electric motor. At the other end of the cables hangs a **counterweight**, which balances the weight of the car. This means the motor has to use much less force. Smaller lifts are often pushed up **hydraulically** with an oil piston.

Modern lifts are very safe. If a cable breaks or the car goes too fast, a **safety gear** grips the rails and holds the car. A **door sensor** notices when someone is standing in the doorway and opens the door again. A sign says how many people and how many kilograms may travel. If the lift gets stuck, you press the **alarm button** and wait calmly for help. In a fire you always take the stairs, because the lift can get stuck in the smoke.

Simple goods lifts with ropes and muscle power existed in ancient times, for example in the Colosseum in Rome. The breakthrough came in 1853 with **Elisha Otis** in the USA. He invented a safety brake and demonstrated it in public by having the rope of his platform cut. Only then did people dare to use lifts. Soon afterwards the first skyscrapers appeared in American cities.

One of the biggest lift companies in the world comes from Switzerland: **Schindler**, founded in 1874 in Lucerne. A special lift is the **Hammetschwand Lift** on the Bürgenstock above Lake Lucerne. It opened in 1905 and travels more than 150 metres up the outside of a rock face. It is regarded as the highest free-standing outdoor lift in Europe.

In skyscrapers lifts shoot upwards at high speed. A **display** in the car shows the floor. New systems ask for your destination before you get in and assign passengers to the right lift. Lifts are also very important for people in wheelchairs, with pushchairs or with heavy luggage. As well as lifts there are **escalators**, which carry lots of people up at a slant.

begriffe.erklaerung: The space in which you travel in the lift.
A heavy weight at the other end of the cable that balances the car.
An emergency brake that holds the car if it travels too fast.
The vertical tunnel in the building in which the lift travels.
An old circulating lift with open cars that move round in a loop all the time.

gewusst: During his demonstration Elisha Otis had the supporting rope cut while he himself was standing on the platform.
In the past there was often a lift boy in lifts who operated them for the passengers.
A paternoster never stops; you simply step into a car as it passes.

teile.einleitung: District heating is heat produced at a central place and delivered to many buildings through a network of pipes. It is used to heat flats and warm water. In Switzerland much district heating comes from waste incineration plants, wood or waste heat.
wichtigste: District heating is produced centrally and delivered to many buildings through pipes.
It usually flows as hot water in well-insulated pipes.
In many Swiss cities, waste incineration plants supply a large share of the district heating.
In the house, a heat exchanger passes the heat on to the building's own heating.
A house with district heating needs no boiler of its own and no oil tank.
The Refuna district heating network in the lower Aare valley uses heat from the Beznau nuclear power station.
In rural heating networks, wood chips are often used for heating.

abschnitte.text: Instead of every house having its own heating, the heat is produced at a central place. From there it flows through a **district heating network** to homes, schools, hospitals and companies. The network can supply a few houses or whole parts of a city. In Switzerland smaller networks are often called **heating networks** (Wärmeverbund). The heat is used for heating and hot water.

abschnitte.titel: How the heat gets into the house
abschnitte.text: Usually hot water is pumped through thick, well-**insulated pipes** under the street. In the cellar of every connected house there is a **heat exchanger**. There the hot water gives off its heat to the house's heating water, without the two mixing. The cooled water flows back to the central plant and is heated up again. This creates a cycle like the blood in the body.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the heat come from?
abschnitte.text: In many Swiss cities such as Zurich, Bern or Basel, **waste incineration plants** supply a large share of the district heating. Burning rubbish produces a lot of heat that would otherwise be lost. Such heat, produced as a by-product of a process, is called **waste heat**. Industrial plants, data centres and sewage treatment works also give off waste heat. In the countryside, many heating networks use **wood chips** from their own forests.

In the lower Aare valley in the canton of Aargau there is the **Refuna** district heating network. It uses heat from the Beznau nuclear power station. A network of pipes connects several municipalities in the region with the power station. In this way heat is used that is produced anyway when generating electricity.

A house with district heating needs no **boiler** of its own and no oil tank. This saves space in the cellar, and there are fewer exhaust fumes in the neighbourhood. If the heat comes from rubbish, wood or waste heat, it is better for the climate than heating oil. But building a district heating network is expensive, because streets have to be dug up. That is why it is worthwhile mainly where many houses stand close together.

Many Swiss cities are currently greatly expanding their district heating networks. In this way they want to replace oil and gas heating and cut emissions of **CO₂**. Some networks also use heat from lakes, rivers or groundwater with large heat pumps. When you see big roadworks with thick pipes in the street, district heating is often being laid.

begriffe.erklaerung: Device that passes heat from one water circuit to another without them mixing.
Heat produced as a by-product of a process.
Smaller network that supplies several buildings together with heat.
Plant in which rubbish is burned and the heat is used for electricity and heating.

gewusst: In many cities, the rubbish we throw away becomes heat for thousands of flats.
The pipes of a district heating network are so well insulated that the water cools only a little on the way.
Even the waste heat from computers in data centres can heat houses.

teile.einleitung: A number trick is a calculating stunt that at first looks like magic. But behind it there are always simple rules of mathematics. With number tricks you can amaze your friends or calculate faster in your head.
wichtigste: Many number tricks work with any starting number at all.
In the mind-reading trick, after doubling, adding 10, halving and subtracting the starting number, the answer is always 5.
A three-digit number written twice in a row is always divisible by 1001.
In the 1089 trick the result is always 1089.
With a trick you can multiply numbers by 11 in a flash in your head.
The Kaprekar constant 6174 appears for almost all four-digit numbers.
If you know the algebra behind a trick, you can explain it and invent your own.

abschnitte.text: Ask someone to think of a number, double it, add 10, halve the result and subtract the number they thought of. The result is always 5. The reason: x becomes 2x + 10, halved x + 5, and after subtracting x, 5 is left. With a **variable** such as x you can see through such tricks and prove them.

When multiplying a two-digit number by 11, you write the sum of the digits in the middle. For 23 · 11 you write 2, then 2 + 3 = 5, then 3, giving 253. Numbers ending in 5 are squared like this: multiply the tens digit by the next number up and add 25 on the end. For 35 · 35 you work out 3 · 4 = 12 and add 25, which gives **1225**.

Take a three-digit number whose first and last digits differ by at least 2, for example 732. Subtract the **reversed number**: 732 − 237 = 495. Then add the reverse of the result: 495 + 594 = 1089. Whichever suitable number you start with, the answer at the end is always 1089.

In the 20th century the Indian mathematician D. R. Kaprekar discovered a special number. You arrange the digits of a four-digit number that is not made of all the same digits in descending and ascending order and subtract the smaller number from the larger. If you repeat this, you reach **6174** in at most seven steps. After that you stay there, because 7641 − 1467 gives 6174 again.

Some calculations give amazing patterns. 37 · 3 = 111, 37 · 6 = 222 and 37 · 9 = 333. Even more impressive is 12345679 · 9 = 111111111. If you write a three-digit number twice, such as 347347, it is the same as 347 · **1001**, and because 1001 = 7 · 11 · 13, the number is also divisible by 7, 11 and 13.

Number tricks are fun and show that mathematics is not only made of worksheets. If you want to explain a trick, you automatically learn **algebra**, that is calculating with letters. Mental arithmetic tricks help in everyday life, for example when shopping or estimating. Many magicians also use mathematical tricks for card tricks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A letter such as x that stands for any number.
The number you get when you read the digits backwards, for example 237 for 732.
The number 6174, at which Kaprekar’s trick always ends.
The part of mathematics in which you calculate with letters and equations.

gewusst: For three-digit numbers there is a similar Kaprekar number, namely 495.
The mind-reading trick also works with fractions and negative numbers.

teile.einleitung: When splitting a number, you divide it into two or more smaller numbers that together make the whole number again. So you can split 10 into 6 and 4, or 245 into 200 + 40 + 5. If you can split numbers confidently, mental arithmetic becomes much easier.
wichtigste: A number can be split in many different ways.
Added together, the parts always make the whole number again.
The number house is a popular aid for splitting numbers.
Even numbers can be split into two equal numbers, for example 18 into 9 and 9.
Numbers with several digits are split into hundreds, tens and units.
Splitting numbers helps with calculations that cross the ten.
Including 0 and taking order into account, 5 can be split into two numbers in 6 ways.

abschnitte.text: Splitting a number means breaking it into **parts**. You can split 7, for example, into 5 and 2, into 4 and 3 or into 6 and 1. What all the splits have in common is that the parts add up to 7 again. You can also split into three parts: 12, for example, is 4 + 4 + 4.

In the **number house** there is a number in the roof at the top, for example 9. On each floor there are two numbers that together make the roof number. If 4 is on the left, 5 belongs on the right. In this way you can write down all the ways of splitting a number neatly one below the other.

If you split 5 into two numbers and include 0, there are 0 + 5, 1 + 4, 2 + 3, 3 + 2, 4 + 1 and 5 + 0. That is 6 possibilities, if you count 1 + 4 and 4 + 1 as different. In general there are exactly n + 1 such **splits** for a number n. If you arrange them cleverly, you see a nice staircase pattern.

Larger numbers are split according to their **place values**. 73 is 70 + 3, and 245 is 200 + 40 + 5. This way of writing shows how many hundreds, tens and units there are in a number. It also helps with written calculation, where you work place by place.

Splitting is the key to calculations that **cross the ten**. For 8 + 5 you split the 5 into 2 and 3: first 8 + 2 = 10, then 10 + 3 = 13. Especially important are the ways of splitting 10, also called number bonds to ten, such as 6 and 4 or 7 and 3. If you know them by heart, you calculate much faster.

Splitting is used in higher mathematics too. In **prime factorisation** you write a number as a product of prime numbers, for example 12 = 2 · 2 · 3. A famous conjecture by Christian Goldbach from 1742, still unproven today, says that every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two prime numbers. Computers have checked this for huge numbers, but a proof is still missing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A picture with a number in the roof and the ways of splitting it on the floors below.
Two numbers that make exactly 10 together, such as 3 and 7.
The value of a digit depending on its place, that is hundreds, tens or units.
A prime number that is contained in a number as a factor, such as 2 and 3 in 12.

gewusst: The number 10 can be split into two numbers in 11 ways if 0 is included and the order matters.
Every odd number can be split into two numbers that follow each other directly, for example 9 into 4 and 5.
Goldbach’s conjecture is one of the oldest unsolved puzzles in mathematics.

teile.einleitung: A parachute is a large canopy made of fabric that brings a falling person or a load gently to the ground. It does this by using the resistance of the air. Without parachutes, parachute jumps, rescues from aircraft and many landings of space capsules would be impossible.
wichtigste: A parachute slows the fall because the air pushes against the large canopy.
The canopy is made of light but very strong fabric, usually nylon.
In 1797 André-Jacques Garnerin jumped from a balloon in Paris and landed with a parachute.
Parachutists always carry a second parachute as a reserve.
You open the canopy while you are still high enough above the ground.
Many space capsules slow down with parachutes shortly before landing.
The paraglider is a relative of the parachute with which you can take off from mountains and fly for a long time.

abschnitte.text: Anyone who jumps out of an aircraft falls faster and faster until the **air resistance** is as great as the force of gravity. Without a canopy a person reaches about 200 kilometres per hour this way. When the parachute opens, the surface suddenly becomes much larger and the air brakes strongly. After that you sink at only a few metres per second, about as fast as jumping off a wall. This speed is called the **rate of descent**.

A parachute consists of the **canopy**, many thin lines and the harness in which the jumper sits. The canopy is sewn from light, tear-resistant fabric such as nylon. Silk used to be used. Modern sports parachutes are rectangular wings made of two layers of fabric that fill with air. With two steering lines you can steer them and land gently.

As early as around 1485, the artist and inventor **Leonardo da Vinci** drew a parachute shaped like a pyramid. In 1797 the Frenchman André-Jacques Garnerin jumped from a balloon in Paris and landed safely with a parachute. Later parachutes became important for rescuing pilots from aircraft. Today parachuting is also a popular sport.

Every parachutist carries a **main parachute** and a **reserve parachute**. If the main parachute does not open properly, you can cut it away and pull the second one. Many jumpers also have a small device that opens the reserve automatically if you are too low. The canopy must be opened while you are still high enough above the ground. Beginners often jump first as a tandem with an experienced instructor.

Space capsules coming back from space slow down with huge parachutes shortly before landing. Racing aircraft and dragsters sometimes use **drag chutes** too. Aid supplies are dropped from aircraft with parachutes. In nature, dandelion seeds fly through the air on tiny umbrellas, far away from the parent plant.

The **paraglider** looks similar to a parachute but is built for flying. You take off on foot on a mountain slope and can fly for hours in rising warm air. Paragliding is very popular in Switzerland, for example above Interlaken or in Valais. Many tourists take a tandem flight with a pilot there.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air slows down a moving object.
The actual fabric parachute that fills with air.
A second parachute for emergencies.
A jump in which a guest is attached to an experienced jumper.
A steerable wing with which you take off from a mountain and fly for a long time.

gewusst: Leonardo da Vinci drew a parachute more than 300 years before anyone really jumped with one.
Without a parachute a person falls as fast as a car on the motorway, even faster.
Dandelion seeds work on the same principle as a parachute.

teile.einleitung: Fly-by-wire is a control system for aircraft in which the pilot's commands are sent electrically via computers to the control surfaces. In the past the control columns were connected directly to the control surfaces by cables and rods. Today almost all modern airliners and fighter aircraft fly with fly-by-wire.
wichtigste: With fly-by-wire, control commands are sent electrically via computers to the control surfaces.
Concorde already had an analogue fly-by-wire system.
The Airbus A320 was the first airliner with fully digital fly-by-wire controls.
The General Dynamics F-16 was the first mass-produced fighter aircraft with fly-by-wire.
In Airbus cockpits a sidestick replaces the classic control yoke.
Flight envelope protection prevents dangerous flight situations such as a stall.
Several independent computers make sure that a single failure is not dangerous.
With fly-by-light, the signals travel through fibre-optic cables.

abschnitte.text: The English expression means roughly “flying by wire”. When the pilot moves the control stick, the movement is converted into electrical **signals**. These go to **flight control computers**, which calculate how the control surfaces should move. Electric or hydraulic actuators then move the elevators, ailerons and rudder. There is usually no longer a direct mechanical connection.

In older aircraft, the control stick and control surfaces were connected by **control cables**, rods and pulleys. This technology is heavy and needs frequent maintenance. Electrical lines are lighter, and the computer can fine-tune the aircraft's movements. **Concorde**, which flew in scheduled service from 1976, already had an analogue fly-by-wire system. At the end of the 1980s the **Airbus A320** was the first airliner with fully digital controls.

In Airbus cockpits there is no longer a large control yoke in front of the pilot. Instead there is a small **sidestick** at the side, similar to a joystick in computer games. The captain steers with the left hand, the co-pilot with the right. This leaves room in front of the pilots for a fold-out table. Boeing, on the other hand, still uses a control yoke in its fly-by-wire aircraft.

The computers constantly monitor whether the aircraft is flying safely. **Flight envelope protection** prevents dangerous situations, such as climbing too steeply, turning too sharply or a **stall**. Because the controls are so important, there are several computers independent of each other. If one fails, the others take over, so a single failure does not lead to loss of control. This is called **redundancy**.

The American **General Dynamics F-16** was the first mass-produced fighter aircraft with fly-by-wire. Many modern fighter jets are deliberately built to be slightly unstable so that they are very agile. Without computers making corrections many times every second, a human could not fly them at all. The Swiss Air Force's F/A-18 also has fly-by-wire controls.

A further development is called **fly-by-light**. Here the control signals travel as light signals through fibre-optic cables instead of copper wires. Optical fibres are even lighter and are not affected by electrical interference, for example from a lightning strike. So far this technology is used in only a few aircraft.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small control stick at the side of the pilot's seat.
Dangerous situation in which the wings suddenly stop producing lift.
Systems present more than once, so that if one part fails another takes over.
Movable flaps on the aircraft with which it is steered.
Control system in which the signals travel through fibre-optic cables.

gewusst: Many modern fighter aircraft could not be kept stable in the air by any human without computer help.
Some modern cars already steer electrically; this is called steer-by-wire.
The sidestick in an Airbus is operated with only one hand.

teile.einleitung: An arch bridge is a bridge whose main part is formed by a curved arch. The arch carries the weight of the bridge and the vehicles sideways into the ground through compression, a principle the Romans had already mastered.
wichtigste: In a bridge arch it is mainly compression that acts.
Right at the top in the middle of a stone arch sits the wedge-shaped keystone.
Until the arch is closed, centring is needed.
The abutments must take not only the weight but also the sideways thrust of the arch.
The point where the arch rests on the abutment is called the springing.
The Romans built many stone arch bridges and aqueducts.
The Sydney Harbour Bridge in Australia is a steel arch bridge from 1932.
The Rialto Bridge in Venice is a well-known covered stone arch bridge.

abschnitte.text: In an arch all the stones press against each other; this is called **compression**. The weight is passed outwards and downwards along the line of the arch. Stone and concrete can withstand compression very well but hardly any tension, which is why the arch suits these materials perfectly. You can try it out: a sheet of paper bent into an arch and wedged between two books carries much more than a flat sheet.

Right at the top in the middle sits the wedge-shaped **keystone**, which holds the stone arch together. The point where the arch rests on the abutment is called the **springing**. The **abutments** on the bank or slope must not only carry the weight but also the sideways thrust of the arch. If they gave way, the arch would be pushed apart.

An arch only carries a load once it is completely closed. That is why first a wooden or steel **centring** in the shape of the arch is built. The stones are laid on it or the concrete is poured. Only when the keystone is in place or the concrete has hardened is the centring removed.

The **Romans** built many stone arch bridges and aqueducts, that is water channels over valleys, such as the famous Pont du Gard in France. Some Roman bridges are still used today. The Rialto Bridge in Venice was built of stone at the end of the 16th century and even has shops on it. With steel, much bigger arches later became possible, for example in the **Sydney Harbour Bridge** in Australia, opened in 1932.

Switzerland has many famous arch bridges. The **Landwasser Viaduct** near Filisur in the Grisons is a stone railway bridge of the Rhaetian Railway from 1902, whose train goes straight into a tunnel in the rock face. The **Salginatobel Bridge** near Schiers by Robert Maillart from 1930 is an elegant concrete bridge regarded as a masterpiece of bridge building. In the Schöllenen Gorge on the Gotthard, too, arch bridges span the river Reuss.

begriffe.erklaerung: The top, wedge-shaped stone in the middle of an arch.
A solid base at the end of a bridge on which the arch rests.
A temporary framework that supports the arch during construction.
The point where the arch rests on the abutment.
A bridge that carries a water channel across a valley.

gewusst: Some Roman stone arch bridges are almost 2000 years old and are still in use.
The Salginatobel Bridge was declared an international historic civil engineering landmark by an American engineering society.
A stone arch holds up without any mortar, just because the wedge-shaped stones press against each other.

teile.einleitung: The Carnot cycle is an imagined, ideal cycle for heat engines such as steam engines or motors. It shows the most work that can be obtained from heat and is therefore a basic building block of thermodynamics.
wichtigste: The Carnot cycle consists of two isothermal and two adiabatic changes of state.
Sadi Carnot described it in 1824 in his work “Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu”.
The efficiency is η = 1 − T_k / T_w, with temperatures in kelvin.
100 per cent efficiency would only be possible with a cold reservoir at 0 kelvin.
A higher upper temperature improves the efficiency.
No real engine reaches the Carnot efficiency, because real processes are irreversible.
In the T-s diagram the Carnot cycle is a rectangle.

abschnitte.text: A **heat engine** takes in heat from a hot place and gives off part of it to a cold place. The rest is turned into mechanical **work**, for example to turn a wheel. The Carnot cycle is an **ideal cycle** in which a gas goes through the same four steps again and again. It runs without friction and without losses, so it only exists in thought. Even so, it is very useful as a yardstick for real engines.

First the gas expands at a high, constant temperature: the **isothermal expansion**. In doing so it takes in heat from the hot reservoir. Then comes the **adiabatic expansion**, in which no heat is exchanged and the gas cools down. Then it is compressed at a low temperature and gives off heat: the isothermal compression. Finally it is compressed further without heat exchange and warms up again to the starting temperature.

The **efficiency** says what share of the heat becomes work. For the Carnot cycle, η = 1 − T_k / T_w, where T_w is the hot and T_k the cold temperature, measured in **kelvin**. With 600 kelvin at the top and 300 kelvin at the bottom this gives 50 per cent. A hundred per cent would only be possible if the cold reservoir were at **0 kelvin**, absolute zero. That is why the efficiency is increased by raising the upper temperature or lowering the lower one.

In the **p-V diagram**, with pressure and volume, the cycle forms a closed loop. The area inside this loop corresponds to the work given off in each cycle. In the **T-s diagram**, with temperature and entropy, the Carnot cycle looks like a simple rectangle. The horizontal sides are the isothermal steps, the vertical ones the adiabatic steps.

The French engineer **Sadi Carnot** lived from 1796 to 1832. In his time steam engines drove industry, but nobody knew exactly how good they could be. In 1824 he published the work “Réflexions sur la puissance motrice du feu”, roughly “Reflections on the Motive Power of Fire”. His ideas were only properly understood years after his early death. They later led to the **second law of thermodynamics**.

Real engines and power stations never reach the Carnot efficiency, because **friction**, heat conduction and other irreversible processes cost energy. But the Carnot efficiency shows the limit that no engine can exceed. If the cycle runs backwards, it becomes the model for **refrigerators** and **heat pumps**. These use work to pump heat from cold to warm, like many heating systems in Swiss homes.

begriffe.erklaerung: At a constant temperature.
Without heat exchange with the surroundings.
The share of the energy put in that comes out as useful work.
A unit of temperature that starts at 0 at absolute zero; 0 degrees Celsius is about 273 kelvin.
A sequence of steps after which the gas is back in its starting state.

gewusst: Sadi Carnot died at only 36, long before his ideas became famous.
No engine in the world can ever turn all of the heat into work.
A heat pump is basically a heat engine running backwards.

teile.einleitung: A computer is a machine that processes, stores and outputs data according to a program. Inside, every computer calculates only with the two digits 0 and 1, but incredibly quickly. Whether laptop, smartphone or games console: computers are almost everywhere today.
wichtigste: A computer processes data according to the instructions of a program.
Inside, a computer calculates only with the digits 0 and 1, the binary system.
A byte consists of 8 bits.
In 1941 Konrad Zuse built the Z3, the first working program-controlled computer.
Ada Lovelace is regarded as the first programmer in history.
In 1989 the World Wide Web was invented at CERN near Geneva.
You should never tell anyone your password.

abschnitte.text: A **computer** takes in data, processes it and outputs a result. What exactly it should do is written in a **program**, also called software. The devices themselves are called **hardware**. A computer includes, for example, a processor, working memory, storage for files and a screen.

On the **keyboard** you type letters, numbers and commands. With the **mouse** you move the pointer on the screen and click on things. On tablets and smartphones your finger on the touchscreen does this job. The Swiss company Logitech, founded in 1981 in the canton of Vaud, became world-famous for computer mice.

Inside, a computer knows only two states: current on or current off. That is why it uses the **binary system** with the digits 0 and 1. Such a digit is called a **bit**, and 8 bits make a byte. With many billions of bits a computer can store texts, pictures, music and videos.

Around 1843 **Ada Lovelace** wrote a program for Charles Babbage’s calculating machine and is therefore regarded as the first programmer. In 1941 **Konrad Zuse** built the Z3 in Berlin, the first working program-controlled computer. The first computers were as big as a room; the American ENIAC of 1946 weighed about 27 tonnes. Only transistors and microchips made computers small, so that today every smartphone contains a powerful computer.

In 1989 Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web at **CERN** near Geneva, so that researchers could exchange information more easily. The Swiss computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** of ETH Zurich invented the programming language Pascal around 1970. From 1950 the Zuse Z4 also stood at ETH, and in 1956 the first Swiss computer, the ERMETH, was completed there. Today computer science and programming are part of the school curriculum in Switzerland.

A good **password** is long, contains letters, numbers and symbols, and is never told to anyone. You should use a different password for every account. You should not open unknown attachments, because they can contain **malware**. Regular updates protect the computer from new dangers.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the parts of a computer that you can touch.
Programs that tell the computer what to do.
The smallest unit of information, either 0 or 1.
The “brain” of the computer, which carries out the calculation steps.
A language in which people write instructions for a computer.

gewusst: A smartphone today calculates many millions of times faster than the computers with which people flew to the Moon in 1969.
The word “bug” for a program error is said to go back to a moth that was found in a computer in 1947.
The world’s first website from CERN can still be viewed on the internet today.

teile.einleitung: Electrical resistance describes how strongly a material or component slows down electric current. The greater the resistance, the less current flows for the same voltage. It is measured in ohms, named after the physicist Georg Simon Ohm.
wichtigste: Electrical resistance is measured in ohms.
The unit is named after Georg Simon Ohm.
Ohm’s law is U = R · I.
A wire twice as long has twice the resistance.
A thicker wire of the same material has a lower resistance.
When a metal wire gets warmer, its resistance rises.
With 100 ohms and 0.2 amperes there is a voltage of 20 volts across the resistor.

abschnitte.text: Current consists of electrons moving through a conductor. On the way they bump into the atoms of the material and are slowed down. This braking effect is called **electrical resistance**. You can compare it with water in a hose: a narrow hose lets less water through than a wide one. The symbol for resistance is R, and the unit is the **ohm**, with the symbol Ω.

Voltage U, resistance R and current I are linked: **U = R · I**. If 0.2 amperes flow through 100 ohms, there is a voltage of 20 volts. If there are 12 volts across a resistor and 0.5 amperes flow, the resistance is 12 divided by 0.5, that is, 24 ohms. Electricians and electronics technicians calculate with this formula every day.

The resistance of a wire depends on its length, its thickness and the **material**. A wire twice as long has twice the resistance. A thicker wire has a lower resistance, because the electrons have more room. Copper and silver conduct very well, rubber and glass hardly at all; they are **insulators**.

When a metal wire gets warmer, its resistance rises, because the atoms jiggle more. Conversely, current in a resistor produces heat. Toasters, kettles and hairdryers use this, with a **heating wire** that glows inside them. Certain materials lose their resistance completely at very low temperatures; this is called **superconductivity**.

In electronics there are small components whose only job is to have a particular resistance. They limit, for example, the current through a light-emitting diode so that it does not break. Coloured rings on the component show its value; this is the **colour code**. With a rotary control, for example the volume knob, you change the resistance by hand.

**Georg Simon Ohm** was a German physicist and teacher who lived from 1789 to 1854. In the 1820s he used wires of different lengths to study how voltage and current are linked. At first his discovery was hardly noticed. Today Ohm’s law is one of the most important rules of electrical engineering.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of electrical resistance, symbol Ω.
The driving force that pushes the electrons through the conductor, measured in volts.
How much charge flows per second, measured in amperes.
A material that hardly conducts current, for example plastic.

gewusst: The filament of an old light bulb has a much greater resistance when hot than when cold.
Superconductors conduct current entirely without resistance, but for this they have to be extremely cold.
The symbol for the ohm is the Greek letter omega.

teile.einleitung: The foundation is the lowest part of a building, which sits in the ground and carries all the weight. Later you hardly see it, but without a foundation a house would sink, become crooked or even collapse. That is why it is always built first.
wichtigste: A foundation spreads the weight of the house over the ground so that it does not sink.
The foundation is built first, even before the walls.
Today foundations are mostly made of concrete, often reinforced with steel.
A skyscraper needs an especially strong foundation, because it is very heavy.
Foundations must lie deep enough so that frost does not damage them.
Many old houses in Venice stand on wooden piles.
The saying “built on sand” means that something is unsafe.

abschnitte.text: A **foundation** is the part of a structure that carries the whole load down into the **subsoil**. This includes the weight of the walls, ceilings and roof, but also furniture, people and snow on the roof. The foundation spreads this weight over a large area, rather like snowshoes that stop you sinking into the snow. Without this spreading, the house would press into the ground and crack.

Under single columns a **pad foundation** is built, under walls a long strip foundation. Many modern houses stand on a **raft**, a thick concrete slab under the whole building. If the ground is soft, long **piles** are driven or drilled deep into the earth until they reach firm ground. Such pile foundations even carry very tall towers and large bridges.

Today foundations are mostly made of **concrete**, a mixture of cement, sand, gravel and water that sets rock-hard. To stop it breaking, steel bars are placed inside; this is then called **reinforced concrete**. The ancient Romans already knew a kind of concrete and built huge structures with it. Earlier houses often had foundations of stacked natural stones.

When wet soil freezes, the water in it expands and can lift and damage a foundation. That is why a foundation must lie deeper than the frost line, in Switzerland often about 80 centimetres to more than a metre deep, and even deeper in the mountains. Before building, experts examine the ground carefully; this is called a **geological survey**. In areas with earthquakes, such as Valais or near Basel, buildings are also made earthquake-resistant.

Many houses in **Venice** stand on millions of wooden piles stuck in the muddy ground of the lagoon. Under water and without air the wood hardly rots, so it has lasted for centuries. The **Leaning Tower of Pisa**, on the other hand, started to tilt while it was still being built, because its foundation on soft ground was not deep enough. That is why the saying “built on sand” means that something is unsafe and could easily collapse.

begriffe.erklaerung: Lowest part of a structure, which carries the weight down into the ground.
The ground on which a building stands.
Concrete with steel bars set inside it, which is especially stable.
Foundation made of long piles that reach down to firm ground.
Depth down to which the ground can freeze in winter.

gewusst: The foundations of very tall skyscrapers often reach several dozen metres deep into the ground.
Wood lasts so long under water because fungi and bacteria can hardly work without oxygen.
The word “foundation” comes from the Latin “fundus”, which means “bottom” or “ground”.

teile.einleitung: A drone is an aircraft without a pilot on board that is remote-controlled or flies by itself. The best known are small quadcopters with four propellers that take photos and videos from the air. But drones are also used for transport, surveying and rescue missions.
wichtigste: A drone is an unmanned aircraft.
A quadcopter has 4 propellers.
Inertial sensors and satellite navigation keep a drone stable in the air and in position.
In the open category, drones in Switzerland may normally fly no higher than 120 m above the ground.
In Switzerland drone pilots register with the Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA).
To fly a drone that must be registered on your own, you must be at least 12 years old.
BVLOS means a flight beyond the pilot’s line of sight.
From 2017 Swiss Post used drones in Lugano to carry laboratory samples between hospitals.

abschnitte.text: The word drone stands for an **unmanned aircraft**, that is, an aircraft with no people on board. There are drones with wings that fly like small planes, and ones with several rotors, so-called **multicopters**. The most common design is the quadcopter with four propellers. It is controlled with a remote control, a mobile phone or a pre-programmed flight plan.

On a quadcopter two propellers turn clockwise and two anticlockwise. In this way their turning forces cancel each other out, and the drone does not spin round unintentionally. To turn about its **vertical axis**, it changes the speed of the two pairs of propellers differently. For movements forwards, backwards or sideways, individual propellers turn faster, and the drone tilts slightly in the desired direction.

Small measuring devices, the **inertial sensors**, detect every tilt and acceleration many times a second. A computer can then make up for gusts of wind at once. With **satellite navigation** such as GPS the drone knows its position and can hover at one spot in the air. Many drones fly back to their starting point automatically if there are problems.

Drones film sports events, survey land and inspect power lines or bridges. Farmers use them to watch their fields, and rescue teams search for missing people with thermal imaging cameras. From 2017 **Swiss Post** used drones in Lugano to carry laboratory samples between hospitals. Armed forces also use drones, for example for reconnaissance.

In Switzerland the **Federal Office of Civil Aviation (FOCA)**, in German BAZL, is responsible for drones. Anyone who flies a drone that must be registered has to register there and be at least 12 years old. In the open category you may normally fly no higher than 120 metres above the ground and must keep the drone in sight. Flights beyond the line of sight are called **BVLOS** and need special permission. Near airports and over crowds of people strict restrictions apply.

begriffe.erklaerung: A drone with four propellers.
Federal Office of Civil Aviation (in German BAZL), the Swiss authority for everything that flies.
A measuring device that detects tilt and acceleration.
Beyond visual line of sight: a flight in which the drone is out of the pilot’s sight.

gewusst: The name drone comes from the male honeybee, which also buzzes loudly.
A quadcopter can only turn because its propellers run at different speeds.
Drones with thermal imaging cameras can find missing people even at night.

teile.einleitung: Automation means that machines carry out tasks on their own that people used to do by hand. From the washing machine to the industrial robot to the self-driving car, programs and sensors control many processes today. Automation has greatly changed the world of work and continues to do so.
wichtigste: In automation, machines take over tasks without people constantly having to step in.
Open-loop control carries out a sequence; closed-loop control also measures and corrects continuously.
James Watt regulated the speed of his steam engine with a centrifugal governor.
From 1804 the Jacquard loom controlled weaving patterns with punched cards.
In 1913 Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line in car manufacturing.
In factories, programmable logic controllers (PLCs) control many machines.
Industry 4.0 stands for networked production with cyber-physical systems.

abschnitte.text: Automation means that a technical system carries out a task **by itself**. For this it needs sensors that measure, a controller that decides and **actuators** such as motors or valves that act. A simple example is a street lamp that switches itself on when it gets dark. Big examples are factories in which robots weld cars together. The word comes from the Greek “automatos”, meaning “moving by itself”.

With **open-loop control** a process runs according to plan without checking the result. A toaster with a timer is an example. With **closed-loop control** the result is measured and corrected continuously. A heating thermostat measures the room temperature and heats more if it gets too cool. A well-known type of controller is the **PID controller**, whose letters stand for proportional, integral and derivative.

As early as 1788 **James Watt** used a centrifugal governor that kept the speed of his steam engine constant. From 1804 Joseph-Marie Jacquard built a loom that controlled patterns with **punched cards**. This idea later influenced the first calculating machines. In 1913 **Henry Ford** introduced the moving assembly line in his car factory. As a result, making a Ford Model T became much faster and cheaper.

In modern factories a **programmable logic controller**, PLC for short, takes control of machines. Its sequence is set by a program and can easily be changed. Industrial robots weld, paint, pack and sort round the clock. The Swiss company ABB is one of the big manufacturers of industrial robots. **Industry 4.0** means factories in which machines, products and computers are networked and exchange data.

At home, too, many things are automated, such as the washing machine, the dishwasher and the robotic lawnmower. Stations and airports use automatic baggage systems and ticket machines. For **automated driving**, the SAE association distinguishes six levels from 0 to 5. Level 5 means full automation, in which no person has to drive any more. In Switzerland some metros and airport trains, for example in Lausanne and at Zurich Airport, already run without a driver.

Automation makes work safer, more accurate and often cheaper. Machines can take over dangerous or monotonous tasks. At the same time some jobs disappear while new professions arise. In Switzerland, for example, young people can train as **automation technicians** (Automatiker). It remains important that people monitor the systems and can recognise faults.

begriffe.erklaerung: A detector that measures something, for example temperature or light.
A component that moves or switches something, such as a motor.
A process that measures the result and corrects it continuously.
Programmable logic controller, a programmable control computer for machines.

gewusst: The punched cards of the Jacquard loom are regarded as forerunners of computer programs.
In ancient Greece Heron of Alexandria already built automatic temple doors.
The M2 metro in Lausanne has been running without a driver since 2008.

teile.einleitung: The angle bisector is a line that divides an angle into two exactly equal parts. Every point on it is the same distance from both arms. It can be constructed very precisely with compasses and a ruler.
wichtigste: The angle bisector divides an angle into two equal parts.
An angle of 74° becomes two angles of 37° each.
All the points on it are the same distance from both arms.
It is the line of symmetry of the two arms.
The construction starts with an arc around the vertex.
A triangle has three bisectors of its interior angles; they meet at the centre of the incircle.
The bisectors of two adjacent angles on a line are perpendicular to each other.

abschnitte.text: The **angle bisector** passes through the vertex of an angle and divides it exactly in the middle. If an angle measures 74°, two angles of 37° each are formed. With a right angle, two angles of 45° are formed. You can imagine folding the angle exactly down the middle.

The angle bisector is the **line of symmetry** of the two arms. If you reflect one arm in it, it lands exactly on the other. That is why every point on the angle bisector is the same **distance** from both arms. This property is used in many constructions.

First you draw an **arc** with the compasses around the vertex, cutting both arms. Around these two points of intersection you now draw two arcs of the same size, which cross inside the angle. The line from the vertex through this crossing point is the angle bisector. This makes it more accurate than with a set square alone.

A triangle has three interior angles and therefore three angle bisectors. They all meet at one point, the centre of the **incircle**. The incircle is the largest circle that fits inside the triangle and touches all three sides. In an equilateral triangle this point coincides with the centre of the circumcircle.

In a square the bisector of a corner angle is a diagonal. Two adjacent angles on a line add up to 180°, so their bisectors form a right angle of 90°. The line y = x in the coordinate system is also an angle bisector, namely that of the two axes. In practice, carpenters, for example, use the angle bisector when they join two strips of wood exactly in a corner.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line that divides an angle into two equal halves.
The point where the two arms of an angle meet.
A circle inside a triangle that touches all three sides.
A line in which a shape can be reflected onto itself.

gewusst: The corners of a picture frame are often cut at an angle of 45°, that is exactly along the angle bisector.
Bisecting an angle with compasses and a ruler is easy, but dividing it exactly into three is in general impossible with them.
You can also find the angle bisector by folding a piece of paper.

teile.einleitung: The landline is the telephone network in which a telephone is permanently connected to a line in the house. Long before there were mobile phones, everyone made calls over the landline. Many households and companies still have a landline connection today.
wichtigste: A landline telephone is connected to a fixed line in the house.
On old telephones you dialled the number with a rotary dial.
When making a call you hold the handset to your ear.
If you pick up the handset and the line is free, you hear a humming tone.
The area code shows the region; 031, for example, stands for Bern.
In the past all telephone numbers were listed in the thick telephone directory.
When out and about, people made calls from a telephone box.
In Switzerland you reach the fire brigade on 118.

abschnitte.text: With a landline, the telephone is connected to the telephone network by a line. The line runs from the house via cables to the **telephone exchange**. By contrast, a mobile phone works by radio in the **mobile network**. Because the telephone is attached to the line, you can only use it at home or in the office. Many landline telephones today, however, are cordless and have a base station.

A classic telephone consists of the unit and the **handset**, which you hold to your ear. Inside the handset are a small loudspeaker and a microphone. On old telephones you dialled the number with a **rotary dial**, which you had to turn for each digit. Later buttons were added. If you pick up the handset and the line is free, you hear a humming tone, the dialling tone.

Swiss landline numbers begin with an **area code** that shows the region. 031 stands for the Bern region, 044 for Zurich and 022 for Geneva. After that come seven more digits. In the past all numbers were listed with name and address in the thick **telephone directory**. Important emergency numbers are 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 144 for the ambulance.

Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone in 1876. Soon telephone lines were built in many cities. At first, female operators connected the calls by hand with plugs. Later automatic exchanges took over this work. When out and about, people made calls from a **telephone box** with coins or a Taxcard.

Today landline calls in Switzerland mostly run digitally over the internet; this is called **IP telephony**. For this the telephone is connected to the router. Most public telephone boxes have disappeared because almost everyone has a mobile phone. Nevertheless many companies, hospitals and older people still use the landline. It is considered reliable and often has good sound quality.

begriffe.erklaerung: Part of the telephone you hold to your ear, with a loudspeaker and a microphone.
Turning disc on old telephones with which you dialled the number.
The first digits of a telephone number, which show the region.
Humming tone that shows the line is free.
Small booth with a public telephone.

gewusst: In the past, operators connected every call by hand with a plug.
With a rotary dial, dialling a 0 took longest, because you had to turn it furthest.
An old telephone directory for a big city listed hundreds of thousands of names.

teile.einleitung: Cube buildings are structures made of cubes of the same size, stacked next to and on top of each other. At school they are used to learn how to work out amounts and to picture three-dimensional solids. You look at them from the front, from the side and from above and draw building plans for them.
wichtigste: A cube building consists of many cubes of the same size.
You can find the number of cubes by counting, adding or multiplying.
A large cube made of 2 by 2 by 2 small cubes needs 8 cubes.
A building plan shows the view from above with a number on each square.
The number on a square says how many cubes are stacked there.
From above you cannot see well how tall a building is.
Cube buildings train spatial awareness.

abschnitte.text: A cube building is a solid made entirely of **cubes** of the same size. The cubes lie face to face, so not at a slant or out of line. You can build towers, walls, stairs or whole houses. At school, wooden cubes, linking cubes or building blocks are used for this.

With simple buildings you just count: a tower of 4 cubes with 2 more on top has 6 cubes. With regular shapes **multiplication** helps: a wall of 2 rows of 3 cubes each has 2 · 3 = 6 cubes, and 3 towers of 4 cubes each need 12 cubes. A staircase 1, 2 and 3 cubes high has 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 cubes. A large cube made of 2 · 2 · 2 small cubes needs 8, and one made of 3 · 3 · 3 already 27.

A cube building looks different from every side. A distinction is made between the **front view**, the side view and the plan view from above. From above you can see which squares are occupied, but not how tall the building is. That is why you often need several views to understand a building exactly. Cubes hidden right at the back or inside cannot be seen from any direction.

A **building plan** shows the building from above as a grid of squares. On each square you write a number that says how many cubes are stacked there. If you add up all the numbers, you know the total number of cubes. With such a plan someone else can rebuild the building exactly.

Many puzzle games are based on cube buildings. The **Soma cube** consists of seven pieces that can be put together to form a large cube of 27 small cubes. Construction sets with interlocking bricks and computer games with block worlds work in a similar way. Such games develop imagination and logical thinking.

If you understand cube buildings, you can picture solids in space better. This is needed later by, for example, architects, engineers, draughtspeople and tradespeople who build from plans. Spatial thinking also helps when packing a car boot or filling a shelf. In the Swiss primary school curriculum, cube buildings belong to the area of shape and space.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid with six square faces of equal size.
The view of a solid directly from above.
A drawing from above that shows how many cubes are stacked on each square.
The ability to picture solids and their position in space in your head.

gewusst: For a large cube with 10 small cubes along each edge you already need 1000 small cubes.
The Soma cube was thought up in 1933 by the Danish inventor Piet Hein.
From only two views you can sometimes build several different buildings that look exactly the same.

teile.einleitung: A shape-memory alloy is a metal that can remember its original shape. If you bend it and then heat it, it returns to its old shape as if by magic. Such metals are used in medicine, construction and engineering.
wichtigste: Shape-memory alloys return to an imprinted shape when heated.
The best-known shape-memory alloy is called nitinol and is made of nickel and titanium.
The effect is based on a change between martensite and austenite in the crystal lattice.
With pseudoelasticity, nitinol can be stretched by several per cent and springs back immediately.
With the two-way effect, a component switches between two shapes when heated and cooled.
Nitinol stents for blood vessels unfold by themselves inside the body.
Empa has developed a shape-memory steel that can be used to prestress concrete.
Copper zinc aluminium alloys also show a shape-memory effect.

abschnitte.text: An **alloy** is a mixture of several metals. Shape-memory alloys have an amazing property: they remember a shape that is imprinted on them when they are made. If you bend such a wire at room temperature and then heat it, it returns to its imprinted shape. That is why they are also called **memory metals**. The best known is **nitinol**, made of nickel and titanium.

The atoms in a metal are arranged in a regular **crystal lattice**. In shape-memory alloys, this lattice can have two different arrangements. At lower temperature the bendable form, **martensite**, is present; at higher temperature the rigid form, **austenite**. When heated, the lattice flips into austenite, and the component takes on its original shape again. The temperature at which this happens is called the transformation temperature.

With the **one-way effect**, a bent part returns to its shape once when heated and stays that way.
