Around 1860 bicycles in France got pedals on the front wheel. After that came penny-farthings with a huge front wheel. Around 1885 the safety bicycle with a chain drive appeared, which already looked almost like today's bicycles.

A **bike helmet** protects your head in a fall. A red light must shine at the back and a white one at the front so that you can be seen well at dusk. Anyone who cycles must know the rules of the road, such as hand signals when turning. In Switzerland many children take a **cycling test** at school. On cycle paths and cycle lanes you are safer, separated from the cars.

There are **mountain bikes** for forest tracks, racing bikes for fast rides on the road and city bikes for town. An **e-bike** has an electric motor that helps when you pedal. With cargo bikes you can carry shopping or even children. Tandems have room for two people, one behind the other. Children often first learn to ride on a balance bike without pedals, just like Drais's invention.

Switzerland has a dense network of signposted cycle routes, which you can recognise by red signposts. The **SwitzerlandMobility** project shows many of these routes on a map. Especially in cities such as Basel, Bern or Winterthur, many people cycle to work or school every day. Cycling makes no noise, causes no exhaust fumes and keeps you fit.

begriffe.erklaerung: Karl Drais's running machine without pedals, the forerunner of the bicycle.
Part with which you can make pedalling easier or harder.
Old bicycle with a very large front wheel.
Bicycle with an electric motor that helps when you pedal.

gewusst: Karl Drais's running machine is said to have been invented when horses were scarce because of a famine.
Cycling is one of the most energy-efficient ways of moving under your own power.
Worldwide there are estimated to be more than a billion bicycles.

teile.einleitung: ANYmal is a four-legged walking robot from Switzerland that is a little reminiscent of a dog. It was developed at ETH Zurich and can walk on its own over stairs, scree and uneven ground.
wichtigste: ANYmal walks on four legs, which makes it a walking robot.
It was developed at the Robotic Systems Lab of ETH Zurich.
The ETH spin-off ANYbotics, founded in 2016, produces ANYmal commercially.
In industry ANYmal mainly carries out automatic inspection rounds.
Through reinforcement learning in computer simulations it learned to walk robustly.
In 2021 the CERBERUS team won the DARPA Subterranean Challenge with ANYmal robots.
The ANYmal X version is explosion-proof.

abschnitte.text: ANYmal has four legs that are moved by powerful electric motors in the joints. This means it can climb steps, step over obstacles and keep its **balance** on sloping ground. Wheels would often get stuck in such places. The robot is about the size of a medium-sized dog and carries its sensors and batteries in its body.

ANYmal was created at the **Robotic Systems Lab** of ETH Zurich, which works on robots for difficult terrain. Students and researchers worked for years on the legs, control and software. In 2016 members of the team founded the company **ANYbotics** in Zurich. Today this company builds the robot and sells it to companies in many countries.

So that ANYmal walks safely, the researchers trained it with **reinforcement learning**. Here a computer program tries out countless movements in a simulation and is rewarded for good steps. In the virtual world you can practise as much in hours as in years in the real world. What has been learned is then transferred to the real robot. In this way, in an experiment in 2022, ANYmal climbed the Etzel in the canton of Schwyz faster than the walking time given for people.

ANYmal mainly carries out **inspection rounds** in industrial plants, for example in power stations, refineries or on oil and gas platforms. With cameras, a thermal camera and microphones it checks gauges, looks for hot spots and listens for unusual noises from machines. This means people have to go to dangerous or remote places less often. The **ANYmal X** version is explosion-proof and may therefore also work where flammable gases can occur.

The American research agency DARPA held the **Subterranean Challenge**, a competition in caves, tunnels and underground facilities. The robots had to find objects on their own there and draw a map. In 2021 the international team **CERBERUS**, in which ETH Zurich took part, won with several ANYmal robots. This victory made the Swiss robot famous worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: A robot that moves on legs instead of wheels.
A kind of machine learning in which a program gets better through trial and reward.
A new company founded out of a university or another company.
A careful check of whether everything is in order.
A way of building in which a device produces no sparks that could ignite flammable gases.

gewusst: ANYmal learned to walk in simulation before taking its first steps on real ground.
If ANYmal falls over, it can usually get itself back up with its legs.
The name ANYmal plays on the English word “animal” and on “any”.

teile.einleitung: Additive manufacturing is the technical term for what many people call 3D printing. An object is built up layer by layer from material, instead of being milled out of a block. In this way toys, spare parts, prostheses and even rocket parts are made directly from a computer file.
wichtigste: In additive manufacturing a part is built up layer by layer.
Additive means adding, because material only goes where it is needed.
Chuck Hull invented stereolithography in the 1980s.
In the most common home method, a plastic wire is melted in a hot nozzle.
The building instructions come from a computer file, often in STL format.
Overhangs often need support structures, which are removed afterwards.
Metal parts can also be printed from powder with lasers.

abschnitte.text: In traditional methods such as milling or drilling, material is taken away until the shape is finished. In **additive manufacturing** it is the other way round: material is added, layer by layer. Each layer is often only a fraction of a millimetre thick. In the end hundreds or thousands of layers make a solid object.

First the part is designed on the computer with a CAD program. The shape is then usually saved as an **STL file**, which describes the surface as a mesh of many small triangles. Software called a slicer cuts the model into thin slices. The printer then builds these slices one after another.

In **fused filament fabrication**, FDM or FFF for short, a plastic wire is melted in a hot nozzle and laid down as if with a hot-glue gun. In stereolithography a beam of light hardens liquid resin layer by layer. In selective laser sintering a laser solidifies plastic powder; the loose powder supports the part, so no support structures are needed. In selective laser melting a laser melts metal powder completely.

Parts that would float in the air, such as the arms of a figure, often need **support structures** during printing. They are broken off or washed out after printing. A big advantage is that shapes can be made that are hardly possible with other methods, such as hollow spaces inside or lattices. With **topology optimisation**, the computer calculates organically shaped parts that are light and yet strong.

In 1984 the American **Chuck Hull** applied for a patent for stereolithography and founded the company 3D Systems. At the end of the 1980s Scott Crump developed fused filament fabrication. From 2005 the RepRap project made cheap home printers well known, some of which can even print parts for themselves. Today 3D printers are found in schools, libraries and workshops.

In medicine, custom-made prostheses, hearing-aid shells and dental splints are printed. The aerospace industry uses printed metal parts because they are light. In architecture, concrete parts and even whole small houses are printed; such methods are being researched at ETH Zurich too. For hobbyists the 3D printer is handy for making spare parts or figures themselves.

begriffe.erklaerung: Adding; material is added bit by bit.
Computer-aided design, that is drawing parts on the computer.
The plastic wire on a spool that is melted in the 3D printer.
A program that breaks a 3D model down into thin layers.
A temporary framework that holds up overhanging parts during printing.

gewusst: Some 3D printers print with chocolate or dough instead of plastic.
A 3D printer has already been used on the International Space Station so that astronauts can make tools themselves.
The name stereolithography means roughly three-dimensional stone printing.

teile.einleitung: In 3D printing a machine makes a real object by laying material down layer by layer. A model on the computer serves as the template. In this way toys, spare parts, prostheses and even houses are made.
wichtigste: A 3D printer builds objects layer by layer.
Because material is added, this is called additive manufacturing.
Home printers usually melt plastic wire that is wound on a reel.
The popular plastic PLA is usually made from maize starch or sugar cane.
Chuck Hull invented stereolithography in the 1980s.
The STL file format is very often used for 3D models.
With layers of 0.2 mm, an object 3 cm high needs 150 layers.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary printer puts ink on a flat sheet. A **3D printer**, on the other hand, builds a solid with length, width and height. It lays thin layers on top of each other until the object is finished. Because material is added and not cut away, this is called **additive manufacturing**. In milling or turning, by contrast, material is removed.

First you draw a **3D model** on the computer or download one. It is often saved in the **STL** file format. A program called a slicer cuts the model into many thin slices. Then the printer works through each layer one by one. At 0.2 mm per layer, an object 3 cm high needs 150 layers and often several hours.

Most home printers work with **fused filament fabrication**. Here a plastic wire, the **filament**, is fed from a reel into a hot nozzle, where it is melted. PLA, which is usually made from maize starch or sugar cane, is popular. In stereolithography a beam of light hardens liquid resin layer by layer. Other methods fuse metal powder together with a laser.

The American **Chuck Hull** invented stereolithography and applied for a patent in 1984. Shortly afterwards he founded the company 3D Systems. At about the same time other methods using powder and melted plastic were developed. For a long time the machines were expensive and found only in industry. Only from about 2010 did cheap printers for the home become widespread.

Engineers print **prototypes**, that is first test models of new products. In medicine, custom-made prostheses, dental splints and hearing-aid shells are made. In aviation, light metal parts for aircraft engines are printed. Shoes, jewellery and spare parts for old devices can also be printed. At ETH Zurich researchers are even working on building with printed concrete.

3D printing is worthwhile above all for one-off items and complicated shapes. You can use exactly as much material as is needed. For large numbers, however, injection moulding is usually faster and cheaper. Printing produces fine particles, so the room should be well ventilated. Schools in Switzerland are using 3D printers more and more in the subject **Design and Technology**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Production in which material is added layer by layer.
Plastic wire on a reel that is melted in the printer.
A program that breaks a 3D model down into thin layers.
A first test model of a new product.
A method in which light hardens liquid resin layer by layer.

gewusst: Printing has already been done with a 3D printer on the International Space Station ISS.
In several countries whole houses have already been built from printed concrete.
PLA may be made from plants, but it hardly breaks down in a garden compost heap.

teile.einleitung: George de Mestral was a Swiss engineer who invented Velcro. He got the idea when he had to pick burrs out of his dog's fur after an outing. Today his invention is found in shoes, jackets and bags, and it has even been used in space travel.
wichtigste: George de Mestral came from Switzerland and was born in the canton of Vaud.
He studied in Lausanne and worked as an engineer.
After an outing, burrs were stuck in his dog's fur.
He examined the burrs closely with a microscope.
He had the idea for Velcro in 1941.
It took about ten years from the idea to the patent application.
He gave his invention the name Velcro.

abschnitte.text: George de Mestral was born in 1907 in the **canton of Vaud**. Even as a teenager he liked tinkering, and he applied for a patent for a toy aeroplane. He studied at the technical university in **Lausanne** and became an **engineer**. As well as technology, he was also interested in nature and hunting. He died in 1990 in French-speaking Switzerland.

In 1941 de Mestral came back from an outing with his dog. Many **burrs**, the seed heads of a plant, were stuck in the dog's fur and on his clothes. Instead of just being annoyed, he wanted to know why they stuck so well. Under the **microscope** he saw that the burrs have tiny hooks. These hooks get caught in hairs and loops of fabric.

De Mestral wanted to recreate this idea: one strip with lots of tiny hooks and a second with lots of tiny **loops**. If you press the two together, they hold firmly, and you can pull them apart again. When an invention copies nature, this is called **bionics**. Velcro is considered one of the best-known examples of it.

Putting it into practice was harder than expected. For many years de Mestral searched for the right material and a machine that could make the tiny hooks. Finally he found that **nylon** worked well. It took about ten years from the idea to the patent application. He called his invention **Velcro**, from the French words “velours” for velvet and “crochet” for hook.

Today Velcro fastenings are found on children's shoes, jackets, blood pressure cuffs and rucksacks. They have also been used in space travel to hold objects in place in weightlessness. The name Velcro is still a well-known brand today. George de Mestral is one of the most famous examples of Swiss inventiveness.

begriffe.erklaerung: Plant whose seed heads stick to fur and clothes with tiny hooks.
Fastening made of a strip of hooks and a strip of loops.
Official protection that secures an invention for its inventor for a certain time.
Technology that imitates ideas from nature.
Brand name for the hook-and-loop fastening, from “velours” and “crochet”.

gewusst: Velcro came about because someone wondered about burrs in a dog's fur instead of just being annoyed.
The name Velcro is made up of the French words for velvet and hook.
On space stations, Velcro strips help to hold objects in place in weightlessness.

teile.einleitung: BBC Brown Boveri was a large Swiss industrial company from Baden in the canton of Aargau that built generators, turbines, motors and many other electrical machines. In 1988, together with the Swedish company ASEA, BBC gave rise to today’s global group ABB.
wichtigste: Brown, Boveri & Cie. was founded in 1891 in Baden.
Charles Brown was the engineer, Walter Boveri the businessman.
From 1901 BBC mainly built steam turbines together with turbogenerators.
Around 1910 BBC was the largest company in Swiss mechanical engineering.
From the 1920s BBC produced the exhaust turbocharger, based on an invention by Alfred Büchi.
In 1900 BBC founded a subsidiary in Mannheim, which from about 1930 was bigger than the parent company.
In 1967 BBC merged with Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon (MFO).
In 1988 BBC merged with the Swedish company ASEA to form ABB.

abschnitte.text: Charles Eugen Lancelot Brown and Walter Boveri founded the company Brown, Boveri & Cie. in **Baden** in 1891. Brown was a gifted engineer and inventor, Boveri a skilful **businessman** who organised the money and the business side. Both had previously worked at Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon. Baden was well placed on the river Limmat and on the railway.

At first BBC built generators, motors and transformers and supplied whole power stations. From 1901 **steam turbines** together with turbogenerators became its main business. With them BBC supplied equipment for power stations in many countries. The electrification of the Swiss railways also brought the company many orders.

By around 1910 BBC was already the largest company in Swiss mechanical engineering. As early as 1900 the company founded a subsidiary in **Mannheim** in Germany, which from about 1930 was even bigger than the parent company in Baden. Later, companies in France, Italy and other countries were added. The town of Baden grew with the company from a spa town into an industrial town.

The Swiss engineer **Alfred Büchi** invented exhaust turbocharging. Here the exhaust gas of an engine drives a small turbine, which forces fresh air into the engine and so makes it more powerful. BBC produced such **turbochargers** from the 1920s, at first for large ship and locomotive engines. Turbochargers from Baden are still among the best-known products of the BBC tradition today.

In 1967 BBC merged with **Maschinenfabrik Oerlikon** (MFO) from Zurich. In 1988 BBC joined with the Swedish company ASEA, and **ABB** was formed, which stands for Asea Brown Boveri. ABB has its headquarters in Zurich and is one of the largest technology groups in Europe. In Baden, buildings, villas and the Langmatt Museum recall the BBC era.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two companies joining together to form a new one.
A machine in which hot steam drives a bladed wheel.
A machine that turns movement into electric current.
A component that uses the exhaust gases to force more air into an engine.
A company that belongs to another company.

gewusst: Charles Brown was only 28 years old when he co-founded the company.
The Langmatt Museum in Baden shows the art collection of the family of Sidney Brown, a brother of Charles Brown.
The letters ABB stand for Asea Brown Boveri and so still recall the two founders today.

teile.einleitung: A period of time is the length of time between two points in time, for example from the start of a film to the end. In everyday life we constantly calculate periods of time: how long does the bus journey take, when will the cake be ready, how many days do the holidays last? If you are good at calculating them, you will not miss a train.
wichtigste: A point in time says when something happens; a period of time says how long it lasts.
An hour has 60 minutes, and a minute has 60 seconds.
So an hour has 3600 seconds.
A day has 24 hours, and a week has 7 days.
Periods of time are easiest to calculate in steps up to the next full hour.
With periods of time over midnight, the time starts again at 0.00.
A year has 365 days, a leap year 366 days.

abschnitte.titel: Point in time and period of time
abschnitte.text: A **point in time** is a particular moment, for example 14:00. A **period of time** is the length of time between two points in time. If a film starts at 14:00 and ends at 15:30, it lasts 1 hour 30 minutes. Points in time are read off a clock; periods of time often have to be worked out. On Swiss timetables times are written with a point, for example 8.47.

With time you do not calculate in the decimal system, because an hour has 60 minutes. That is why it is best to calculate in steps up to the next full hour. A train leaves at 8.47 and arrives at 10.12: up to 9.00 it is 13 minutes, up to 10.00 one hour, then another 12 minutes. Together that makes 1 hour 25 minutes. This method is called **counting on** in steps.

The bus leaves at 7:40 and arrives at 8:05, so the journey takes 25 minutes. A cake that goes into the oven at 15:30 for 40 minutes is ready at 16:10. If a bus leaves every 15 minutes from 6.05, the fifth bus leaves at 7.05. A night train that leaves at 23.40 and travels for 50 minutes arrives at 0.30. With problems like this a **timeline** on which you draw the steps helps.

Longer periods of time are measured in days, weeks, months and years. If today is Monday, in 3 days it will be Thursday. If today is 3 May, in a week it will be 10 May. Five weeks of summer holidays are 5 times 7, that is 35 days. Because the Earth needs a little more than 365 days to go once round the Sun, almost every four years there is a **leap year** with a 29 February.

In Switzerland punctuality is especially important, above all on the railways. The well-known SBB **station clock** was designed in 1944 by Hans Hilfiker. Its red second hand with the round end is reminiscent of a signalling disc. It goes round in about 58 seconds and then waits briefly until all the clocks jump to the next minute together. Watches and stopwatches from Switzerland are also famous worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of time between two points in time.
A particular moment that you can read off a clock.
A line on which you mark times in order.
A year with 366 days, because there is a 29 February.
A small unit of time; 60 seconds make a minute.

gewusst: A day has 86,400 seconds.
Dividing the hour into 60 minutes goes back to the Babylonians, who calculated with the number 60.
Because the Earth does not turn completely evenly, an extra leap second has been added to some years.

teile.einleitung: A postage stamp is a small adhesive token with which you pay the postage for a letter or a card. Stamps have existed for almost 200 years, and many people collect them because of their beautiful pictures and exciting history.
wichtigste: The first postage stamp in the world appeared in Great Britain in 1840.
In 1843 the canton of Zurich was one of the first to issue stamps.
The famous Basel Dove appeared in 1845.
The value on a Swiss stamp shows how much it costs.
The stamp goes at the top right of the envelope.
The post office postmarks the stamp so that it cannot be used again.
Someone who collects stamps is called a philatelist.
Today, instead of a stamp, you can also write a code from your phone on the letter.

abschnitte.text: A stamp shows that the **postage**, that is the price for transport, has been paid in advance. The printed value shows how much it costs. You stick it at the top right of the envelope so that the post office’s sorting machines can find it easily. The post office then postmarks the stamp so that it cannot be used a second time.

In the past it was usually the recipient who had to pay, and the price depended on the distance. The Englishman Rowland Hill suggested that the sender should pay a uniform amount with a stamp stuck on the letter. In 1840 the world’s first postage stamp, the **Penny Black**, appeared in Great Britain. It showed the portrait of the young Queen Victoria on a black background.

Switzerland was one of the first countries with stamps. In 1843 the canton of **Zurich** issued the stamps “Zürich 4” and “Zürich 6”, and Geneva followed in the same year. In 1845 the famous **Basel Dove** appeared in Basel, one of the first multicoloured stamps in the world, with a white dove in embossed printing. From 1850 there were federal stamps for the whole of Switzerland.

Someone who collects stamps is called a **philatelist**, and collecting stamps is called philately. Collectors keep their stamps in albums and handle them with tweezers so that they are not damaged. Rare old stamps or stamps with printing errors are especially valuable. Well-preserved old Swiss cantonal stamps such as the Basel Dove fetch high prices at auctions.

Swiss Post issues new **special stamps** every year on themes such as nature, anniversaries or art. For some years now you have also been able to pay the postage with your mobile phone. You then get a code that you write on the letter by hand instead of sticking on a stamp. Even so, printed stamps remain popular with many people.

begriffe.erklaerung: The charge for sending a letter or parcel.
Someone who collects and studies stamps.
The post office’s print that cancels the stamp.
The small teeth along the edge where stamps are torn apart.
A stamp on a particular theme or for a special occasion.

gewusst: The first stamps had no perforation and had to be cut out with scissors.
Swiss stamps bear the word “Helvetia” because the country has four national languages.
The Basel Dove was the first stamp in the world to be printed in several colours.

teile.einleitung: An excavator, often called a digger, is a powerful construction machine that digs out and moves earth, stones and rubble. Without excavators it would be almost impossible to build foundation pits, roads and tunnels.
wichtigste: Excavators dig big holes on building sites.
At the front of the arm is the bucket, with which the excavator digs.
Pistons filled with oil move the strong arm; this is called hydraulics.
Many large excavators run on tracks so that they do not sink into the ground.
The upper part of many excavators can turn right round.
A mini excavator even fits into small gardens.
A walking excavator can climb steep slopes with its legs.
The bucket-wheel excavator digs with a giant wheel full of buckets.

abschnitte.text: A typical excavator has an **undercarriage** with tracks or wheels and on top of it an upper structure with the cab and engine. The upper structure can turn right round, so the excavator can dig and unload the material beside itself without driving away. Attached to the upper structure is the arm, which consists of the boom and the stick. Right at the front hangs the **bucket**.

The arm is not moved by ropes but by **hydraulic cylinders**. A pump presses oil into the cylinders and so pushes strong pistons out or pulls them in. Because oil can hardly be compressed, very great forces can be produced in this way. The operator controls everything with two levers, the joysticks, in the cab.

Many large excavators run on **crawler tracks**. The tracks spread the heavy weight over a large area, so the excavator does not sink into soft ground. Wheeled excavators, on the other hand, are faster and may drive on the road. For gardens and tight spaces there are **mini excavators**, which often weigh only one to two tonnes.

Instead of tracks, the **walking excavator** has movable legs with wheels or feet. With them it can climb steep slopes, stream beds or mountains. It was invented by the Swiss Ernst Menzi, and his company in the St Gallen Rhine Valley became world-famous with the “Menzi Muck”. Walking excavators help, for example, to build avalanche barriers on slopes and to build mountain paths.

The biggest excavators are **bucket-wheel excavators** in open-cast lignite mines. A huge wheel with many buckets turns and digs away earth non-stop, which is carried off on conveyor belts. Bagger 288 in Germany is about 96 metres high and more than 200 metres long. It is one of the largest mobile machines in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A technology in which liquids such as oil under pressure transmit great forces.
An endless belt of links on which heavy vehicles travel.
The long arm of an excavator or crane.
An excavator with movable legs that can climb in steep terrain.
Extracting coal or rock in an open pit at the surface.

gewusst: A walking excavator can even lever itself up with its arm and climb over obstacles.
Bagger 288 moves so slowly that someone out for a walk could easily overtake it.
Instead of a bucket, excavators can also carry grabs, hammers or shears to demolish houses.

teile.einleitung: Escher Wyss was a famous Zurich engineering company founded in 1805. It built steamships, turbines and machines and became known worldwide especially for equipment for hydropower stations. The Escher-Wyss-Platz in Zurich still recalls the company today.
wichtigste: Hans Caspar Escher and Salomon von Wyss founded the company in Zurich in 1805.
Escher Wyss started out with a mechanical spinning mill.
From 1835 the company built steamships that sailed on many lakes.
In 1856 Escher Wyss set up a branch in Ravensburg in southern Germany.
In 1860 the company closed its spinning mill, because engineering had become more important.
In the 20th century Escher Wyss was a world leader in equipment for hydropower stations.
In 1969 Sulzer took over the company.
The Escher-Wyss-Platz in Zurich's industrial district recalls the company.

abschnitte.text: In 1805 **Hans Caspar Escher** and **Salomon von Wyss** founded the company in Zurich. It started with a **mechanical spinning mill**, where machines turned cotton into yarn. The spinning machines needed a workshop of their own to build and repair them. From this workshop a large engineering business gradually grew.

From 1835 Escher Wyss built **steamships**. The ships sailed on Swiss lakes and also on waters abroad. Some were delivered in parts and only assembled at the lake. Some historic paddle steamers from that time still sail on Swiss lakes today.

Engineering became more and more important, so Escher Wyss closed the spinning mill in 1860. In 1856 the company had already set up a branch in **Ravensburg** in southern Germany. Among other things, Escher Wyss made paper machines, steam engines and turbines. At the end of the 19th century the works moved to what is now Zurich's **industrial district**.

In the 20th century Escher Wyss was a world leader in equipment for **hydropower stations**. The company built huge **turbines** that use water power to drive generators. Such installations stand in power stations in Switzerland and in many other countries. Parts of the hydropower business now belong to the Austrian group Andritz.

In 1969 the Winterthur group **Sulzer** took over the company. Later the factory halls in Zurich were no longer needed, and the district changed a great deal. Today there are flats, offices, restaurants and cultural venues there. The **Escher-Wyss-Platz** recalls in its name the company that once shaped the district.

begriffe.erklaerung: Factory where fibres such as cotton are spun into yarn.
Industry that designs and makes machines.
Wheel with blades that is driven by water or steam.
Part of a city where many factories used to stand.

gewusst: Escher Wyss started as a yarn factory and became one of the best-known engineering companies in the world.
Steamships were sometimes transported in separate parts and only assembled at the lake.
Today the Escher-Wyss-Platz is an important traffic hub in Zurich's District 5.

teile.einleitung: A two-way radio is a device that lets people talk to each other without cables using radio waves. It sends and receives, so it is a transmitter and a receiver in one. Police, fire brigades, pilots and mountain guides rely on two-way radios every day.
wichtigste: A two-way radio carries the voice through the air on radio waves.
A small hand-held radio is called a walkie-talkie.
To speak, you press the talk button.
With a simple radio, only one person can speak at a time.
Both radios must be set to the same channel.
The aerial sends and receives the radio waves.
Police and fire brigades often use radios at work.
In great danger, people call “Mayday” over the radio.

abschnitte.text: A two-way radio turns the voice into **electromagnetic waves** that spread through the air. Another radio catches these waves and turns them back into sounds. Unlike the telephone, you need no cable for this and usually no mobile network. Every radio has a **transmitter**, a receiver, a microphone, a loudspeaker and an aerial. Small hand-held radios are called **walkie-talkies**.

When you want to speak, you press the **talk button** and hold it down. When you let go, you listen again. With simple radios, only one person can speak at a time; this is called **half-duplex**. That is why people often say “Over” at the end, so the other person knows it is their turn. Both devices must be set to the same **channel**, otherwise they cannot hear each other.

The **aerial** sends and receives the radio waves. The higher it is, the further the radio reaches, because mountains and houses block the waves. Small toy walkie-talkies often reach only a few hundred metres to a few kilometres. For greater distances there are **relay stations** on mountains that pass radio messages on. In the Swiss Alps this is important, because valleys and peaks disturb reception.

Police, fire brigades, ambulance services and civil protection talk by radio during operations. In Switzerland these emergency services use the shared digital radio network **Polycom**. Pilots talk by radio with air traffic control in the control tower. Mountain guides, workers on large building sites, ski instructors and the army also use radios. Radio amateurs even talk by radio in their free time with people on other continents.

If an aircraft or a ship is in great danger, the crew calls “**Mayday**” three times over the radio. The word comes from the French “m'aidez”, which means “help me”. Everyone who hears the distress call must then keep quiet and help if they can. For less urgent problems there is the call “Pan-Pan”. In the past, distress calls on ships were also sent with the Morse signal SOS.

Around 1895 the Italian **Guglielmo Marconi** achieved the first radio transmissions over longer distances. At first only Morse signals were sent, later the voice too. In the Second World War portable radios were developed for soldiers, and this gave rise to the walkie-talkie. Today radios are small, light and often digital.

begriffe.erklaerung: Small radio that you hold in your hand.
Button that you hold down while speaking.
Particular frequency on which radios talk to each other.
International distress call in voice radio.
Installation that receives radio messages and sends them on.

gewusst: The word Mayday comes from French and means roughly “help me”.
Radio amateurs can talk halfway round the world with home-made aerials.
On the International Space Station there are radios with which astronauts sometimes talk to school classes.

teile.einleitung: A construction crane is a tall lifting machine that lifts heavy loads such as concrete buckets, steel girders or building blocks on building sites and takes them to the right place. With their long arms, cranes shape the look of every big building site.
wichtigste: A crane lifts heavy loads on the building site.
The long arm of a crane is called the jib.
The load hangs on a hook on a steel cable.
Heavy concrete blocks on the short end stop the crane from tipping over.
The tall crane that turns round at the top is called a tower crane.
On large cranes the crane operator often sits in a cab high up.
In very strong wind a crane must not work, because the load swings dangerously.
In German the crane is named after the crane bird (Kranich), which has a long neck.

abschnitte.titel: How a tower crane is built
abschnitte.text: The most common construction crane is the **tower crane**. It consists of a tall tower made of steel lattice and a horizontal **jib** at the top that can turn round. A trolley runs back and forth along the jib, and the steel cable with the hook hangs from it. Heavy concrete **counterweights** hang on the short counter-jib.

abschnitte.titel: Why it does not tip over
abschnitte.text: A crane works like a seesaw. The load on the long jib pulls downwards, and the concrete blocks on the short end pull on the other side. In this way the crane stays in **balance**. The further out the load hangs, the less heavy it may be, which is why every crane has a table of the permitted loads.

On large cranes the crane operator sits in a cab high up and climbs up via a ladder in the tower. Today, however, many construction cranes are also operated from the ground by **radio remote control**. In Switzerland you need special training with an exam to operate a tower crane. In very strong wind the crane is switched off so that the jib can turn freely like a weathervane.

The Romans already built wooden cranes driven by a **treadwheel**. People walked inside it like hamsters in a wheel and so wound up a rope. In the Middle Ages such cranes helped to build cathedrals. Modern tower cranes appeared in the 20th century, and in 1949 the company Liebherr built one of the first tower cranes that were easy to put up.

As well as the tower crane, there is the **mobile crane**, which is mounted on a lorry and can quickly drive to a building site. Its jib can be extended like a telescope. In ports, large container cranes lift containers off ships. The name crane comes from the bird, the **crane**, because the long jib is reminiscent of its neck.

begriffe.erklaerung: The long horizontal or sloping arm of a crane.
Heavy blocks that balance the weight of the load.
A carriage that runs back and forth on the jib and carries the cable.
A tall crane with a jib that turns, typical of building sites.
A crane on a vehicle that can quickly travel from place to place.

gewusst: In the evening tower cranes are set so that they can turn freely in the wind; this is safer than holding them fixed.
Crane operators sometimes sit more than 50 metres up and have the best view of the building site.
Many tower cranes grow with the building by having new tower sections fitted.

teile.einleitung: The computer mouse is a small input device that you use to move a pointer across the screen and click on things. It made using computers much easier, and a well-known mouse company even comes from Switzerland.
wichtigste: Douglas Engelbart is regarded as the inventor of the computer mouse.
The symbol on the screen that follows the mouse is called the mouse pointer.
A double click with the left button usually opens a file.
In Windows the right mouse button usually opens the context menu.
With the wheel between the buttons you scroll through pages.
Older mice had a ball on the underside; today’s mice photograph the surface.
Wireless mice often connect by radio, for example via Bluetooth.

abschnitte.text: A computer mouse is an **input device** that you slide across the desk with your hand. It transfers every movement to the **mouse pointer** on the screen. With the left button you click on things, and a **double click** usually opens a file or a program. In Windows the right button opens the **context menu** with suitable commands. With the mouse wheel you scroll through long pages.

Older mice had a **ball** underneath, which turned two small wheels when the mouse was moved. Because dust collected there, they often had to be cleaned. An **optical mouse** has a light and a tiny camera sensor instead. It photographs the surface thousands of times a second and compares the pictures. The **dpi** value shows how sensitively the mouse reacts to movement.

The American **Douglas Engelbart** developed the mouse in the 1960s at the Stanford Research Institute in California. The first model was a small wooden box with two wheels and a button. In 1968 he presented it to the public in a famous demonstration. Because the cable looked like a tail, the device was given the name **mouse**. It really became well known in the 1980s with Apple’s computers.

Research on the mouse was also done in Switzerland, for example at ETH Zurich and at EPFL in Lausanne. The company **Logitech** was founded in 1981 in Apples in the canton of Vaud. It became world-famous for computer mice and had already made more than a billion of them by 2008. Today Logitech also makes keyboards, webcams and headsets.

Many mice today are **wireless** and transmit via a small USB receiver or via **Bluetooth**. Gaming mice have extra buttons and very precise sensors. On laptops a **touchpad** often replaces the mouse, and on tablets and mobile phones your finger on the touchscreen does. For people with hand pain there are ergonomic mice that you hold almost upright.

begriffe.erklaerung: A device with which you give the computer commands, such as a keyboard or mouse.
The small arrow on the screen that follows the mouse.
A menu with suitable commands that opens with the right mouse button.
Short for “dots per inch”, a measure of how sensitive the mouse is.
Moving the screen content up or down.

gewusst: The first computer mouse was made of wood.
An optical mouse often works badly on glass or mirrors, because the sensor cannot detect anything there.
The name mouse came about because the cable looked like a mouse’s tail.

teile.einleitung: Battery storage is a large installation made of many rechargeable batteries that stores electrical energy and feeds it back into the grid when needed. Such stores help to use electricity from the sun and wind when it is needed.
wichtigste: Lithium-ion batteries dominate in newly built large grid storage today.
For stationary storage, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) is often used, which needs no cobalt and is regarded as especially safe.
The Hornsdale Power Reserve in South Australia came into service in 2017 as the largest lithium-ion installation in the world at the time.
A redox flow battery stores energy in liquid electrolytes in external tanks.
A store with 2 MW of power and 8 MWh of capacity can feed in at full power for 4 hours.
Lithium-ion grid storage has an efficiency of about 80 to 90 per cent per cycle.
The dangerous, self-reinforcing heating of a cell is called thermal runaway.
With vehicle-to-grid, the batteries of parked electric cars serve as storage for the grid.

abschnitte.text: Battery storage consists of thousands of individual **battery cells** connected together in cabinets or containers. It also includes inverters, which turn the direct current of the batteries into alternating current for the grid, as well as cooling and control. Small battery stores sit in the cellars of houses with solar panels. Large **grid storage** systems fill whole fields with containers.

Solar panels produce a lot of electricity at midday but none in the evening. Battery storage takes in the surplus electricity and releases it later. It also reacts in fractions of a second and so helps to keep the **grid frequency** stable. This is important, because the electricity produced and used in the grid must always be exactly equal.

With storage, two quantities are distinguished. The **power** in megawatts (MW) says how much electricity it can deliver at the same time. The **capacity** in megawatt-hours (MWh) says how much energy fits into it altogether. So a store with 2 MW and 8 MWh can feed in at full power for 4 hours. When charging and discharging, about 10 to 20 per cent of the energy is lost as heat.

Today mainly **lithium-ion batteries** are built, for stationary installations often with the cell chemistry lithium iron phosphate (LFP), which needs no cobalt. An alternative is the **redox flow battery**, which stores its energy in liquid electrolytes in large tanks. If you want to store more energy, you simply build bigger tanks. A famous example of lithium-ion storage is the Hornsdale Power Reserve in South Australia, which came into service in 2017.

If damaged or overheated, lithium-ion cells can go into **thermal runaway**, in which they keep heating up and catch fire. That is why storage systems have temperature monitoring and fire suppression systems. An idea for the future is **vehicle-to-grid**, in which parked electric cars feed electricity back into the grid. In Switzerland battery storage complements the pumped-storage power stations in the Alps, which have long stored large amounts of energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A battery that can be charged again.
A device that turns direct current into alternating current.
How much energy a store can hold altogether.
The share of energy that comes back out after storage.
A liquid or substance in a battery through which charged particles move.

gewusst: The Hornsdale Power Reserve was built by the company Tesla, and its boss had promised to finish it in 100 days.
A battery store can react to fluctuations in the grid faster than any power station with turbines.
The battery of an electric car often stores more energy than a household uses in a whole day.

teile.einleitung: Biotechnology uses living cells, microorganisms or their building blocks to make useful products. For thousands of years people have baked bread or made cheese with yeast and bacteria, and that is already biotechnology. Today researchers can even change genes in a targeted way and so develop new medicines and vaccines.
wichtigste: Biotechnology combines biology with technology.
Bacteria, yeasts and cells work like tiny factories.
In 1982 human insulin was the first genetically engineered medicine approved for people.
The Swiss scientist Werner Arber received the Nobel Prize in 1978 for discovering restriction enzymes.
In 1996 Dolly the sheep was born, the first mammal cloned from an adult body cell.
For the gene scissors CRISPR/Cas9, Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.
Green biotechnology means biotechnology in plant breeding and farming.

abschnitte.text: **Biotechnology** means using living things or parts of them technically. Often they are tiny **microorganisms** such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi. They make substances we need, for example medicines, enzymes for washing powder or ingredients for food. Production often takes place in a **bioreactor**, a container in which temperature, food and oxygen are precisely controlled.

Thousands of years ago people were already using yeast for baking and brewing beer, and bacteria for yoghurt and cheese. This process is called **fermentation**. In 1928 Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin, which is made by a mould. Since the 1970s it has been possible to change the genetic material of living things in a targeted way with **genetic engineering**.

Experts like to divide biotechnology into colours. **Red biotechnology** concerns medicine and drugs. **Green biotechnology** deals with plant breeding and farming. White biotechnology makes substances for industry, such as enzymes or bioplastics. Blue biotechnology researches living things from the sea.

The Swiss scientist **Werner Arber** discovered restriction enzymes, which cut DNA at particular points, and received the Nobel Prize for it in 1978. In 1983 Kary Mullis developed the **polymerase chain reaction** (PCR), with which sections of DNA can be copied in a targeted way. In 1996 Dolly the sheep was cloned in Scotland. The gene scissors **CRISPR/Cas9** brought Emmanuelle Charpentier and Jennifer Doudna the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.

Many people with diabetes need insulin. Since 1982 **human insulin** has been made by genetically modified bacteria; before that it was obtained from the pancreases of pigs and cattle. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2023 for modified nucleosides. Their research made possible the **mRNA vaccines** that were used in the coronavirus pandemic.

Switzerland is an important location for biotechnology, especially around Basel with the pharmaceutical companies Roche and Novartis. ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne also do research in this field. In farming Switzerland is cautious: since a popular vote in 2005 there has been a **moratorium** on growing genetically modified plants. The opportunities and risks of genetic engineering are still being debated today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A molecule in every cell that stores the genetic information.
A section of DNA with the blueprint for a particular characteristic.
A container in which microorganisms or cells make products under controlled conditions.
A living thing with exactly the same genetic material as another.
A temporary ban or postponement for a certain time.

gewusst: Dolly the sheep was named after the singer Dolly Parton.
Many washing powders contain enzymes from bacteria that remove stains even at low temperatures.
With PCR you can make billions of copies from a tiny amount of DNA in a few hours.

teile.einleitung: A number sequence is a series of numbers that follow one another according to a particular rule. If you discover the rule, you can say which number comes next. Number sequences are a popular puzzle and an important topic in mathematics.
wichtigste: A number sequence follows a fixed rule.
In 5, 10, 15, 20, 5 is always added, so 25 comes next.
In 20, 18, 16, 14, 2 is always taken away, so 12 comes next.
The odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7 continue with 9.
In 1, 2, 4, 8 the number is always doubled, so 16 comes next.
The individual numbers of a sequence are called terms.
The famous Fibonacci sequence also occurs in nature.

abschnitte.text: A **number sequence** is an ordered series of numbers. Each number in it is called a **term** of the sequence. The terms are linked by a rule. If you know the rule, you can continue the sequence as far as you like. Many sequences are infinitely long.

In many sequences you add the same number each time. In 3, 6, 9, 12 it is 3 each time, so 15 comes next. In 10, 20, 30, 40 it is 10, so 50 comes next. Such sequences are called **arithmetic sequences**. They often match the sequences from the **times tables**.

A sequence can also get smaller. In 100, 90, 80, 70, 10 is taken away each time, so 60 comes next. In 20, 18, 16, 14, 2 is taken away and the next term is 12. Such sequences are called **decreasing**. The easiest way to recognise the rule is to work out the **difference** between two neighbours.

In 1, 2, 4, 8 each number is doubled, so 16 comes next and then 32. If you always multiply by the same number, it is called a **geometric sequence**. Such sequences grow very fast. An old legend tells of a chessboard: you put one grain of rice on the first square and twice as many on each following square. On the 64th square there would be more than nine quintillion grains, more rice than there is in the world.

The **Fibonacci sequence** goes 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. Each number is the sum of the two before it. It is named after the Italian mathematician Leonardo Fibonacci, who lived around 1200. In sunflowers and fir cones you often find spirals with Fibonacci numbers. Another well-known sequence is the **square numbers** 1, 4, 9, 16, 25.

abschnitte.titel: What number sequences are good for
abschnitte.text: Number sequences train logical thinking. They often come up in **intelligence tests** and entrance exams. Sequences can be used to describe how savings grow with interest or how bacteria multiply. In higher mathematics people study whether sequences get closer to a certain value. This value is called the **limit**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single number in a number sequence.
A sequence in which the same amount is always added or taken away.
A sequence in which you always multiply by the same number.
A sequence in which each number is the sum of the two before it.

gewusst: The On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS) collects more than 300,000 different number sequences.
The number of petals of many flowers is a Fibonacci number, such as 3, 5 or 8.
A sheet of paper that could be folded 42 times would be thicker than the distance from the Earth to the Moon.

teile.einleitung: The Energy Strategy 2050 is Switzerland's plan for what its energy supply should look like in future. It aims to save energy, expand renewable energy and replace nuclear power step by step. Swiss voters approved the basis for it in a popular vote in 2017.
wichtigste: The three main goals are saving energy, expanding renewable energy and replacing nuclear power step by step.
In 2011 the Federal Council, under energy minister Doris Leuthard, decided to phase out nuclear power.
Voters approved the revised Energy Act in 2017.
The act came into force on 1 January 2018.
The Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE) is mainly responsible for putting it into practice.
In 2023, with the Climate and Innovation Act, voters approved the goal of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050.
In June 2024 voters approved the Electricity Act (the so-called framework act) for a secure electricity supply with renewable energy.
Energy efficiency means getting the same benefit with less energy.

abschnitte.text: The Energy Strategy 2050 is a long-term plan by the Federal Council and Parliament for Switzerland's energy supply. It is meant to be secure, affordable and environmentally friendly. Its three pillars are: using less energy, using more **renewable energy** and gradually replacing the nuclear power stations. The responsible office is the **Swiss Federal Office of Energy (SFOE)**.

In March 2011, after an earthquake and tsunami in Japan, the nuclear accident at **Fukushima** happened. Shortly afterwards the Federal Council, under energy minister **Doris Leuthard**, decided that no new nuclear power stations should be built in Switzerland. The existing stations may keep running as long as they are safe. This led to a new Energy Act.

A **referendum** was launched against the revised Energy Act. In May 2017 voters approved the act, and it came into force on 1 January 2018. In 2023 came the **Climate and Innovation Act**, with the goal of net zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. In June 2024 voters approved the **Electricity Act**, also called the framework act, which is meant to speed up the expansion of renewable electricity production.

More and more roofs are getting **solar panels**, and the Confederation supports their construction with subsidies. Hydropower, wind power and biomass are also meant to supply more electricity. Buildings are being better insulated, and old oil heating systems are often replaced by heat pumps. At the end of 2019 the Mühleberg nuclear power station became the first Swiss nuclear power station to be taken off the grid.

**Energy efficiency** means getting the same benefit with less energy, for example with LED bulbs or economical appliances. A big task is the electricity supply in winter, when solar panels produce less. That is why reservoirs and storage are also to be expanded. How quickly and by what route the goals should be reached is still being debated in politics.

begriffe.erklaerung: A people's right to demand a vote on a new law.
No more greenhouse gas is emitted than is removed from the air again.
Getting the same benefit with less energy.
Swiss Federal Office of Energy, the responsible federal authority.

gewusst: The Energy Strategy 2050 was drawn up after the Fukushima nuclear accident in 2011.
The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was the first Swiss nuclear power station to be shut down for good.
In Switzerland the people vote directly on important energy and climate laws.

teile.einleitung: A block and tackle is a simple machine made of pulleys and a rope that lets you lift heavy loads with little force. It is found on building cranes, on sailing ships and in workshops. Its trick is amazingly simple: you save force, but in return you have to pull more rope.
wichtigste: A block and tackle consists of pulleys and a rope.
The casing that holds the pulleys is called a block.
With a block and tackle you save force.
In return you have to pull more rope.
A single fixed pulley on the ceiling only changes the direction of pull.
A movable pulley rises together with the load.
If the load hangs on two supporting lengths of rope, you need about half the force.

abschnitte.titel: What is a block and tackle?
abschnitte.text: A block and tackle is one of the oldest **simple machines**, like the lever or the inclined plane. It consists of several pulleys and a rope that runs over them. The pulleys sit in a casing called a **block**. One block hangs firmly at the top, the other hangs on the load. With it a single person can lift loads that are much heavier than themselves.

A **fixed pulley** is attached, for example, to the ceiling and does not move. It saves no force, but it changes the direction of pull, so you can pull downwards instead of upwards. A **movable pulley** hangs on the load and rises together with it. With it, two lengths of rope carry the load, so you need only about half the force. If you combine several pulleys, the force becomes even smaller.

For every bit of force you save, you have to pull more rope. If the load hangs on four lengths of rope, you need only about a quarter of the force. But you have to pull four times as much rope to lift the load by one metre. This rule is called the **golden rule of mechanics**: whatever you save in force, you have to add in distance. A small part of the force is also lost through **friction** in the pulleys.

Pulleys and ropes were already used in ancient times. According to legend, the Greek scholar **Archimedes** moved a ship single-handed with a block and tackle. The Romans built large treadwheel cranes with blocks and tackle, in which people walked as in a hamster wheel. Such cranes also helped in building medieval cathedrals.

abschnitte.titel: Blocks and tackle in everyday life
abschnitte.text: On a **building crane**, a block and tackle lifts heavy loads such as concrete parts or steel girders. On sailing ships, blocks and tackle help to pull in the sails and hold them in place. In car workshops they are used to lift engines out of cars. Mountaineers and rescuers build a block and tackle with ropes and karabiners to recover injured people from a crevasse. Flagpoles and blinds also use pulleys.

begriffe.erklaerung: Casing in which the pulleys of a block and tackle sit.
Pulley that does not move and only changes the direction of pull.
Pulley that moves with the load and saves force.
Simple aid such as a lever or pulley with which you save force.
Whatever you save in force, you have to add in distance.

gewusst: With a block and tackle made of many pulleys, a child can lift a car a little way.
The German name “Flaschenzug” comes from the casing of the pulleys, which is called a “Flasche” (bottle).
When rescuing people from crevasses, mountain guides build blocks and tackle from ropes and karabiners.

teile.einleitung: Scientific notation is a short way of writing very large and very small numbers. Instead of lots of zeros, you write a number between 1 and 10 and multiply it by a power of ten. So 3,400,000 simply becomes 3.4 · 10⁶.
wichtigste: A number in scientific notation has the form a · 10ⁿ.
The number a is always between 1 and 10, with 10 itself not included.
A positive exponent stands for large numbers, a negative one for small numbers.
When multiplying, you multiply the front numbers and add the exponents.
When dividing, you divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents.
Calculators often show this notation with an E, for example 2.5E-3.
Researchers in physics, chemistry and astronomy use it every day.

abschnitte.text: A number in scientific notation consists of two parts. At the front is the **mantissa**, a number from 1 to less than 10, for example 4.5. After it comes a **power of ten** such as 10⁷, which tells you how many times to multiply by 10. So 4.5 · 10⁷ means 45,000,000. A form such as 45 · 10⁶ has the same value but is not considered correct, because 45 is greater than 10.

To convert a large number, you move the decimal point to the left until there is only one digit in front of it. The number of places becomes the **exponent**: for 3,400,000 there are six places, so 3.4 · 10⁶. With small numbers you move the decimal point to the right, and the exponent becomes negative. In this way 7.03 · 10⁻⁵ becomes the decimal number 0.0000703.

When multiplying, you multiply the front numbers together and add the exponents: (2 · 10³) · (4 · 10⁵) gives 8 · 10⁸. When dividing, you divide the front numbers and subtract the exponents: (6 · 10⁸) : (3 · 10²) gives 2 · 10⁶. This is much quicker than writing long numbers with lots of zeros. These rules are called the **laws of indices**.

In astronomy numbers are often unimaginably large. In a vacuum light travels about 3 · 10⁸ metres per second, that is about 300,000 kilometres. The mass of the Earth is about 6 · 10²⁴ kilograms, a number with 24 zeros. Without scientific notation such values would hardly be readable.

Very small things can be described in this way too. An atom is about 10⁻¹⁰ metres across, that is one ten-billionth of a metre. A human hair is about 10⁻⁴ metres thick, roughly a tenth of a millimetre. With negative exponents you can see at once how small something is.

In 2024 Switzerland had about 9 million inhabitants, that is roughly 9 · 10⁶ people. A calculator often shows very large or very small results with the letter **E**, which stands for “times ten to the power of”. The display 2.5E-3 therefore means 2.5 · 10⁻³, which is 0.0025. In Swiss schools this notation is usually learned at lower secondary level.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number such as 10³, in which 10 is multiplied by itself several times.
The small raised number that says how many times you multiply by 10.
The front number between 1 and 10 in scientific notation.
A rule for calculating with numbers with exponents, for example adding the exponents when multiplying.

gewusst: 10⁰ equals 1, because any number to the power of zero gives 1.
More than 2000 years ago the Greek Archimedes thought about how to write down huge numbers, such as the number of grains of sand in the universe.
A famous giant number, 10¹⁰⁰, has its own name: googol.

teile.einleitung: A cube is a geometric solid with six square faces of equal size. It has 8 vertices and 12 edges of equal length. Every child knows the cube from games, for example snakes and ladders, and it is one of the most important solids in geometry.
wichtigste: A cube has 6 square faces of equal size.
A cube has 8 vertices and 12 edges.
All the edges of a cube are the same length.
The volume is edge times edge times edge.
The surface area is six times the area of one square.
On a die, opposite numbers of pips always add up to 7.
There are 11 different nets of a cube.

abschnitte.text: A **cube** is a solid bounded by six **squares** of exactly the same size. It has 8 **vertices** and 12 **edges**, all of which are the same length. At each vertex three faces and three edges meet at right angles. Opposite faces are parallel. Because all the faces are the same, a cube looks the same from every side, however you place it.

The **volume** of a cube is calculated as edge times edge times edge, that is a to the power of 3. A cube with an edge length of 2 cm has a volume of 2 times 2 times 2, that is 8 cm³. This is where the English word “cubed” for “to the power of three” comes from, after the cube. The **surface area** consists of six squares and is 6 times a². With an edge length of 2 cm that is 6 times 4, so 24 cm².

If you cut a cardboard cube open along some edges and unfold it flat, you get a **net of a cube**. It consists of six connected squares. Altogether there are 11 different nets that can be folded back into a cube. A well-known net looks like a cross. Not every arrangement of six squares works, for example not six squares in a row.

The **die** is one of the oldest toys in the world and was known thousands of years ago. Its sides carry 1 to 6 dots, called **pips**. On most dice, opposite sides always add up to 7, so 1 and 6, 2 and 5, 3 and 4. Because all the sides are the same size, every number is equally likely. That is why the die is suitable for games of chance such as snakes and ladders (Leiterlispiel) or “Eile mit Weile”.

Cube shapes can be found in sugar cubes, ice cubes, building blocks and some boxes. The **Rubik’s Cube**, invented by the Hungarian Ernő Rubik in 1974, is one of the best-selling toys in the world. Many crystals, such as those of table salt, have the shape of small cubes. In computer games such as Minecraft the whole world is built from cubes. Units of measurement such as the cubic metre are also based on the cube.

The cube is one of the five **Platonic solids**, solids whose faces are all identical regular polygons. The other four are the tetrahedron, octahedron, dodecahedron and icosahedron. They are named after the Greek philosopher Plato. Another name for the cube is therefore **hexahedron**, which means six-faced solid. The cube is also a special cuboid and a special prism.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line where two faces of a solid meet.
A point where several edges meet.
The surface of a cube spread out flat.
Another name for the cube; it means six-faced solid.
A solid made entirely of identical regular polygons.

gewusst: A Rubik’s Cube has more than 43 quintillion possible positions.
Dice were already known in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia; some were carved from bone.
A cube with an edge length of 1 m holds exactly 1000 litres of water.

teile.einleitung: Rail 2000 (Bahn 2000) is a big project that made rail travel in Switzerland faster and better connected. The people voted for it in 1987, and the first stage came into service in 2004. The idea behind it: trains should meet at the big stations so that there are good connections everywhere.
wichtigste: The Swiss people approved Rail 2000 in 1987 with about 57 per cent voting yes.
The first stage came into service in December 2004.
The principle was: as fast as necessary, not as fast as possible.
Trains are meant to meet at big stations, the hubs, and offer connections.
The journey time between two hubs should therefore be just under an hour or half an hour.
Since then the fastest trains have taken just under an hour from Bern to Zurich.
On the new line from Mattstetten to Rothrist, trains run with ETCS at up to 200 km/h.

abschnitte.text: **Rail 2000** is a plan by the Swiss Federal Railways SBB and the federal government to improve the whole rail network. It was not mainly about record speeds but about good **connections**. The principle was: as fast as necessary, not as fast as possible. On 6 December 1987 the people approved the project with about 57 per cent voting yes.

The idea of Rail 2000 is the **hub principle**. At big stations such as Zurich, Bern, Basel and Lucerne, the trains arrive shortly before the full or half hour and leave again shortly afterwards. This makes changing trains easy. For this to work, the journey time between two **hubs** has to be just under an hour or half an hour. Only then do the trains make the connections at both hubs.

To get the journey times right, lines were upgraded and new ones built. The most important is the **new line** between Mattstetten near Bern and Rothrist in Aargau. Trains run there at up to 200 km/h. Since then the fastest trains have taken just under an hour from Bern to Zurich.

At 200 km/h a train driver can hardly recognise ordinary trackside signals safely any more. That is why the new line uses the European train control system **ETCS**. With it the information is sent by radio directly to a screen in the **driver’s cab**. The system monitors the speed and brakes the train automatically if necessary.

On 12 December 2004 the first stage of Rail 2000 came into service with the new timetable. It was one of the biggest timetable changes in the history of the SBB. Many connections became faster, and on important lines trains now ran **every half hour**. For this the SBB also brought in extra double-decker trains.

After Rail 2000, the Swiss rail network is being expanded in further stages. These also include the base tunnels through the Alps at the Lötschberg and the Gotthard, which are part of the **NRLA** (NEAT). Since 2016 a dedicated **railway infrastructure fund** has made sure that money is available for maintenance and expansion. Today Switzerland is regarded as one of the countries with the densest train services in the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: A big station where many trains meet so that people can change.
A train you can catch after changing without waiting long.
A timetable in which trains leave regularly at the same minute.
A European safety system that sends signals directly into the driver’s cab.

gewusst: With Rail 2000 the aim was not the fastest timetable but the best coordinated one.
On the new line from Mattstetten to Rothrist there are no ordinary trackside signals for the fast trains.
The Swiss regular-interval timetable was introduced as early as 1982, and Rail 2000 built on it.

teile.einleitung: The Gotthard Railway is one of the most famous railway lines in the world and links German-speaking Switzerland with Ticino and Italy. Since it opened in 1882, trains have passed through a long tunnel under the Gotthard massif. Building it was a technical masterpiece, but it also cost many workers their lives.
wichtigste: The Gotthard Railway opened in 1882.
The old summit tunnel between Göschenen and Airolo is about 15 kilometres long.
Alfred Escher was the first president of the Gotthard Railway Company.
The Geneva building contractor Louis Favre led the tunnel construction and died in 1879 before it was completed.
The church of Wassen can be seen from three different heights along the line.
The electrification of the Gotthard Railway was completed in 1922.
Since 2016 most trains have run through the 57-kilometre Gotthard Base Tunnel.

abschnitte.text: The Gotthard Railway runs from Lake Lucerne up through the **Reuss valley** in Uri to Göschenen, through the tunnel to Airolo and down through the **Leventina** into Ticino as far as Chiasso. It is an important part of the north-south link between Germany and Italy. The actual mountain line begins in Erstfeld and ends in Biasca. The highest point is in the summit tunnel at about 1,150 metres above sea level.

The building of the line was driven forward by the Zurich politician and businessman **Alfred Escher**, the first president of the Gotthard Railway Company. The 15-kilometre tunnel was built from 1872 by **Louis Favre** from Geneva. Thousands of workers, many of them from Italy, drilled under harsh conditions with dynamite, pneumatic drills and bad air. Favre died in 1879 during an inspection in the tunnel, a year before the two tunnels met in 1880. About 200 workers lost their lives building the tunnel, and many more fell ill.

Because trains cannot manage steep gradients, the line winds up the mountain in loops. For this the engineers built **spiral tunnels**, in which the train travels in a circle inside the mountain and gains height as it does so. Near **Wassen** in the canton of Uri, the train loops in such a way that you see the village church from three different heights. For many travellers, the “little church of Wassen” was therefore the best-known landmark of the journey.

At first steam locomotives pulled the trains, making a lot of smoke in the long tunnel. After the First World War, when coal was scarce and expensive, the SBB switched to electricity from hydropower. In 1922 the **electrification** of the Gotthard Railway was completed. The goods locomotive nicknamed the **Crocodile** became famous; it got its name from its long bonnets.

In 2016 the **Gotthard Base Tunnel** went into scheduled service; at 57 kilometres it is the longest railway tunnel in the world. It lies much deeper inside the mountain, so trains can run almost without any gradient and much faster. Since then most goods and long-distance trains have run through the base tunnel. The old **mountain line** is now used mainly by regional trains and the Treno Gottardo, and it is very popular with railway fans.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tunnel that passes through a mountain at the highest point of a railway line.
Tunnel in which a train travels in a circle to gain height.
Very long tunnel deep down in the mountain, almost without any gradient.
Converting a railway line to run on electricity.
Valley in the canton of Ticino through which the Gotthard Railway runs southwards.

gewusst: When the tunnel was broken through in 1880, the two tunnels were only a few decimetres out from each other.
The Gotthard Railway was financed jointly by Switzerland, Germany and Italy.
In Erstfeld and Göschenen, monuments remember the workers who died building the tunnel.

teile.einleitung: When comparing numbers, you find out which of two numbers is bigger or smaller, or whether both are equal. There are signs for less than, greater than and equal to. If you can compare numbers, you can also put them in order.
wichtigste: The sign < means “is less than”.
The sign > means “is greater than”.
The sign = means “is equal to”.
Between 45 and 54 the sign < belongs.
Calculations can be compared too: 8 + 5 = 13 and 20 + 30 > 45.
With numbers that have the same number of digits, you compare place by place from left to right.
For whole numbers, a number with more digits is always bigger.

abschnitte.text: There are three signs for comparing: **<** means “is less than”, **>** means “is greater than” and **=** means “is equal to”. The point of the sign always points to the smaller number, and the open side to the bigger one. Many children remember this with a crocodile that always opens its mouth towards the bigger number, because it wants to eat more. So you write 45 < 54 or 710 > 170.

First you look at how many **digits** the numbers have: 109 is bigger than 91, because it has three digits. If both numbers have the same number of digits, you compare from left to right. With 45 and 54 the tens are different; 4 tens are less than 5 tens. If the first digits are the same, you move on to the next **place**.

You can also compare calculations with each other. To do this you first work out both sides. So 8 + 5 equals 13, and 2 times 6 equals 3 times 4, because both give 12. The statement 20 + 30 > 45 is true, because 50 is greater than 45. A statement like this with < or > is called an **inequality**.

If you can compare numbers, you can also **put them in order**. From the smallest to the largest number this is called ascending order, for example 19, 91, 109, 190. The other way round it is called descending order. On the **number line** the smaller number is always further to the left.

The equals sign was invented by the Welsh mathematician **Robert Recorde** in 1557. He chose two parallel lines of the same length, because nothing could be more equal. The signs < and > come from the Englishman Thomas Harriot and were published in 1631. Today people all over the world use these signs.

In everyday life we compare numbers all the time, for example prices in a shop, temperatures or points in a game. With **decimal numbers** you have to be careful: 0.5 is greater than 0.45, even though 45 has more digits. With **negative numbers**, minus 10 is less than minus 2, because it is colder on the thermometer. In sport, too, people measure and compare who was faster or went further.

begriffe.erklaerung: The sign <, for example 3 < 5.
The sign >, for example 9 > 2.
The sign =, which shows that both sides have the same value.
A statement with < or >, for example 20 + 30 > 45.
Ordered from the smallest to the largest number.

gewusst: The equals sign is only about 470 years old.
On a computer “less than or equal to” is often written as the two signs <= one after the other.
With decimal numbers the number with more digits is not always the bigger one.

teile.einleitung: A point of inflection is a place where a graph changes its curvature. Imagine riding your bike on a winding road: at the point of inflection you switch from a left-hand bend into a right-hand bend. In calculus, points of inflection are found with the help of derivatives.
wichtigste: At a point of inflection the curvature changes direction.
The necessary condition is f''(x₀) = 0.
If f'''(x₀) ≠ 0 as well, x₀ is definitely a point of inflection.
The tangent at a point of inflection is called the inflectional tangent.
A point of inflection with a horizontal tangent is called a saddle point.
The graph of x³ has a saddle point at the origin.
With logistic growth, the growth rate is greatest at the point of inflection.

abschnitte.titel: What is a point of inflection?
abschnitte.text: A graph can **curve** to the left or to the right, like a road with bends. At the **point of inflection** the curvature changes from left to right or the other way round. For the graph of f(x) = x³, the curve bends to the right for x < 0 and to the left for x > 0. The change happens at the origin.

The curvature is described by the second **derivative** f''. At a point of inflection x₀, f''(x₀) = 0 must hold; this is the necessary condition. It becomes sufficient if f'''(x₀) ≠ 0 as well. Without this second check you can be fooled, because for x⁴, f''(0) = 0, and yet there is no point of inflection there.

For f(x) = x³ − 6x², f''(x) = 6x − 12. If you set this equal to zero, you get x = 2. Since f'''(x) = 6 is not zero, there is a point of inflection there, and f(2) = 8 − 24 = -16 gives the point (2|-16). For f(x) = x³ − 3x² the point of inflection is at x = 1, and the **inflectional tangent** there has the gradient -3.

If the tangent at the point of inflection is horizontal, it is called a **saddle point** or terrace point. There the gradient is zero, but there is neither a maximum nor a minimum. The best-known example is x³ at the origin. The graph rises before and after it, but in between it has a short flat stretch.

abschnitte.titel: Points of inflection in everyday life
abschnitte.text: Points of inflection show where a development is fastest. With **logistic growth**, for example an animal population with limited food, the number grows slowly at first, then fast and finally slowly again. At the point of inflection the growth rate is greatest. Curvature also plays an important role in the spread of new technologies and in roller coasters and road bends.

begriffe.erklaerung: Describes whether a graph bends to the left or to the right.
Tells you how steep a graph is at a point.
The tangent that touches the graph exactly at the point of inflection.
A point of inflection with a horizontal tangent.

gewusst: Every cubic function has exactly one point of inflection.
The inflectional tangent crosses the graph at the point of inflection instead of just touching it.
Road planners build the transitions between bends so that the curvature changes gently, to keep driving comfortable.

teile.einleitung: An electrical conductor is a substance through which electric current can flow easily. The best conductors are metals such as silver, copper and aluminium. The opposite are insulators such as rubber, glass or plastic, which stop the current.
wichtigste: Metals conduct well because they have many freely moving electrons.
Silver conducts best, but for cables the much cheaper copper is used.
High-voltage lines are often made of aluminium, because it is light and conducts well.
Tap water conducts electricity because salts are dissolved in it as ions.
The human body also conducts electricity, because it contains a lot of salty fluid.
Below a very low temperature, superconductors have no resistance at all.
In Swiss household cables the protective earth conductor is green and yellow and the neutral conductor is blue.

abschnitte.text: A **conductor** lets electric current through almost unhindered. In metals some electrons are not firmly bound to their atoms and can move freely; they are called **free electrons**. If a voltage is applied, they all move in one direction and current flows. Substances without free charge carriers are called **insulators**.

**Silver** conducts best of all, closely followed by copper, gold and aluminium. For electric cables in the home, **copper** is used, because it conducts almost as well as silver but is much cheaper. For overhead high-voltage lines **aluminium** is mostly used, often with a steel core for strength, because it is light and the pylons have less to carry. Gold is found on plug contacts in computers, because it does not corrode.

Completely pure, distilled water hardly conducts electricity. But **tap water** contains dissolved salts that break up into electrically charged particles, the **ions**. These can carry the current.
