The human body also contains a lot of salty fluid and therefore conducts electricity, which is why electrical appliances near the bath and washbasin are dangerous.

Between conductors and insulators lie the **semiconductors** such as silicon, from which computer chips are built. Depending on the conditions they conduct sometimes more, sometimes less. In 1911 the Dutch physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes discovered that mercury loses all its resistance when extremely cold. Such **superconductors** are used today, for example, in the strong magnets of MRI scanners in hospitals and in the particle accelerator at CERN near Geneva.

An electric cable consists of copper wires that are **insulated** with plastic so that they can be touched safely. In Switzerland the wires have standardised colours. The **protective earth conductor**, also called earth, is green and yellow, and the neutral conductor in new cables is blue. The live conductors are usually brown, black or grey.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance through which electric current can flow easily.
A substance that hardly lets current through, for example rubber or plastic.
An electrically charged particle, for example from dissolved salt.
A substance such as silicon that conducts current well only under certain conditions.
A substance that has no resistance at all at a very low temperature.

gewusst: Pencil leads made of graphite conduct electricity, even though they are not metal at all.
Metals conduct less well when they get warm, because the atoms then jiggle more and get in the electrons’ way.
Most superconductors have to be cooled to far below minus 100 degrees, often with liquid helium.

teile.einleitung: Inventors are people who think up and build something new that did not exist before. Their ideas range from printing to the lightning conductor to Velcro. Careful observation, lots of trying things out and sometimes a lucky accident often help.
wichtigste: An inventor creates a new technical solution to a problem.
Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg invented printing with movable type in Mainz.
Samuel Morse invented a code made of short and long signals.
A screw for lifting water is named after the ancient Greek Archimedes.
Leonardo da Vinci drew flying machines more than 500 years ago.
Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning conductor.
The Swiss George de Mestral invented Velcro.

abschnitte.text: An **inventor** develops something new, for example a machine, a tool or a process. An **invention** usually solves a problem or makes life easier. Finding something new that already exists, such as a law of nature, is called a discovery instead. Many inventions come about in teams or build on older ideas.

abschnitte.titel: Inventors of antiquity and the Renaissance
abschnitte.text: The Greek **Archimedes** lived in Syracuse more than 2,200 years ago. The Archimedean screw, used to raise water, is named after him. The Italian **Leonardo da Vinci** was both an artist and an inventor. More than 500 years ago he drew flying machines, parachutes and diving suits, even though most of them were never built.

Around 1450 **Johannes Gutenberg** invented printing with movable type in Mainz, which made books much cheaper. In the 18th century Benjamin Franklin invented the **lightning conductor**, which protects houses from lightning strikes. In the 1830s Samuel Morse developed the telegraph and **Morse code**, made of short and long signals. Around 1879 Thomas Edison improved the light bulb, and he applied for over a thousand patents.

In 1941 **George de Mestral** from French-speaking Switzerland came back from a walk with burrs in his dog's fur and had the idea for **Velcro**. The “Rex” peeler was invented in Davos in 1947 by Alfred Neweczerzal. From 1891 Karl Elsener from Ibach supplied soldier's knives to the Swiss army, and this gave rise to the famous **Swiss Army knife**. Milk chocolate was also invented, in Vevey in 1875, by Daniel Peter.

Anyone who has invented something can apply for a **patent**. A patent forbids others from using the invention without permission for a certain time, usually up to 20 years. In Switzerland the Swiss Federal Institute of Intellectual Property in Bern is responsible for this. Albert Einstein worked at the patent office in Bern from 1902 to 1909, where he examined inventions.

Many inventions start with curiosity and the question of how something could be done better. Inventors observe carefully, just as de Mestral examined the burrs under a microscope. Anyone who takes ideas from nature is practising **bionics**. Mistakes are part of it, because it often takes many attempts before something works.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something new that a person has thought up and built.
Official right that protects an invention for a certain time.
First test model of a new invention.
Technology that copies solutions from nature.

gewusst: The name “Velcro” comes from the French words “velours” for velvet and “crochet” for hook.
The “Rex” peeler has been made almost unchanged since 1947 and is considered a classic of Swiss design.
Many inventions came about by chance, for example penicillin and the microwave oven.

teile.einleitung: Renewable energy is energy from sources that keep renewing themselves, for example sun, wind, water and geothermal heat. By human standards it never runs out. In Switzerland, water from the mountains plays a huge part.
wichtigste: Renewable energy comes from sources that are constantly being replenished.
The most important forms are hydropower, solar energy, wind energy, geothermal energy and biomass.
In Switzerland hydropower supplies most of the electricity.
A solar cell converts sunlight directly into electric current.
Using heat from inside the Earth is called geothermal energy.
Oil, natural gas and coal are not renewable, because they take millions of years to form.
Renewable energy produces hardly any greenhouse gases in operation and so protects the climate.

abschnitte.text: In Switzerland **hydropower** supplies about 55 to 60 per cent of the electricity (as of around 2024). Flowing or falling water drives a turbine, which produces electricity with a generator. In the Alps there are many reservoirs behind high dams. At 285 metres, the Grande Dixence in Valais is the highest **gravity dam** in the world. River power stations, such as those on the Rhine, instead use the constantly flowing water.

A **solar cell** is usually made of silicon and converts sunlight directly into electricity. Many solar cells together form a solar panel, which is mounted on roofs, walls or even on dams. This technology is called **photovoltaics**. Solar collectors can also be used to heat water, for example for the shower. In Switzerland solar energy has been growing especially fast for some years.

Wind energy counts as renewable because the wind keeps forming again, driven by the sun, which warms the air unevenly. A **wind turbine** turns a generator with its rotor blades. One of the largest wind farms in Switzerland is on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura. **Geothermal energy** uses heat from inside the Earth, for example with ground probes and heat pumps for heating houses.

Sun and wind do not always supply the same amount of energy, so electricity has to be stored. A **pumped storage power station** uses surplus electricity to pump water into a lake higher up. When electricity is needed later, the water is let back down to run through turbines. One example is the Nant de Drance power station in Valais, which went into operation in 2022. Batteries also store electricity, for example in electric cars.

Burning oil, **natural gas** and coal produces carbon dioxide, which warms the Earth. Renewable energy helps to slow down **climate change**. Switzerland has decided to emit net zero greenhouse gases by 2050. To do this, more solar panels, wind turbines and heat pumps are to be built. Saving energy is also part of it, because the cleanest energy is the energy you do not need at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology with which solar cells convert sunlight into electricity.
Using heat from inside the Earth.
Power station that pumps water uphill to store energy for later.
Machine that converts rotation into electric current.
Plants, wood or waste from which energy is obtained.

gewusst: At 285 metres, the Grande Dixence dam is almost as tall as the Eiffel Tower.
Wood is also a renewable source of energy, because trees grow back.
In Iceland a large share of houses are heated with geothermal heat.

teile.einleitung: Biogas is a flammable gas produced when bacteria break down plant remains, manure or waste without oxygen. It can be used to produce electricity, heat and even fuel for vehicles, all from renewable sources.
wichtigste: The main component of biogas is methane.
Bacteria break down the biomass without oxygen.
On farms biogas is often produced from slurry and manure.
The fermentation takes place in a container called a digester.
A combined heat and power plant produces electricity and heat from biogas.
The digestate left over is often used as fertiliser.
Purified biogas that can be fed into the natural gas grid is called biomethane.
In sewage treatment plants sewage gas is produced, which is a form of biogas.

abschnitte.text: Biogas is a mixture of gases that is about half to three quarters **methane**. The rest is mainly carbon dioxide, along with small amounts of other gases such as hydrogen sulphide, which smells of rotten eggs. Methane is also the main component of natural gas and burns well. Biogas also forms naturally, for example in swamps, where it rises as marsh gas.

In a biogas plant, slurry, manure, green waste or food scraps go into a large, airtight container, the **digester**. Inside, bacteria break down the biomass without oxygen; this is called **anaerobic digestion**. The digester is kept warm at about body temperature and stirred constantly. The gas produced collects at the top under a hood.

Biogas is often burned in a **combined heat and power plant**, an engine with a generator. It produces electricity and heat at the same time, which can be used to heat houses or animal sheds. Biogas can also be purified and the carbon dioxide removed. The resulting **biomethane** is fed into the natural gas grid or used as fuel for gas cars and buses.

On many Swiss farms there are biogas plants that are run mainly on slurry and manure. In this way less methane escapes from the farm manure into the air, because methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. The **digestate** left over smells less strongly than fresh slurry. It is spread on the fields as fertiliser, so completing the cycle.

Biogas is also produced in **sewage treatment plants**, where it is called sewage gas. It forms when the sewage sludge ferments in digestion towers. Many treatment plants produce a large part of their own electricity needs with it. In Switzerland green waste from green-waste collections is also turned into biogas in digestion plants.

begriffe.erklaerung: A flammable gas, the main component of biogas and natural gas.
An airtight container in which fermentation takes place.
Plants, animal manure and other material from living things.
An installation that produces electricity and heat at the same time.
What is left after fermentation and is used as fertiliser.

gewusst: Methane is also produced in the stomachs of cows, because similar bacteria work there as in a biogas plant.
In Switzerland some gas cars and buses run on biogas made from kitchen waste.
In ancient China and India people already used simple pits to get flammable gas from manure.

teile.einleitung: Number puzzles are tricky problems in which you use logic and calculation to find a number. They come as brain-teasers, number sequences or puzzle grids such as sudoku. They are fun and train mathematical thinking.
wichtigste: In number puzzles you look for an unknown number with the help of clues.
Many puzzles are solved by working backwards.
For “times 3 plus 4 gives 25”, the number you are looking for is 7.
In the sequence 2, 6, 18, 54 the rule is times 3, so 162 comes next.
In the Fibonacci sequence, 8 and 13 are followed by 21.
Sudoku is one of the most popular number puzzles in the world.
Equations can also be used to solve difficult number puzzles.

abschnitte.text: In this puzzle someone describes what they have done to a number they are thinking of. It is best solved by **working backwards** with the inverse operations. If “times 3 plus 4” gives 25, you work out 25 minus 4 equals 21 and then 21 divided by 3 equals 7. So the number thought of is 7. Plus becomes minus, and times becomes **divided by**.

With sequences you have to find the hidden rule. In 2, 6, 18, 54 each number is **multiplied by 3**, so 162 comes next. 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 are **square numbers**, and the next is 36. In 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 each number is the sum of the two before it, so 21 comes next. A good trick is to write down the gaps between the numbers.

Two numbers add up to 20, and their difference is 6. If you take the difference away from the total, 14 is left, which is two equal parts of 7. So the smaller number is 7 and the larger 13. Such problems can also be solved with an **equation**. The check is: 13 plus 7 is 20, 13 minus 7 is 6.

On a farm there are hens and rabbits with 10 heads and 28 legs altogether. If all 10 animals were hens, they would have only 20 legs. The 8 missing legs come from the fact that each rabbit has 2 more legs. So there are 4 rabbits and 6 hens. This **assumption method** is a classic calculation trick that already appears in an old Chinese maths book.

Some puzzles ask about the **digits** of a number. A two-digit number has a **digit sum** of 9, and the tens digit is twice as big as the units digit. So the units digit must be 3 and the tens digit 6, which gives 63. For the check you work out 6 plus 3 equals 9. Similar problems are cryptarithms, in which letters stand for digits.

In **sudoku** you have to fill a grid of 9 by 9 squares so that each digit from 1 to 9 appears only once in every row, every column and every block. The puzzle became popular worldwide from 2004. In kakuro you fill in digits so that given sums are produced. A **magic square** has the same sum in all its rows, columns and diagonals. A famous example can be seen in the engraving “Melencolia I” by Albrecht Dürer from 1514.

begriffe.erklaerung: You start with the result and undo each calculation.
The sum of all the digits of a number.
A calculation with an equals sign in which an unknown number is sought.
A square of numbers in which all the lines give the same sum.

gewusst: The name sudoku comes from Japanese and means roughly “the digits may only appear once”.
In Albrecht Dürer’s magic square the year 1514 appears in the bottom row.
A sudoku needs at least 17 given numbers to have exactly one solution.

teile.einleitung: The pencil is one of the simplest and most important writing tools in the world. Although in German it is called a “Bleistift” (lead pen), it contains no lead at all, but a core of graphite and clay in a casing of wood.
wichtigste: The pencil lead is made of graphite and clay.
The casing is usually made of wood.
Pencil lines are removed with a rubber.
A blunt pencil is made sharp again with a sharpener.
HB is a medium grade of hardness; B means soft and black.
Many pencils are hexagonal so that they do not roll off the table.
The pencil company Caran d’Ache is based in Geneva.

abschnitte.text: A pencil consists of the **lead** and a **wooden casing**, often made of cedar wood. The lead is a mixture of **graphite** and **clay** that is fired. It is laid in a groove in the wood and glued to a second wooden board. Then the pencils are cut out and varnished. Many pencils are **hexagonal**, so that they do not roll off the table and sit well in the hand.

On the pencil there is a code for the hardness of the lead. **H** stands for hard; such pencils draw fine, pale lines. **B** stands for soft and black; these pencils are popular for drawing and shading. **HB** is in the middle and is the typical school pencil. The more clay there is in the lead, the harder it is; the more graphite, the softer.

In the 16th century a large deposit of pure graphite was found at **Borrowdale** in England. At the time people thought the shiny substance was a kind of lead, which is where the German name “Bleistift” comes from. Because good graphite became scarce, the Frenchman **Nicolas-Jacques Conté** developed a new method in 1795. He mixed graphite powder with clay and fired the mixture. This made it possible for the first time to produce different grades of hardness.

The best-known Swiss pencil company is **Caran d’Ache** in Geneva. It was founded in 1915 and still makes pencils, coloured pencils and fountain pens today. The name goes back to the Russian word for pencil. Many Swiss children know its coloured pencils from school. Other big manufacturers include Faber-Castell and Staedtler in Germany.

A **rubber** rubs the graphite particles off the paper and picks them up. In the past breadcrumbs were used for this. In a **sharpener** a sharp blade cuts the wood and lead to a point again. Unlike a ballpoint pen, a pencil also writes upside down and in space. That is why it is very popular with architects, craftspeople and artists.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft, grey form of carbon that rubs off on paper.
The core inside that writes on the paper.
Says how hard or soft a lead is, for example H, HB or B.
A tool with a blade that makes pencils sharp.

gewusst: There is not a scrap of lead in a pencil.
With a single pencil you can draw a line many kilometres long.
Graphite is the same element as diamond, namely carbon, only arranged differently.

teile.einleitung: A gearbox is an assembly in a machine that transmits rotation and changes it in the process. It can make a rotation faster or slower, stronger or weaker, and change its direction. Gearboxes are found in cars, bicycles, clocks, blenders and wind turbines.
wichtigste: A gearbox converts speed and torque.
The most common kind of gear is the spur gear, with teeth on the outside and parallel shafts.
A bevel gear usually turns a rotation through 90 degrees.
In a worm gear, a screw meshes with a gearwheel and produces a strong reduction.
The outer wheel of a planetary gear, with teeth on the inside, is called the ring gear.
In many cars, the rack and pinion turns the rotation of the steering wheel into a sideways movement.
The differential allows wheels to turn at different speeds on bends.
An automatic gearbox changes gear by itself.

abschnitte.text: A gearbox connects a drive, for example a motor, to the part that is supposed to move. In doing so it changes the **speed**, that is, how fast something turns. At the same time the **torque** changes, that is, how much force there is in the rotation. If a gearbox makes the rotation slower and stronger, this is called a **reduction**. If it makes it faster, it is called stepping up.

Most gearboxes work with **gearwheels** whose teeth mesh with each other. If a small gearwheel drives a large one, the large one turns more slowly but with more force. The ratio of the teeth decides the **gear ratio**. If one wheel has 10 teeth and the other 40, the large one turns only once while the small one turns four times. The most common form is the **spur gear**, with the teeth on the outside and the shafts parallel.

A **bevel gear** has cone-shaped gearwheels and usually turns a rotation through 90 degrees, for example in a hand drill. In a **worm gear**, a screw meshes with a gearwheel, which gives a very strong reduction. A planetary gear has a sun gear in the middle, planet gears around it and a **ring gear** with teeth on the inside around the outside. In a rack and pinion, a rotation is turned into a straight-line movement. This is how the wheels of many cars are steered.

A car engine only runs well within a certain range. With different **gears**, the gearbox makes sure the car has enough power when pulling away and can drive fast on the motorway. With a manual gearbox, the driver chooses the gears with the clutch and gear lever. An automatic gearbox changes gear by itself. The **differential** on the drive axle lets the outer wheel turn faster than the inner one on bends.

The gears on a **bicycle** are also a gear system made of sprockets and a chain. In a low gear it is easier to get up a hill, but you have to pedal faster. In mechanical clocks, tiny gearwheels make sure the hands move at exactly the right speed. Wind turbines often have a gearbox that speeds up the slow rotation of the rotor for the generator. Blenders, drills and escalators also contain gears.

begriffe.erklaerung: How many times something turns per minute.
How much force there is in a rotation.
Ratio by which a gearbox changes the speed.
Outer wheel of a planetary gear with teeth on the inside.
Gear that lets wheels turn at different speeds on bends.

gewusst: With a worm gear, a small motor can move a heavy gate.
Without a differential, a car's tyres would scrub on every bend.
The roughly 2,000-year-old Antikythera mechanism already contained many small gearwheels.

teile.einleitung: When crossing the ten, you calculate past a whole ten, for example in 8 + 5. You first go to the next tens number and then carry on. This calculation trick makes difficult sums easy and is one of the most important steps in arithmetic in the first years of school.
wichtigste: You cross the ten when the result goes past the next ten.
You first calculate up to 10 and then carry on with the rest.
To do this you split a number into two parts.
For 8 + 5 you split the 5 into 2 and 3.
In subtraction, too, you first go back to the ten.
Well-learned number bonds to ten help you calculate quickly.

abschnitte.text: You are **crossing the ten** when you have to go past a tens number such as 10, 20 or 40 while calculating. With 8 + 7 you go past 10 and land on 15. With 23 + 4, on the other hand, you stay in the same ten, so there is no crossing. Children usually learn about crossing the ten in their first and second years at school.

The most important trick is **splitting**. With 8 + 5, 8 is still 2 short of 10, so you split the 5 into 2 and 3. You work out 8 + 2 = 10 and then 10 + 3 = 13. For 9 + 4 you work out 9 + 1 + 3 and also get 13. For 7 + 6 you split the 6 into 3 and 3 and get 13.

Two numbers that make 10 together are called **number bonds to ten** or partner numbers. These are 1 and 9, 2 and 8, 3 and 7, 4 and 6, and 5 and 5. If you know them by heart, you can see at once how much is missing to 10. It works the same with bigger numbers: 38 is 2 short of 40, so for 38 + 5 you work out 38 + 2 + 3 = 43.

There is crossing the ten in subtraction too. For 14 minus 6 you first take away 4 and land on 10; then you take away another 2 and get 8. For 15 minus 7 you work out 15 minus 5 = 10 and then 10 minus 2 = 8. For 62 minus 8 you first go back to 60 and then another 6, and the result is 54.

In lessons, **twenty frames**, bead frames or counters help to make the crossing visible. On a bead frame you first slide the beads of one row up to 10 and then take beads from the next row. Many materials are coloured in groups of five so that you can recognise amounts at a glance. In time you calculate without materials, just in your head.

begriffe.erklaerung: Calculating past a whole tens number.
Dividing a number into smaller parts, for example 5 into 2 and 3.
Two numbers that make 10 together.
A frame with 20 dots in two rows of 10.

gewusst: Adults also use the method of going via 10 in mental arithmetic, often without noticing.
There are only five pairs of number bonds to ten if you ignore the order.
Crossing the ten is linked to our decimal system; in other number systems the boundary would be somewhere else.

teile.einleitung: The incandescent light bulb is an electric lamp in which a thin wire gets so hot that it glows. In German it is called a “Birne” (pear) because its glass bulb looks like a pear. For over 100 years it was the most important source of light in homes all over the world.
wichtigste: In a light bulb a thin wire glows; this is the filament.
A light bulb needs electricity to shine.
Around 1879 Thomas Edison made the light bulb practical for everyone.
A light bulb gets hot because it turns most of its energy into heat.
LED lamps use much less electricity than light bulbs.
Before electric light, many street lamps burned gas.
In German the light bulb is called a “Glühbirne” because it looks like a pear (“Birne”).

abschnitte.text: When **electricity** flows through the very thin wire, it gets hotter than 2,000 degrees and starts to glow brightly. This wire is called the **filament** and today is usually made of tungsten, a metal that only melts at about 3,400 degrees. To stop the wire burning up, the glass bulb contains not normal air but a protective gas or a vacuum. Over time the wire gets thinner until it burns through. Then the bulb has blown.

Even before Edison, several inventors built light bulbs, for example the Englishman **Joseph Swan**. But their lamps only lasted a short time. Around 1879 the American **Thomas Edison** presented a light bulb with a filament made of carbonised fibre that burned long enough. He also built power stations and wires so that the lamps could get electricity at all. In this way electric light became practical for everyone.

Before the light bulb, people used candles, oil lamps and paraffin lamps. In the 19th century many **gas lamps** lit up the cities. A lamplighter went through the streets in the evening and lit them. Open flames were dangerous and caused fires again and again. Electric light made life in the evening safer and brighter.

A light bulb turns only about 5 per cent of its energy into light; the rest becomes **heat**. That is why it gets so hot when it is on that you can burn your fingers on it. Because it wastes so much electricity, most classic light bulbs have not been allowed to be sold in Switzerland and the EU since about 2012. Special lamps that can withstand heat are still available for ovens.

Today most lighting comes from **LED lamps**. LED stands for light-emitting diode, a component made of semiconductors. For the same amount of light, an LED lamp uses about 80 to 90 per cent less electricity than a light bulb. It also lasts much longer, often more than 15,000 hours. Even so, the light bulb is still a symbol of a good **idea**; you often see it in comics above a character's head.

begriffe.erklaerung: The thin wire in the light bulb that glows.
Metal with a very high melting point from which filaments are made.
Light-emitting diode, an economical light source made of semiconductor material.
A space with almost no air in it.

gewusst: In a fire station in California, a light bulb has been burning almost without a break since 1901.
Edison and his team tested thousands of materials before they found a long-lasting filament.
In comics, the light bulb symbol above someone's head means: someone has had an idea.

teile.einleitung: Homing pigeons are bred domestic pigeons that reliably fly back home from great distances. People used this ability for centuries to deliver messages, long before there were telephones and the internet.
wichtigste: Homing pigeons are especially good at finding their way home.
The pigeon carries the message in a small tube on its leg.
A homing pigeon can only take messages to its own home.
Pigeons live in a loft.
The ring on its leg shows who a homing pigeon belongs to.
In wartime homing pigeons were popular because they need neither electricity nor cables.
The Swiss Army had homing pigeons until the 1990s.
A pigeon race is a race flying home.

abschnitte.text: Homing pigeons are descended from the wild **rock dove** and have been bred over centuries for their homing instinct. They are strong fliers with great stamina and powerful breast muscles. A well-trained homing pigeon often flies at 60 to 80 kilometres per hour and can cover several hundred kilometres in a day. Every pigeon wears a **ring** on its leg with a number, which shows who it belongs to.

Exactly how homing pigeons find their way home has not yet been fully worked out. They probably use the position of the **sun** and the Earth’s **magnetic field** to find their way. Near home they also recognise landscapes, rivers and roads. The important thing is: a homing pigeon always flies back only to its own **loft**.

To send a message, the pigeons were first taken to the place from which you wanted to write. The message was written on thin paper and put into a small tube on the leg. Then the pigeon was released and took the message home. People used pigeons in this way even in ancient times, and in the 19th century, for example, Paul Julius Reuter’s news service sent stock market prices by pigeon.

In wars homing pigeons were valuable because they need neither electricity nor cables and can hardly be intercepted. In the First and Second World Wars they delivered many important messages, and some pigeons even received awards for it. The **Swiss Army** also had a pigeon service. It kept homing pigeons until the 1990s, when they were replaced by modern radio technology.

Today homing pigeons are kept mainly for sport. In a **pigeon race** many pigeons are taken together to a faraway place and released at the same time. The winner is the pigeon that flies home fastest. Today arrival is measured with electronic chips in the ring, and in Switzerland, too, there are clubs of pigeon fanciers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small house or room in which pigeons live.
The ability to find the way home from an unfamiliar area.
The wild pigeon from which all domestic pigeons are descended.
A ring on the leg with a number to identify the pigeon.
Someone who keeps animals and breeds them on purpose.

gewusst: In the First World War the homing pigeon Cher Ami saved almost 200 trapped soldiers with a message.
Around 1850 the news agency Reuters used homing pigeons to send news faster than the post.
Some homing pigeons find their way home even from more than 1000 kilometres away.

teile.einleitung: ETH Zurich, the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich, is one of the best-known universities in the world for engineering and natural sciences. It was opened by the Confederation in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic School. Many famous researchers, including several Nobel Prize winners, have studied or taught here.
wichtigste: ETH Zurich was opened in 1855 as the Federal Polytechnic School.
In 1950 ETH rented Konrad Zuse's Z4, one of the first working computers in continental Europe.
From 1956 ERMETH was in use, the first computer built at ETH itself.
Around 1980 Niklaus Wirth developed the Lilith workstation with a graphical interface and a mouse.
Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen graduated from ETH as a mechanical engineer in 1868.
ETH professor Wolfgang Pauli received the Nobel Prize in 1945 for the exclusion principle.
ETH runs the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre (CSCS) in Lugano.
Since 2009 the ETH spin-off Climeworks has been building plants that filter carbon dioxide directly from the air.

abschnitte.text: ETH Zurich is a federal university and, together with **EPFL** in Lausanne, belongs to the ETH Domain. Here you can study, for example, computer science, physics, chemistry, architecture, mechanical engineering or environmental sciences. More than 20,000 students from many countries are enrolled. In international rankings ETH is regularly among the best universities in Europe.

After the federal state was founded in 1848, Switzerland wanted its own technical university. In 1855 the **Federal Polytechnic School** opened, which later received the name ETH. The main building in the centre of Zurich was designed by the architect **Gottfried Semper**. Later the large **Hönggerberg** campus on the edge of the city was added.

Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen graduated from ETH as a mechanical engineer in 1868 and later discovered the rays named after him. **Albert Einstein** also studied here and later briefly taught as a professor. In 1945, as an ETH professor, the physicist **Wolfgang Pauli** received the Nobel Prize for the exclusion principle. In total, more than 20 Nobel Prize winners are connected with ETH.

In 1950 ETH rented the **Z4** built by the German inventor Konrad Zuse, one of the first working computers in continental Europe. From 1956 **ERMETH** was in use, the first computer that ETH had built itself. The computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** invented the programming language Pascal and around 1980 developed the Lilith workstation with a graphical interface and a mouse. Today ETH runs the national supercomputing centre **CSCS** in Lugano.

Every year many young companies, so-called **spin-offs**, emerge from ETH. One example is **Climeworks**, which since 2009 has been building plants that filter carbon dioxide directly from the air. Besides Zurich, ETH also has sites in other cities. The Department of Biosystems Science and Engineering (D-BSSE) is in Basel, and the CSCS is in Lugano.

begriffe.erklaerung: Old name for a university of technology.
World-famous award for outstanding achievements in science, literature and peace.
Very fast large computer for huge calculations, also called a supercomputer.
Young company founded out of a university.

gewusst: Albert Einstein failed the ETH entrance exam at his first attempt.
Konrad Zuse's Z4 was calculating in Zurich in the 1950s, when there were hardly any computers in continental Europe.
Niklaus Wirth of ETH invented the programming language Pascal, with which generations learnt to program.

teile.einleitung: Photolithography is a process that uses light to transfer tiny patterns onto a silicon disc. This is how the billions of transistors in computer chips are made. You can think of it as an extremely fine way of photographing blueprints.
wichtigste: In photolithography a pattern is transferred onto a wafer with light.
The wafer is covered with a light-sensitive layer, the photoresist.
The template with the pattern is called a photomask.
The shorter the wavelength of the light, the finer the structures can be.
DUV light at 193 nanometres is widespread; for the finest chips, EUV light is used.
The only maker of EUV machines for mass production is the Dutch company ASML (as of 2026).
A chip goes through many dozens of exposure steps before it is finished.

abschnitte.text: First a **wafer**, a thin disc of silicon, is coated with **photoresist**. Then light is shone through a **photomask**, which contains the desired pattern. Lenses shrink the pattern greatly and project it onto the resist. Where light falls, the resist changes chemically. In this way the pattern is “photographed into” the resist.

After exposure the resist is developed, rather like a photo film in the past. With a **positive resist**, the exposed areas are dissolved and removed. With a negative resist it is the other way round: the exposed areas stay. In the uncovered areas, the material underneath can now be etched away or substances added. Then the remaining resist is removed, and the next step begins.

abschnitte.titel: The shorter the light, the finer
abschnitte.text: How small the structures can be depends on the **wavelength** of the light. According to the Rayleigh criterion, the smallest structure width is proportional to the wavelength divided by the numerical aperture of the lens. For a long time **DUV light** of 193 nanometres from an argon fluoride laser was used. In **immersion lithography**, ultrapure water sits between the lens and the wafer, which makes even finer patterns possible. An exposure machine that exposes the wafer field by field is called a stepper.

For the most modern chips, **extreme ultraviolet light** (EUV) with a wavelength of only 13.5 nanometres is used. It is produced when a powerful laser hits tiny droplets of tin. Because almost all materials strongly absorb EUV light, these machines work with **mirrors** instead of lenses and in a vacuum. The only maker of such machines for mass production is the company **ASML** from the Netherlands. An EUV machine is as big as a bus and costs several hundred million francs.

The word lithography means “stone writing”. Originally it referred to a **printing process** using stone plates that was invented around 1800. From the 1950s the idea was transferred to semiconductors using light. Since then the structures on chips have kept getting smaller. Today they are often many thousands of times thinner than a human hair.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin, round disc of silicon on which chips are made.
A light-sensitive layer that changes when exposed to light.
A template with the pattern that is transferred onto the wafer.
The distance between two crests of a light wave.
An extremely dust-free room in which chips are made.

gewusst: A single speck of dust on the wafer can make a whole chip useless, which is why people work in clean rooms wearing protective suits.
In an EUV machine, tens of thousands of tin droplets are fired at with a laser every second.
Rooms for photolithography are often lit yellow, because yellow light does not change the photoresist.

teile.einleitung: A battery is a small store of energy that produces electric current from chemical substances. It supplies torches, remote controls, watches and toys with electricity, even where there is no socket.
wichtigste: The current in a battery comes from chemical substances inside it.
A battery has a positive terminal and a negative terminal.
A small round battery of the AA type has 1.5 volts.
Wristwatches usually contain button cells.
The 9-volt battery has two snap connectors on top.
In Switzerland you take empty batteries back to the shop or to a collection point.
Button cells must be kept away from small children.

abschnitte.text: In a battery there are two different substances, the **electrodes**, separated by a conducting material, the **electrolyte**. The two substances react chemically with each other when the circuit is closed. In the process electrons travel from the **negative terminal** through the device to the **positive terminal**. So current flows until the substances are used up. An ordinary battery cannot then be recharged, unlike a rechargeable battery.

The most common is the round **AA** cell with 1.5 volts; the AAA is a little smaller. Larger cells such as C and D are found in powerful torches. The **9-volt battery** has the shape of a small cuboid with two snap connectors on top; you find it, for example, in smoke alarms. Watches, car keys and scales contain flat **button cells**. If you put a battery in the wrong way round, the device usually does not work.

At the end of the 18th century Luigi Galvani in Italy observed how frogs’ legs twitched when they touched metals. His fellow countryman **Alessandro Volta** found out that the current came from the metals. Around 1800 he built the **voltaic pile**, a stack of zinc and copper plates with soaked cardboard in between. That was the first battery in the world. The unit of voltage, the **volt**, is named after him.

Button cells are very dangerous for small children if they are swallowed. They can cause serious injuries in the gullet within a short time. That is why they are stored safely, and in an emergency you immediately call the emergency number or **Tox Info Suisse** on 145. It is also dangerous to connect batteries together or throw them into a fire.

Batteries contain metals and substances that can harm the **environment**. That is why they never belong in ordinary rubbish. In Switzerland every shop that sells batteries must take back empty batteries free of charge. Recycling is paid for by an **advance recycling fee** when you buy them. In recycling plants metals such as zinc, manganese and iron are recovered.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of electrical voltage.
One end of the battery, positive or negative.
A small, flat, round battery, for example for watches.
A substance inside the battery through which charged particles can move.
A closed path through which current can flow.

gewusst: The first battery in the world was a tower of metal plates and wet cardboard.
A battery slowly discharges by itself even in the cupboard, which is why there is often a use-by date on it.
Even a single swallowed button cell can be life-threatening for a toddler.

teile.einleitung: A radio cell is the area that a single mobile phone mast supplies with radio signal. A mobile network consists of thousands of these cells, lying next to each other like honeycomb. When you are on the move with your phone, you are passed from cell to cell without noticing.
wichtigste: A radio cell is the coverage area of a mobile phone aerial.
Mobile networks are divided into many cells so that the same frequencies can be used again in distant cells.
In planning models, radio cells are usually drawn as hexagons.
In cities radio cells are smaller, because many more people need capacity there at the same time.
A site with three directional aerials supplies three separate cells.
Very small cells in homes are called femtocells.
From the identifier of the radio cell, the network operator can work out the approximate location of a phone.
With cell breathing, the range of a cell shrinks when it is very busy.

abschnitte.text: Each **mobile phone aerial** supplies only a certain area with radio signal, the radio cell. A phone always connects to the cell with the best reception at that moment. It is then said to be **registered** there. If you move, for example on a train, the call is automatically passed to the next cell. This passing on is called **handover** and takes only fractions of a second.

Only a few **frequencies** are available for mobile phones. If a single huge aerial supplied a whole country, they would quickly be fully used. If the network is divided into many small cells, the same frequencies can be reused in cells that are far enough apart. In planning models cells are drawn as **hexagons**, because they fit together without gaps like honeycomb. The **cluster size** tells you over how many neighbouring cells the frequencies are spread before they repeat.

In cities radio cells are usually small, sometimes only a few hundred metres across. There very many people need capacity at the same time, for example at stations or in stadiums. In the countryside cells are much larger and can reach several kilometres. Very small cells are called microcells or picocells. **Femtocells** are run, for example, in a flat via the internet connection.

Many mobile phone sites have three **directional aerials** pointing in different directions. In this way a single mast supplies three separate cells; this is called **sectorisation**. This increases capacity without having to build new masts. When a cell is very busy, its range can shrink; this is called **cell breathing**. Neighbouring cells then take over some of the users.

Each radio cell has its own **identifier**. Because the network operator knows which cell a phone is registered in, it knows the phone's approximate location, even without GPS. In town this location is more accurate than in the countryside, because the cells are smaller. For emergency calls this helps the rescue services to find people faster. For data protection reasons, however, such data may only be handed over under strict rules.

In Switzerland, Swisscom, Sunrise and Salt run their own mobile networks with many thousands of aerials. Because of the mountains, especially many sites are needed so that valleys and tunnels are covered too. In long railway tunnels such as the Gotthard Base Tunnel, special aerials provide reception. Switzerland has strict **limits** on radiation from aerials.

begriffe.erklaerung: Area that a mobile phone aerial supplies with radio signal.
Automatic passing of a call to the next radio cell.
Very small radio cell, for example in a flat.
Dividing an aerial site into several separate cells.
Particular range of radio waves on which signals are sent.

gewusst: On a train journey from Zurich to Bern, a phone changes radio cell many times without you noticing.
The hexagons of radio cells exist only on paper; in reality the boundaries are irregular.
In a full football stadium, network operators sometimes put up extra aerials.

teile.einleitung: In mathematics the root is the inverse of raising to a power. The square root of 25 is 5, because 5 · 5 = 25. With roots you can, for example, work out the side length of a square from its area.
wichtigste: The square root of a number is the non-negative number which, multiplied by itself, gives that number.
The sign for the root is √.
The square root of 0.09 is 0.3, because 0.3 · 0.3 = 0.09.
In the real numbers you cannot take the square root of negative numbers.
The equation √x = −3 has no real solution.
There are also third, fourth and higher roots.
Roots can be written as powers with a fraction in the exponent.

abschnitte.text: The **square root** of a number a is the number which, multiplied by itself, gives a and is not negative. √16 = 4, because 4 · 4 = 16. The number under the root sign is called the **radicand**. Because a square root is never negative, the equation √x = −3 has no solution. Also, for every real number √(x²) = |x|, that is the absolute value of x.

Roots may be multiplied: √2 · √18 = √36 = 6. With adding you have to be careful, because √(16 + 9) = √25 = 5, but √16 + √9 = 7. Identical roots can be combined like identical things: because √8 = 2√2, √2 + √8 gives exactly 3√2. This trick is called **partly taking the root**.

As well as the square root there is the **cube root**, the third root: the cube root of 27 is 3, because 3 · 3 · 3 = 27. The fourth root of 81 is 3, because 3 · 3 · 3 · 3 = 81. Roots can also be written as powers: the square root of a is a to the power of 1/2. Similarly, a to the power of 3/4 means the fourth root of a³.

Many roots do not work out exactly. √2 is about 1.41421, and the decimal places never stop and do not repeat. Such numbers are called **irrational numbers**, because they cannot be written as a fraction. This was already discovered in ancient Greece, for example among the followers of Pythagoras, and it caused great astonishment at the time.

Almost 4000 years ago the Babylonians could calculate √2 astonishingly accurately, as a clay tablet with cuneiform writing shows. Today’s sign √ dates from the 16th century and was used by the German arithmetic master Christoph Rudolff. It is said to have developed from a decorated small r, for the Latin word **radix**, which means root. Today roots are simply worked out with a calculator.

If you want to make a square flower bed of 49 m², the root tells you that each side is 7 m long. With Pythagoras’ theorem you calculate lengths, such as the diagonal of a screen, and you need a root to do so. Roots also come up in physics, for example when calculating falling times. Engineers and architects use them every day.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number under the root sign.
A number made by multiplying a whole number by itself, for example 9 or 16.
A number that cannot be written as a fraction and whose decimal places never end, for example √2.
The distance of a number from zero; it is always positive or zero.

gewusst: The German word for root, Wurzel, translates the Latin radix, which also gave us the word radish.
√2 is exactly the ratio of the diagonal to the side in every square.
A chessboard has 64 squares, and √64 = 8 is the number of squares in each row.

teile.einleitung: Electric voltage is, so to speak, the “pressure” that drives electric current through a cable. Without voltage no current flows and no lamp lights up. It is measured in volts, named after the Italian scientist Alessandro Volta.
wichtigste: The symbol for voltage is U (in English often V), and the unit is the volt (V).
The unit volt is named after Alessandro Volta, who built the first battery around 1800.
A voltage arises when there is a difference in electric charge between two points.
A voltmeter is connected in parallel with the component.
A socket in Switzerland supplies 230 volts, a car battery 12 volts.
The SBB overhead line carries 15,000 volts, and the Swissgrid transmission network up to 380,000 volts.
Alternating voltage up to 50 volts counts as extra-low voltage and is largely harmless.

abschnitte.text: Electric voltage arises when there is more negative charge on one side than on the other, as at the two **terminals** of a battery. The charges “want” to even out, and if you connect them with a wire, current flows. You can imagine it like water in two tanks: the greater the difference in height, the more strongly the water flows. The voltage corresponds to this **difference in height**, and the current to the flowing water.

Alessandro Volta (1745 to 1827) was a physicist from Como in Italy. Around 1800 he stacked copper and zinc discs alternately, with cardboard soaked in salt water between them. This **voltaic pile** was the first battery that supplied current continuously. In his honour the unit of voltage is called the **volt**.

Voltage is measured with a **voltmeter** or a multimeter. You connect it **in parallel** with the component, that is, with one cable before and one cable after the component. In this way the device measures the difference between two points. In formulas voltage is written with the letter U, for example U = 230 V.

A small AA battery has 1.5 volts, a mobile phone battery about 3.7 volts and a car battery 12 volts. The socket in Switzerland supplies 230 volts of **alternating voltage**. The SBB overhead line above the tracks carries 15,000 volts. Swissgrid carries electricity over long distances at up to 380,000 volts, because less energy is lost in the lines at high voltage. A **lightning bolt** can even reach many millions of volts.

Alternating voltages above 50 volts can be dangerous for people; below that it is called **extra-low voltage**. That is why many toys run on batteries or small power supplies. You must never tinker with sockets and cables. High-voltage lines and railway overhead lines are deadly even without touching them, because the current can jump across as an **electric arc**. That is why you must never climb onto railway wagons or electricity pylons.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of electric voltage, abbreviated V.
A connection of a power source; there is a positive and a negative terminal.
A device is connected alongside the component, not into the line.
A voltage that constantly changes direction, as at the socket.
Low voltage up to 50 volts alternating voltage, which is considered largely harmless.

gewusst: A bird can sit calmly on a high-voltage line, because there is hardly any voltage between its two feet.
The electric eel can produce electric shocks of several hundred volts with its body.
Our heart and our brain also work with tiny electric voltages, which doctors can measure with an ECG.

teile.einleitung: In engineering, a spring is a component that changes shape under a force and then returns to its original shape. Springs are found in ballpoint pens, mattresses, cars and watches. They can store energy, cushion shocks or push things back.
wichtigste: A spring changes shape under a force and then springs back into shape.
Robert Hooke described how the stretch of a spring is proportional to the force.
The spring constant is given in newtons per metre.
A spring of 200 N/m needs a force of 10 N to stretch by 0.05 m.
A tensioned spring contains elastic energy.
In mechanical watches, the mainspring stores the energy for the drive.
If a steel spring is stretched far too much, it stays permanently deformed.

abschnitte.text: A spring is an **elastic** component, usually made of spring steel. If you press, pull or twist it, it gives way and builds up a counterforce. When you let go, it returns to its original shape. This property is called elasticity. Springs come in many shapes and sizes, from tiny watch springs to huge springs under railway carriages.

In the 17th century the English scientist **Robert Hooke** discovered that the stretch of a spring is proportional to the force. Double the force therefore means double the stretch. If a spring is stretched by 2 centimetres with 3 newtons, it stretches by 4 centimetres with 6 newtons. As a formula you write F = D times s, where D is the **spring constant** in newtons per metre. So a spring of 200 N/m needs 10 newtons for 0.05 metres.

The **coil spring** is a wire wound in a spiral and is the most common kind of spring. The **leaf spring** consists of several strips of steel lying on top of each other and is used in lorries and trailers. A spiral spring is rolled up flat like a snail. Disc springs look like small domed washers and can withstand very large forces. There are also gas springs, for example on office chairs or car tailgates.

A tensioned spring contains **elastic energy**. This energy is released when the spring relaxes. In a mechanical wristwatch, the wound **mainspring** stores the energy for the drive, often for more than a day. Wind-up toy cars, mousetraps and crossbows also use stored spring energy. Swiss watchmakers are famous for their fine watch springs.

A spring only behaves elastically up to a certain limit. If a steel spring is stretched far too much, it goes beyond the **elastic limit** and stays permanently deformed. Then Hooke's law no longer applies. Anyone who has ever pulled out a ballpoint pen spring knows this. Engineers therefore design springs so that they are never overloaded in everyday use.

In a car, coil springs or leaf springs cushion the bumps in the road, together with **shock absorbers**. Mattresses and sofas often contain many small springs. Clothes pegs, staplers, door handles and trampolines also work with springs. A spring balance also uses Hooke's law to measure weights.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability of a material to return to its shape after being deformed.
Tells you how stiff a spring is, given in newtons per metre.
Rule according to which the stretch of a spring is proportional to the force.
Energy stored in a tensioned spring.
Spring made of several strips of steel lying on top of each other.

gewusst: Robert Hooke first published his discovery as a Latin letter puzzle so that nobody could steal it.
With a spring balance you can measure weights, because the stretch matches the force exactly.
A trampoline often has more than a hundred springs all the way round.

teile.einleitung: The angle sum is the result of adding up all the interior angles of a shape. For a triangle it always comes to exactly 180°, whether it is acute, obtuse or right-angled. With this simple rule you can calculate missing angles without measuring them.
wichtigste: In every triangle the interior angles add up to 180°.
In every quadrilateral the angle sum is 360°.
For a polygon with n corners the formula is (n − 2) · 180°.
A pentagon therefore has an angle sum of 540°.
A triangle can never have two right angles.
An exterior angle of a triangle is as big as the two interior angles not next to it put together.
On a curved surface such as a sphere, the 180° rule does not apply.

abschnitte.text: An **interior angle** is an angle that lies inside a shape at a corner. If you add up all the interior angles, you get the **angle sum**. In a triangle it is always 180°, exactly as much as a straight angle, a straight line. This applies to tiny triangles in your exercise book just as much as to huge triangles on a football pitch.

You can try the rule out yourself with paper. Cut out a triangle, tear off the three corners and lay them next to each other. The three points together form a straight line, that is 180°. In geometry it is proved with a **parallel** to one side through the opposite corner. The Greek mathematician Euclid described this theorem more than 2000 years ago.

If you know two angles, you find the third by subtracting both from 180°. If one acute angle in a **right-angled triangle** measures 34°, the other measures 180° − 90° − 34° = 56°. In an **isosceles triangle** the two base angles are equal: with an angle of 40° at the top, each base angle measures 70°. If the base angles are 52° each, 76° is left for the top.

Every quadrilateral can be divided into two triangles with a diagonal, so its angle sum is 2 · 180° = 360°. A pentagon can be divided into three triangles and has 540°. In general, the formula for an **n-sided polygon** is (n − 2) · 180°. So a hexagon, like a honeycomb cell, has 720°, and in a regular hexagon each angle measures 120°.

If you extend one side of a triangle beyond a corner, an **exterior angle** is formed. Together with the interior angle at that corner it makes 180°. That is why it is as big as the other two interior angles together: with 50° and 60°, the exterior angle at the third corner measures 110°. If you add up all the exterior angles of a polygon, the result is always 360°, that is one whole turn.

abschnitte.titel: When the rule does not apply
abschnitte.text: The 180° rule only applies on a flat plane. If you draw a huge triangle on a **sphere**, for example on the Earth, the angle sum is greater than 180°. A triangle from the North Pole to two points on the equator can even have three right angles. Such geometries are important for pilots and for surveying the Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: An angle that lies inside a shape at a corner.
An angle outside a corner that together with the interior angle makes 180°.
The two equal angles on the base of an isosceles triangle.
An angle of exactly 180°; it looks like a straight line.

gewusst: If the angles of a triangle are in the ratio 1 : 2 : 3, they are 30°, 60° and 90°, so the triangle is right-angled.
On the globe a triangle can have three right angles and therefore an angle sum of 270°.
With the angle sum you can check whether a drawing shows a possible triangle at all.

teile.einleitung: An iron is a household appliance used to smooth creases out of clothes and cloths. It uses heat, pressure and often steam too, so that the washing looks nice and smooth again.
wichtigste: With an iron you smooth out creases.
The hot, smooth surface underneath is called the soleplate.
In a steam iron the steam comes from water in the tank.
You iron the washing on an ironing board.
The dots in the ironing symbol on the label show how hot you may iron.
Three dots mean the highest temperature.
In the past irons were often heated with glowing charcoal.
During a break you stand the iron upright so that the hot soleplate does not burn anything.

abschnitte.text: Textile fibres consist of long, tiny threads that bend when they are washed and worn. **Heat** and moisture make the fibres soft and flexible. The weight and pressure of the iron then press them flat. As they cool down, the fibres stay in the smooth shape.

abschnitte.titel: How an iron is made up
abschnitte.text: An electric iron contains a **heating element** that warms the **soleplate**. A control with a thermostat makes sure that the set temperature is kept. In a **steam iron**, water from a small tank drips onto the hot soleplate, where it turns to steam. The steam flows through small holes in the soleplate straight into the fabric.

On the label in clothes you will find a small iron symbol. The **dots** in it show how hot you may iron: one dot stands for a low temperature, for example for synthetic fibres, and two dots for a medium one, for example for wool and silk. Three dots mean the highest temperature, which is suitable for cotton and linen. If the iron is crossed out, the garment must not be ironed at all.

Centuries ago people were already smoothing fabrics with heated metal tools. Heavy cast-iron irons were put on the stove, or hollow **charcoal irons** were filled with glowing charcoal. That was hard work, because the iron cooled down quickly or became too hot and left soot. At the end of the 19th century the first electric irons appeared, which made ironing much easier.

An iron gets hotter than 200 degrees Celsius, so you have to be careful. You iron on a stable **ironing board** with a heat-resistant cover. During a break you stand the appliance upright so that the hot soleplate does not burn anything. Children should only iron with adults, and after use you always pull out the plug.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hot, smooth underside of the iron.
A part that turns electricity into heat.
A control that keeps a set temperature constant.
A sign on the label that shows how to treat a garment.
A padded table on which you iron.

gewusst: The name “iron” is a reminder that in the past these appliances really were made entirely of iron.
Many modern irons switch themselves off automatically if they have not been moved for a while.
With an iron you can also transfer iron-on pictures onto T-shirts or fuse fuse beads together.

teile.einleitung: Bandwidth tells you how wide the range of frequencies is that a signal or a line can use. In everyday life it is often also used to mean how much data per second flows over an internet connection, for example.
wichtigste: In the physical sense, bandwidth is measured in hertz.
The classic analogue telephone transmits roughly frequencies from 300 to 3400 Hz.
The 3 dB bandwidth of a filter is the range in which the power drops to no less than half.
According to Nyquist, an ideal channel with bandwidth B can transmit at most 2 · B symbols per second.
According to Shannon and Hartley, a channel with 3 kHz bandwidth and a signal-to-noise ratio of 1000 has a capacity of about 30 kbit/s.
A file of 1 gigabyte needs at least 8 seconds over a 1 Gbit/s line.
Medium-wave transmitters in Europe have a channel spacing of 9 kHz.

abschnitte.text: Every signal, whether music, radio or data, is made of oscillations with different **frequencies**. The bandwidth is the distance between the lowest and the highest frequency that a signal contains or a device can transmit. It is measured in **hertz**, that is oscillations per second. One example is the classic analogue telephone, which transmits roughly frequencies from 300 to 3400 Hz, giving a bandwidth of about 3.1 kHz.

Electronic **filters** let only certain frequencies through. The limit is not sharp, though; the power falls off gradually. That is why the **3 dB bandwidth** is defined as the range in which the power drops to no less than half. A drop of 3 decibels corresponds roughly to halving the power.

The engineer Harry Nyquist showed that an ideal channel with bandwidth B can transmit at most **2 · B symbols** per second without errors. Claude Shannon and Ralph Hartley worked out how **noise** limits the amount of data. According to their formula, a channel with 3 kHz bandwidth and a signal-to-noise ratio of 1000 has a capacity of about 30 kbit/s. The more bandwidth and the less noise, the more data fits through.

In everyday life people talk about bandwidth when they mean the **data rate** of an internet connection, for example 100 Mbit/s or 1 Gbit/s. Here you need to remember that 1 byte consists of 8 bits. A file of 1 gigabyte therefore needs at least 8 seconds over a 1 Gbit/s line. In Switzerland some fibre-optic connections already offer 10 Gbit/s or more.

In radio many transmitters have to share the available frequencies. Medium-wave transmitters in Europe, for example, are given channels with a spacing of 9 kHz. Because frequencies are scarce and valuable, people try to pack as much data as possible into little bandwidth. **Spectral efficiency** tells you how much data rate a method achieves per hertz of bandwidth, and modern mobile networks such as 5G are very good at this.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number of oscillations per second, measured in hertz.
The unit of frequency; 1 hertz means one oscillation per second.
Random interference that is laid over a signal.
The amount of data transmitted per second, for example in Mbit/s.
A unit used to express ratios of power or loudness.

gewusst: Because the telephone only transmits up to about 3400 Hz, voices on the telephone sound thinner than in real life.
Internet providers give speeds in bits, but file sizes are usually shown in bytes, which is why a download takes longer than you might first think.
Claude Shannon is regarded as the father of information theory.

teile.einleitung: Doping means deliberately adding tiny amounts of foreign atoms to a semiconductor such as silicon. This changes how well the material conducts electricity. Without doping there would be no diodes, transistors, computer chips or solar cells.
wichtigste: In doping, foreign atoms are built into a semiconductor crystal.
A silicon atom has 4 valence electrons.
Donor atoms with 5 valence electrons make silicon n-type.
Acceptors such as boron take up an electron and so create holes.
In a p-doped semiconductor the holes, also called defect electrons, are in the majority.
In ion implantation, dopant atoms are shot into the wafer with high energy.
Afterwards the wafer is heated to repair damage to the crystal and activate the dopant atoms.

abschnitte.text: Pure silicon conducts electricity only poorly; it is called an **intrinsic semiconductor**. It conducts only through intrinsic conduction, that is, through a few electrons that break free because of heat. If you add tiny amounts of other atoms, the conductivity rises sharply. These foreign atoms are called **dopant atoms**. Often one foreign atom per million silicon atoms is enough.

A silicon atom has 4 **valence electrons**, with which it bonds to its neighbours. If you build in an atom with 5 valence electrons, such as phosphorus or arsenic, one electron is left over. It can move freely and carry current. Such atoms are called **donors**, because they donate an electron, and the material becomes n-type.

If instead you build in an atom with only 3 valence electrons, for example **boron**, one electron is missing from the bond. This gap is called a **hole** or defect electron. A neighbouring electron can jump into it, and the hole moves on as if it were a positive charge. Such foreign atoms are called **acceptors**, and the material becomes p-type.

In the chip factory the work is done on thin silicon discs, the **wafers**. In **ion implantation**, charged dopant atoms are shot into the wafer in a targeted way with high energy. This damages the crystal, so it is then heated strongly. During this annealing the atoms arrange themselves again and the dopant atoms are activated. An older method is diffusion, in which the atoms move into the crystal at high temperature.

Where a p-doped and an n-doped region meet, a **p-n junction** forms. It is the heart of every diode, every light-emitting diode and every solar cell. Transistors in computer chips consist of several layers that are doped differently. A modern processor contains billions of such tiny regions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The outermost electrons of an atom, which are responsible for bonds.
A foreign atom that gives off an extra free electron.
A foreign atom that takes up an electron and so creates a hole.
A thin, round disc of silicon from which computer chips are made.

gewusst: Even a single foreign atom per million silicon atoms can increase the conductivity enormously.
A hole is really just a missing electron, but it behaves like a positive particle.
Silicon is obtained from quartz sand, one of the most common substances on Earth.

teile.einleitung: Auguste Piccard was a Swiss physicist and inventor who was one of the first people to fly into the stratosphere in a balloon. Later he built submersibles with which people could reach the deepest parts of the oceans.
wichtigste: Auguste Piccard was born in 1884 in Basel and died in 1962 in Lausanne.
He had a twin brother called Jean, who also became a scientist.
He studied at ETH Zurich.
In 1931 he flew almost 16 kilometres high into the stratosphere in a balloon.
In 1932 he set off from Dübendorf on his second high-altitude flight.
He built the deep-sea submersible Trieste.
Hergé used him as the model for Professor Calculus in the Tintin comics.

abschnitte.text: Auguste Piccard was born **in 1884 in Basel**, together with his twin brother **Jean**. Both studied at **ETH Zurich** and became scientists. Auguste became a physicist and from 1922 worked as a professor at the university in Brussels. He was tall and thin and had striking glasses and wild hair. He died in 1962 in Lausanne.

Piccard wanted to study **cosmic rays** at great heights. For this he built a huge hydrogen balloon with an airtight **pressurised cabin** made of aluminium in the shape of a ball. The ball was necessary because the air up there is far too thin to breathe. On 27 May 1931 he set off from Augsburg with his assistant Paul Kipfer and reached a height of almost 16 kilometres. This made the two of them among the first people in the **stratosphere**.

In August 1932 Piccard set off again, this time from **Dübendorf** airfield near Zurich. Together with Max Cosyns he climbed to more than 16 kilometres and set a new record. The two landed safely in northern Italy. The flights showed that people can survive at great heights in a pressurised cabin. This was later important for aircraft and space travel.

After that Piccard turned to the **deep sea**. He transferred the idea of his balloon to the water and invented the **bathyscaphe**, a submersible with a pressure sphere beneath a float. His submersible **Trieste** was built in Italy in 1953. In 1960 his son Jacques Piccard dived in it with Don Walsh into the Mariana Trench, almost 11 kilometres deep. That was the deepest point of the world’s oceans.

The Belgian cartoonist **Hergé** knew Piccard from Brussels. He used him as the model for the absent-minded inventor **Professor Calculus** in the Tintin comics. Hergé, however, drew the character smaller, because the real Piccard would not have fitted into the pictures. In this way Piccard also became world-famous among children.

The love of adventure stayed in the family. His son **Jacques Piccard** built a tourist submarine for Lake Geneva for Expo 64 in Lausanne. His grandson **Bertrand Piccard** flew round the Earth non-stop in a balloon in 1999. Later he flew round the world in the solar-powered aircraft **Solar Impulse** without a single drop of fuel.

begriffe.erklaerung: A layer of the atmosphere from about 10 to 15 kilometres up, in which the air is very thin.
An airtight cabin in which the air pressure is enough to breathe.
A deep-sea submersible with a pressure sphere that works like an underwater balloon.
Very high-energy particles that reach the Earth from space.

gewusst: Three generations of the Piccard family set records in the air or in the water.
In the comic Professor Calculus is smaller than Piccard, because the real scientist was very tall.
At take-off Piccard’s balloon was limp and only swelled into a big ball high up.

teile.einleitung: A number word is a word that expresses a number or an amount, such as eleven, thirty or thousand. With number words we count, give orders of things or say how often something happens. Every language has its own number words, and some of them are quite surprising.
wichtigste: In grammar number words are also called numerals.
Cardinal numbers such as one, two, three say how many there are.
Ordinal numbers such as the first or the second give an order.
In German, for two-digit numbers the units are said first, for example “einundzwanzig” (one and twenty) for 21.
In German, numbers below a million are written as one word.
In Switzerland the German word “dreissig” (thirty) is written with a double s.
In French three is “trois”, and in English five is “five”.

abschnitte.text: Number words name numbers and amounts. The most important are the **cardinal numbers**: one, two, three up to thousand, million and billion. There are also indefinite number words such as many, few or some. They say roughly how much there is, but not exactly.

**Ordinal numbers** show an order, for example in a race: the first, the second, the third. In German they are written as a digit with a full stop, so 2. for “zweite” (second); in English you write 2nd. Fraction words such as a third or a quarter describe parts of a whole. Words such as double, threefold or twice say how often something occurs.

In German the numbers from 13 to 19 end in “zehn” (ten), as in “siebzehn” (seventeen), where “sieben” (seven) becomes “sieb”. In two-digit numbers the units come first, joined with “und” (and): 21 is “einundzwanzig”. All numbers below a million are written together in German, even long ones such as “dreihundertfünfundzwanzig” (325). In Switzerland German is written without the letter Eszett (the “sharp s”), so **“dreissig”** for 30.

In Switzerland’s national languages numbers sound different: three is “trois” in French, “tre” in Italian and “trais” in Romansh. In English five is “five”. In French-speaking Switzerland people say **“septante”** for 70 and “nonante” for 90, but in France “soixante-dix” and “quatre-vingt-dix”. For 80 people say “huitante” in the cantons of Vaud, Valais and Fribourg.

In some Swiss German dialects the number two has different forms depending on the **gender** of the noun, for example “zwee Manne” (two men), “zwo Froue” (two women) and “zwöi Chind” (two children). In standard German people sometimes say “zwo” instead of “zwei” on the telephone so that it is not confused with “drei” (three). The words dozen for twelve and pair for two are also old words for amounts.

After thousand in German come “Million”, “Milliarde”, “Billion” and “Billiarde”. Careful: the English word billion means only a German **“Milliarde”**, that is 1000 million, whereas a German “Billion” is a million million. Many number words are very old and similar in related languages, such as “drei”, three and “tres”. From this, linguists can tell that these languages have a common origin.

begriffe.erklaerung: A number word that gives an amount, such as five or hundred.
A number word that gives an order, such as the third.
The technical term in grammar for a number word.
A number word for a part of a whole, such as a quarter.

gewusst: The longest German number word below a million is “siebenhundertsiebenundsiebzigtausendsiebenhundertsiebenundsiebzig” (777,777).
The German number “elf” (eleven) comes from an old word meaning something like “one left over”, that is one over ten.
A German “Milliarde” is called a billion in English, which often leads to mistakes in translations.

teile.einleitung: An electric motor is a machine that converts electrical energy into energy of movement. To do this it uses the force of magnets and electricity. Electric motors are found in trains, electric cars, washing machines, fans and even electric toothbrushes.
wichtigste: An electric motor converts electrical energy into energy of movement.
The fixed part of an electric motor is called the stator, the rotating part is called the rotor.
In a direct current motor, the commutator keeps reversing the direction of the current in the rotating part.
Michael Faraday discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831.
A generator does the opposite and produces electric current from rotation.
Almost all SBB trains today are driven by electric motors.
Electric motors usually use over 90 per cent of their energy for movement.

abschnitte.text: When current flows through a wire, a **magnetic field** forms around it. If you wind the wire into a coil, it becomes a strong **electromagnet**. Magnets attract or repel each other, depending on which poles face each other. It is exactly these forces that make an electric motor turn.

abschnitte.titel: How an electric motor is built
abschnitte.text: An electric motor consists of two main parts. The fixed part is called the **stator**, the rotating part is called the **rotor**. The magnetic fields of the stator and rotor repel and attract each other, so the rotor turns. In a direct current motor, the **commutator** makes sure the direction of the current in the rotor always changes at the right moment so that the rotation does not stop.

A **generator** works like an electric motor, only the other way round. If you turn its rotor, it produces electric current. This is based on **electromagnetic induction**, which Michael Faraday discovered in 1831. In hydropower stations, flowing water drives huge generators, and electric cars recharge their battery when braking because the motor then works as a generator.

As early as 1821, **Michael Faraday** showed in London that a wire carrying current can rotate around a magnet. In 1834 Moritz Hermann Jacobi built one of the first practically usable electric motors in Königsberg. Towards the end of the 19th century the first electric trams ran. In Baden, Charles Brown and Walter Boveri founded the company **Brown, Boveri & Cie.** in 1891, which soon built electric motors, generators and locomotives worldwide.

Electric motors are quiet, clean and very efficient; they often use more than 90 per cent of their energy for movement. That is why almost all **SBB** trains are driven by electric motors. **Electric cars**, e-bikes, trams and cable cars also run on electricity. At home, electric motors are found in vacuum cleaners, blenders, fridges and hairdryers.

Electric motors produce no exhaust fumes when running. If the electricity comes from water, sun or wind, they are especially climate-friendly. That is why they are replacing more and more petrol and diesel engines. Many modern motors work with strong **permanent magnets** made of special metals, the rare earths.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fixed part of an electric motor.
Rotating part of an electric motor.
Component that reverses the direction of the current in the rotor of a direct current motor.
Machine that produces electric current from rotation.
The creation of current by a changing magnetic field.

gewusst: A modern smartphone contains a tiny electric motor that makes it vibrate.
The famous Swiss locomotive “Crocodile” was built around 1920 for the Gotthard line.
A petrol engine uses only about a third of its energy for movement, whereas an electric motor uses most of it.

teile.einleitung: An analogue-to-digital converter, ADC for short, turns a continuous electrical signal into numbers that a computer can process. It is found in almost every digital device, from the smartphone microphone to the digital camera. Without it, computers could not measure the real, analogue world.
wichtigste: An ADC converts an analogue voltage into a digital numerical value.
The signal is measured at regular intervals; this is called sampling.
The resolution in bits decides how many steps there are: 12 bits give 4096 steps.
Rounding to the nearest step produces the quantisation error.
Flash converters are the fastest but need a great many comparators.
Successive approximation converters find the value bit by bit, as in a binary search.
A sample-and-hold circuit keeps the voltage constant during conversion.

abschnitte.text: An **analogue signal** can take any value at all, like the voltage of a microphone picking up sound. A **digital signal**, on the other hand, consists only of numbers with fixed steps. The ADC is the bridge between the two worlds. The counterpart that turns numbers back into voltage is called a digital-to-analogue converter and is found, for example, in headphone outputs.

The ADC does not measure the signal continuously but at regular intervals of time; this is called **sampling**. The number of measurements per second is called the sampling rate. According to the sampling theorem, you must measure at least twice as often as the highest frequency in the signal.
