Because people can hear sounds up to about 20,000 hertz, the audio CD uses a sampling rate of 44.1 kilohertz.

The **resolution** says with how many bits a measured value is stored. With n bits there are 2 to the power of n steps: 10 bits give 1024 steps, 12 bits already 4096. In a 10-bit converter with a measuring range of 0 to 5 volts, one step is about 4.9 millivolts. Because the real value is rounded to the nearest step, a small **quantisation error** arises, which shows up as a quiet noise.

The **flash converter** compares the voltage with many thresholds at the same time and is therefore the fastest, but for n bits it needs about 2 to the power of n comparators. The **successive approximation** converter homes in on the value bit by bit, rather like a number-guessing game with the clues higher or lower. So that the voltage does not change in the meantime, a sample-and-hold circuit briefly holds it. For very accurate audio measurements delta-sigma converters are often used.

The amount of data follows from the sampling rate and the resolution. For stereo audio at 44.1 kilohertz and 16 bits, it is 44,100 · 16 · 2, that is about 1411 kilobits per second. According to the rule of thumb 6.02 · n + 1.76 dB, an ideal 16-bit converter achieves a signal-to-noise ratio of about 98 decibels. The more bits, the quieter the noise compared with the signal.

ADCs are found in smartphones, where they convert speech from the microphone. In digital cameras they turn the brightness of each pixel into numbers. Digital thermometers, scales, heart rate monitors and laboratory measuring instruments work with them too. In cars, too, many sensors measure in analogue form and send the values to the on-board computer via an ADC.

begriffe.erklaerung: Continuous; a signal can take any value in between.
Shown in numbers with fixed steps, usually as zeros and ones.
How many times per second a signal is measured.
The smallest unit of information; it can be 0 or 1.
A circuit that compares two voltages and says which is greater.

gewusst: A single smartphone contains several analogue-to-digital converters, for example for the microphone, camera and sensors.
The audio CD’s sampling rate of 44.1 kilohertz has to do with the way sound data used to be stored on video tapes.
An 8-bit flash converter already needs 255 comparators.

teile.einleitung: A hard disk drive, HDD for short, is a computer storage device that stores data magnetically on fast-spinning discs. Photos, videos and programs stay stored on it even when the computer is switched off. Today hard disks are often replaced by SSDs, but they are still very important for large amounts of data.
wichtigste: A hard disk stores data magnetically on spinning discs.
A read-write head reads and writes the data.
The figure 7200 rpm means that the discs turn 7,200 times per minute.
A hard disk is non-volatile storage and keeps its data without electricity.
IBM brought out the first hard disk in 1956.
Knocks during operation can damage the disc.
Per gigabyte, hard disks are usually cheaper than SSDs.

abschnitte.text: A hard disk drive is a device that stores data permanently. In English it is called a hard disk drive, **HDD** for short. It is **non-volatile storage**, so the data is kept even without electricity. By contrast, the working memory, RAM, loses its data when switched off. Hard disks are found in computers, servers and external storage devices.

In a tightly sealed case, one or more shiny discs spin; these are the **platters**. Their surface is coated with a thin magnetic layer. A tiny **read-write head** hovers on an arm just above the disc. It magnetises tiny areas that stand for the ones and zeros of the data, and later reads them out again. Usual speeds are 5,400 or 7,200 revolutions per minute.

The gap between the head and the disc is much smaller than the thickness of a hair. If a laptop with a hard disk is dropped while running, the head can touch and damage the spinning disc. This is called a **head crash**, and data is often lost. That is why many laptops have a sensor that moves the head to safety in a fall. You should always keep an extra **backup** of important data.

In 1956 the company IBM brought out the first hard disk, the **IBM 350** system. It was as big as a wardrobe and had 50 large discs. Even so, only about 5 megabytes fitted on it, less than a single mobile phone photo today. Since then hard disks have become much smaller and their storage space millions of times larger. Modern hard disks hold many terabytes.

An **SSD** stores data in memory chips and has no moving parts. It is faster, quieter and less sensitive to knocks. Hard disks, on the other hand, are usually still cheaper per gigabyte. That is why they are often used for large amounts of data, for example in data centres or for backups. If you count 1 terabyte as 1,000 gigabytes, 2 terabytes are exactly 2,000 gigabytes.

begriffe.erklaerung: Abbreviation for hard disk drive.
Tiny component that writes data onto the disc and reads it from it.
Storage that keeps data even without electricity.
Storage made of chips with no moving parts.
Large unit of storage, usually counted as 1,000 gigabytes.

gewusst: The first hard disk of 1956 weighed about a tonne and stored only about 5 megabytes.
The read head hovers on a wafer-thin cushion of air above the spinning disc.
At the outer edge of a disc, the data races past under the head at over 100 kilometres per hour.

teile.einleitung: A time zone is an area of the Earth in which the same clock time applies everywhere. Because the Earth turns, the sun does not rise everywhere at the same time, which is why, for example, it is already evening in Tokyo when it is only midday in Zurich. Switzerland belongs to Central European Time.
wichtigste: The Earth turns once on its axis in 24 hours, that is 15 degrees of longitude per hour.
Time zones are based on Coordinated Universal Time, UTC.
In winter Switzerland uses Central European Time, CET, which is UTC+1.
In summer Switzerland puts the clock forward by one hour to summer time, CEST, that is UTC+2.
Going east the clocks are put forward, going west they are put back.
At the date line in the Pacific the date changes.
Time zones often follow national borders and not exactly the lines of longitude.

abschnitte.text: The Earth turns once on its axis in 24 hours, that is 360 degrees. If you divide 360 by 24, you get **15 degrees** per hour. Where the sun is at its highest, it is midday, and this keeps moving westwards. That is why the Earth was divided into zones, in each of which a shared clock time applies.

In the past every town had its own local time based on the position of the sun. With the **railways** in the 19th century this became a problem, because timetables were confusing. In 1884, at a conference in Washington, countries agreed that the prime meridian runs through the observatory at Greenwich near London. Time zones are counted from there today.

In winter Switzerland uses **Central European Time**, CET, which is one hour ahead of Universal Time, UTC. On the last Sunday in March the clocks are put forward by one hour to summer time, and on the last Sunday in October they are put back again. Voters rejected summer time in a popular vote in 1978, but Switzerland introduced it anyway in 1981. Otherwise the country would have been a time island surrounded by neighbours using summer time.

You can do lots of maths with time zones. In winter London is one hour behind Zurich, so it is 14:00 there when it is 15:00 in Zurich. Tokyo is in UTC+9, so in winter it is 8 hours ahead of Zurich: at 10:00 in Zurich it is 18:00 there. In winter New York is in UTC−5, so 6 hours behind Zurich, and at 18:00 in Zurich it is 12:00 there. If a flight leaves Zurich at 13:00, takes 9 hours and the destination is 6 hours behind, it lands at 16:00 **local time**.

Roughly along the 180th line of longitude in the middle of the Pacific runs the **International Date Line**. Anyone crossing it westwards jumps forward one day; anyone travelling east experiences a day twice. The line bends so that island nations are not split into two days. That is why some Pacific islands are the first in the world to celebrate New Year.

Not all time zones are shifted by whole hours: India is at UTC+5:30 and Nepal even at UTC+5:45. China is as wide as several time zones, but uses only one single time throughout the country. Russia, on the other hand, has eleven time zones. Because of its overseas territories on several continents, France has the most time zones of any country.

begriffe.erklaerung: Coordinated Universal Time, on which all time zones are based.
Central European Time, Switzerland’s winter time, one hour ahead of UTC.
The time in summer, for which the clock is put forward by one hour.
An imaginary line in the Pacific at which the date changes.
The clock time that applies at a particular place at the moment.

gewusst: Anyone flying east round the world from Zurich has to put their watch forward by 24 hours altogether on the way and gets a day back at the date line.
At the South Pole all the lines of longitude, and so all the time zones, meet; the research stations there simply choose a time.
Because of the date line there are hours every day during which three different calendar dates apply on Earth at the same time.

teile.einleitung: A magic triangle is a maths puzzle in the shape of a triangle in which every side must give the same sum. The numbers are in boxes at the corners and along the sides. Whoever finds the missing numbers has made the triangle magic.
wichtigste: In a magic triangle the sum is the same on all three sides.
A simple magic triangle has 6 boxes, three at the corners and three in the middle of the sides.
A number in a corner counts for two sides, because two sides meet there.
Missing numbers are found by subtracting the known numbers from the side sum.
With the numbers 1 to 6, the side sums 9, 10, 11 and 12 are possible.
Magic triangles are relatives of magic squares.
They practise calculation and logical thinking at the same time.

abschnitte.titel: What a magic triangle looks like
abschnitte.text: A simple magic triangle has a box at each **corner** and a box in the middle of each side. That makes 6 boxes altogether. Each side consists of three boxes: two corners and one middle box. The numbers on each side add up to the same **side sum**.

If a number is missing on one side, you subtract the known numbers from the side sum. If the sum is 10 and there are 5 and 1, the 4 is missing. With a sum of 9 and 1 and 6, the 2 is missing; with 12 and 6 and 2, the 4 is missing. With 11 and 4 and 5, the 2 is missing, and with 20 and 10 and 4, the 6 is missing.

The numbers in the corners are especially important, because two sides meet there. Each **corner number** therefore counts towards two sides. If you put the smallest numbers in the corners, all the side sums become small. If you put the largest numbers in the corners, the side sums become large.

A classic task is: arrange the numbers 1 to 6 so that every side has the same sum. This works for the sums 9, 10, 11 and 12. For the sum 9, 1, 2 and 3 go in the corners; for 12, the numbers 4, 5 and 6. Such tasks develop **systematic trying out**.

Magic triangles belong to the family of **magic figures**. The best known is the magic square, in which all the rows, columns and diagonals have the same sum. A famous magic square is shown in the engraving Melencolia I by Albrecht Dürer from 1514. There are also larger magic triangles with four or more boxes on each side.

In Swiss primary schools magic triangles are a popular type of exercise. Even first-year pupils can puzzle with small numbers, while older children solve harder versions. They do lots of additions and subtractions without it feeling like an exercise. They also learn to spot **patterns** and to explain their solutions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number you get when you add up all the numbers on one side.
A number in a corner that belongs to two sides.
A square of numbers in which all the rows, columns and diagonals have the same sum.
Orderly and according to a plan, so that you do not forget anything.

gewusst: With the numbers 1 to 6 there are exactly four different possible side sums.
The oldest known magic square is said to come from China and is called Lo Shu.
In Albrecht Dürer’s magic square the year 1514 appears in the bottom row.

teile.einleitung: Energy engineering deals with how energy is obtained, converted, stored and brought to where it is needed. This includes power stations, power lines, batteries, solar panels and heat pumps. Because the world wants to move away from coal, oil and gas, energy engineering is especially important today.
wichtigste: Energy is never lost, it is only converted from one form into another.
In 2024 hydropower supplied about 60 per cent of Switzerland's domestic electricity production.
Commercial silicon solar modules reach an efficiency of about 20 per cent (as of 2025).
Nant de Drance in Valais is a pumped storage power station.
Electricity is transmitted over long distances at high voltage, because then there are fewer losses in the lines.
A heat pump with a coefficient of performance of 4 delivers 4 kWh of heat from 1 kWh of electricity.
In a hydrogen fuel cell, the only thing produced besides electricity is water.

abschnitte.text: According to the **law of conservation of energy**, energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it is only converted. A power station, for example, turns the energy of moving water into electrical energy. A part is always lost as heat that can no longer be used. **Efficiency** tells you what share of the energy is actually used.

Heat engines such as steam turbines can never turn heat completely into work. The highest possible efficiency is described by the **Carnot efficiency**, named after the Frenchman Sadi Carnot. It depends on the temperature difference: between 600 kelvin and 300 kelvin it is 50 per cent. Real machines always achieve a little less.

**Renewable energy** comes from sources that keep renewing themselves, such as water, sun, wind, biomass and geothermal heat. Silicon solar modules today convert about 20 per cent of sunlight into electricity (as of 2025). Wind turbines use the power of the wind, and **heat pumps** take heat from the air, water or ground. A heat pump with a coefficient of performance of 4 delivers a whole 4 kWh of heat from 1 kWh of electricity.

In Switzerland **hydropower** supplied about 60 per cent of domestic electricity production in 2024. On top of this come nuclear power stations such as Beznau, Gösgen and Leibstadt, and more and more solar panels. At 285 metres, the Grande Dixence dam in Valais is the highest gravity dam in the world. With the **Energy Strategy 2050**, which voters approved in 2017, Switzerland wants to phase out nuclear power step by step and expand renewable energy.

Electricity has to be produced exactly when it is needed, which is why storage is required. A **pumped storage power station** such as Nant de Drance in Valais pumps water into an upper lake when there is surplus electricity and lets it flow back down through turbines when needed. Batteries and hydrogen can also store energy. In a **fuel cell**, hydrogen reacts with oxygen, producing electricity and water.

Over long distances electricity is transmitted at **high voltage**, in Switzerland for example at 380,000 volts. For the same power, less current then flows and there are fewer losses in the lines. Electricity is paid for in **kilowatt hours**. A device with a power of 2 kW uses 6 kWh in 3 hours; at 30 centimes per kWh, that costs 1.80 francs.

begriffe.erklaerung: The share of the energy put in that is really used.
The amount of energy a 1,000-watt device uses in one hour.
Power station that stores energy by pumping water into a higher lake.
Device that takes heat from the surroundings and uses it for heating.
Energy from sources that do not run out, such as the sun or water.

gewusst: In about one hour the sun sends more energy to Earth than the whole of humanity uses in a year.
The caverns of Nant de Drance lie deep inside the mountain, so you can hardly see the big power station from outside.
A heat pump works like a fridge in reverse.

teile.einleitung: CERN near Geneva is one of the largest research centres in the world for particle physics. Thousands of researchers from many countries study there what everything in the universe is made of, and along the way the World Wide Web was even invented here.
wichtigste: CERN was officially founded in 1954.
The abbreviation originally stood for “Conseil européen pour la recherche nucléaire”.
The site is in Meyrin near Geneva, right on the border with France.
The largest particle accelerator is the Large Hadron Collider, with a circumference of about 27 kilometres.
In 1983 the W and Z bosons were discovered at CERN.
In 2012 the Higgs boson was detected at CERN.
In 2016 Fabiola Gianotti became the first woman Director-General of CERN.

abschnitte.text: CERN is the **European Organization for Nuclear Research**. The name comes from the French “Conseil européen pour la recherche nucléaire”. It was officially founded in **1954** so that European countries could do peaceful research together after the Second World War. Today it has more than 20 member states, including Switzerland. The headquarters is in **Meyrin** in the canton of Geneva, and part of the facilities extends into France.

At CERN tiny particles such as protons are brought almost to the speed of light in **particle accelerators**. Then they are made to collide, and huge **detectors** record what is produced. The largest accelerator is the **Large Hadron Collider** (LHC). Its ring-shaped tunnel is about 27 kilometres long and lies about 100 metres underground. Strong, very cold magnets keep the particles on their path.

In 1973 the neutral weak currents were discovered with the bubble chamber **Gargamelle**. In 1983 the **W and Z bosons** were found, for which Carlo Rubbia and Simon van der Meer received the Nobel Prize in 1984. Van der Meer had invented stochastic cooling for this, in order to collect enough antiprotons. In 1995 artificial **antihydrogen atoms** were produced for the first time at CERN. In 2012 the long-sought **Higgs boson** was detected.

In 1989 an invention that changed the world was made at CERN: the Briton **Tim Berners-Lee** developed the **World Wide Web** so that researchers could exchange information more easily. Georges Charpak received the Nobel Prize in 1992 for the multiwire proportional chamber, a particle detector. Technology from particle physics also helps in medicine today, for example in imaging and cancer treatment.

Thousands of people from all over the world work and do research together at CERN. In 2016 the Italian **Fabiola Gianotti** became the first woman Director-General. She had previously played an important part in detecting the Higgs boson. Since 2026 the Briton Mark Thomson has led CERN. The working languages are English and French.

Anyone who wants to visit CERN can go to the **Science Gateway** visitor centre. The building was designed by the Italian architect **Renzo Piano** and opened in 2023. There are exhibitions, experiments and workshops for school classes and families. Also well known is the **Globe of Science and Innovation**, a large wooden building in the shape of a sphere.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the smallest building blocks of matter.
A machine that makes tiny particles extremely fast.
A measuring device that records particles and their tracks.
A particle that explains why other particles have mass.
The counterpart of normal matter, in which the particles have the opposite charge.

gewusst: The very first website in the world ran on a computer at CERN.
The magnets in the LHC are colder than outer space between the stars.
The LHC tunnel passes under the border between Switzerland and France several times.

teile.einleitung: In assembly line production, a product moves on a belt from workstation to workstation. At each station someone always does the same task, until at the end the finished product comes out. This method became famous in 1913 through Henry Ford and his Model T car.
wichtigste: In assembly line production the workpiece moves while the workers stay at fixed places.
As early as 1901 Ransom E. Olds used an assembly line with fixed stations, but still without a moving belt.
In 1913 Henry Ford introduced the moving assembly line for his Model T.
This cut the assembly time of a Model T from about 12 hours to about 1.5 hours.
From 1908 to 1927 about 15 million Ford Model Ts were built.
The time allowed per task at a station is called the cycle time.
In 1936 Charlie Chaplin criticised monotonous assembly line work in the film “Modern Times”.

abschnitte.text: An **assembly line** is a moving belt or chain that carries workpieces onwards. Production is broken down into many small steps. Each person does only one step, for example tightening a screw or fitting a wheel. A fixed **cycle time** is available for each step, after which the workpiece moves on. This creates an even flow of work.

abschnitte.titel: Henry Ford and the Model T
abschnitte.text: The American car maker **Henry Ford** wanted to build a car that many families could afford. His engineers were inspired by the **slaughterhouses of Chicago**, where animal carcasses moved on hooks from worker to worker. In 1913 Ford introduced the moving belt at the Highland Park factory near Detroit. After that, assembling a Model T took only about 1.5 hours instead of about 12. The car became much cheaper as a result, and by 1927 about 15 million had been built.

Work on the line was hard and monotonous, and many workers quickly quit. So in 1914 Ford introduced the **five-dollar day**, a very high wage for the time. The rate of people quitting fell, and the workers could now afford a car themselves. This model of mass production and mass consumption through higher wages is called **Fordism**. It strongly shaped the economy in the 20th century.

Anyone who does the same task all day quickly gets tired and bored. Charlie Chaplin showed this in 1936 in his film **“Modern Times”**, in which he tightens screws on the line for so long that he goes mad. Physical complaints caused by repetitive movements are also a problem. Later companies tried to make the work more varied, for example with **teamwork**. Today robots take over many especially monotonous or heavy tasks.

abschnitte.titel: The assembly line conquers the world
abschnitte.text: Companies in Europe soon took up the new method. In Germany, from 1924 the Opel “Laubfrosch” (“Tree Frog”) was the first car made on an assembly line. Today it is not only cars that are made on assembly lines, but also household appliances, food, mobile phones and much more. Modern lines are often highly **automated** and controlled by computers. In Swiss factories too, for example in the food or watch industry, products pass along assembly lines.

begriffe.erklaerung: A moving belt that carries workpieces from station to station.
The time allowed at each station for one task.
Making very large numbers of the same product.
An economic model made up of assembly line work, good wages and mass consumption.

gewusst: For a long time the Ford Model T was only available in black, because black paint dried fastest.
The idea for the assembly line came, of all places, from slaughterhouses, where animals were taken apart rather than something being put together.
The Opel “Laubfrosch” got its nickname because of its green colour.

teile.einleitung: Simple machines are aids that let you do heavy work with less force. They include, for example, the lever, the inclined plane, the wedge and the pulley system. They are ancient and are still found today in many tools and devices.
wichtigste: Simple machines make work easier.
With a lever, such as a long bar, you can lift a heavy stone.
With a pulley system you can pull heavy loads up on a rope with little force.
A ramp on which you can push things up more easily is called an inclined plane.
The blade of an axe is a wedge.
Gears are wheels with teeth that mesh with each other.
What you save in force, you have to make up for in distance.

abschnitte.text: **Simple machines** are the basic building blocks of mechanics. They have no motor, but change the direction or the size of a force. The classic simple machines include the **lever**, inclined plane, wedge, screw, pulley and wheel and axle. Many complicated machines are put together from them.

A lever is a bar that moves about a **pivot**. The longer the side you press on, the less force you need. That is why you can lift a heavy stone with a long bar. Seesaws, scissors, pliers and the **wheelbarrow** also work as levers. With a wheelbarrow you carry soil around the garden on just one wheel.

An **inclined plane** is a ramp on which you can push loads up more easily than lifting them straight up. Mountain roads with many bends also use this principle. A **wedge** consists of two inclined planes and, for example as the blade of an axe, splits wood. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a pin.

A single fixed **pulley** only changes the direction of the force, so that you can pull downwards to lift something up. In a **pulley system** several pulleys are combined. With four supporting sections of rope you need only about a quarter of the force. Pulley systems are found on cranes, on sailing ships and in workshops.

The wheel and axle, for example a door knob or a crank, increases a turning force. **Gears** are wheels with teeth that mesh with each other and so pass on rotations. A large and a small gear can make a movement faster or more powerful. Gears are found in bikes, clocks and machines, and Swiss watches are famous for their tiny gears.

Simple machines save force, but not work. This is described by the **golden rule of mechanics**: what you save in force, you have to make up for in distance. Anyone pushing on a long ramp needs less force but covers a longer distance. More than 2200 years ago the Greek scholar Archimedes was already studying the laws of the lever.

begriffe.erklaerung: The point about which a lever turns.
Something that can move, slow down or change the shape of an object.
A combination of several pulleys and a rope for lifting heavy loads.
The part of physics that deals with forces and movements.

gewusst: Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a long enough lever and a fixed point he could move the Earth.
Your forearm also works like a lever, with the elbow as the pivot.
When building the Egyptian pyramids, the workers probably used ramps, that is, inclined planes.

teile.einleitung: The numbers up to 1000 include all the numbers from 0 to 1000. As well as tens and units, hundreds now come in. If you have mastered them, you can read, write and compare three-digit numbers and calculate with them in your head.
wichtigste: Three-digit numbers are made up of hundreds, tens and units.
The smallest three-digit number is 100, the largest is 999.
1000 is made up of 10 hundreds or 100 tens.
The number 325 is called three hundred and twenty-five.
A zero shows that a place is empty, as in 708.
You can count forwards and backwards in steps of a hundred, ten or one.
A place value chart helps you put numbers in the right order.

abschnitte.text: A three-digit number has three **places**. In 325 there are 3 hundreds, 2 tens and 5 units, that is 300 + 20 + 5. In the **place value chart** you write H for hundreds, T for tens and U for units above the columns. 1000 is as much as 10 hundreds, and a thousand is abbreviated as Th.

The digit **zero** keeps a place free. In 708 there are no tens, so there is a 0 there, and you say seven hundred and eight. Without the zero it would be 78, a completely different number. Zero as a placeholder was invented in India and came to Europe via Arab scholars in the Middle Ages.

Three-digit numbers are said starting from the hundreds: three hundred and twenty-five for 325. In German the units then come before the tens here too. In German, number words up to a million are written together as one single word. Long words such as “neunhundertneunundneunzig” (nine hundred and ninety-nine) show how practical digits are.

In **steps of a hundred** it goes 200, 300, 400, 500. Counting backwards in steps of ten, you count for example 530, 520, 510, 500. To compare numbers, you look first at the hundreds, then at the tens and finally at the units. In this way you quickly see that 650 lies between 600 and 700.

You can lay out numbers with **hundred squares**, tens rods and unit cubes. Ten hundred squares stacked on top of each other make a large thousand cube. On the number line up to 1000 you can see how far apart numbers are. The thousand book, in which each page shows a hundred numbers, is also a popular aid.

We come across three-digit numbers everywhere in everyday life. Swiss postcodes have four digits, but house numbers, page numbers or heights on hiking trails often have three. A bike can easily cost several hundred francs. In Switzerland children usually learn the numbers up to 1000 in their third year at school.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of a hundred units or ten tens.
The value a digit gets from its place in the number.
A table with columns for thousands, hundreds, tens and units.
A number with three digits, from 100 to 999.

gewusst: There are exactly 900 three-digit numbers, from 100 to 999.
A thousand cube made of small unit cubes contains 1000 cubes.
The Romans wrote 1000 as M, from the Latin word mille for thousand.

teile.einleitung: Bluetooth is a radio technology with which devices exchange data wirelessly over short distances. It is used, for example, to connect headphones, speakers, watches or a mouse to a phone or computer.
wichtigste: Bluetooth is designed for radio connections over short distances.
It transmits in the frequency range around 2.4 gigahertz.
The company Ericsson began developing it in 1994.
The name comes from a Danish king.
The logo is made of two runes.
Connecting two devices for the first time is called pairing.
Bluetooth LE stands for Low Energy and saves power.

abschnitte.text: Bluetooth is a **radio standard** for short distances, usually about 10 metres. Instead of cables, the devices send radio waves back and forth. It is used to connect **wireless headphones**, speakers, keyboards, smartwatches or the hands-free system in a car. For the internet connection at home, on the other hand, you need Wi-Fi or a fibre-optic line. Bluetooth is meant more for exchanges between devices that are close by.

For two devices to understand each other, they first have to get to know each other. This first connection is called **pairing** (in German “Koppeln”). Often you have to press a button or confirm a code to do this. After that the devices remember each other and later connect automatically. In this way Bluetooth stops strange devices from simply listening in.

Bluetooth uses the frequency range around **2.4 gigahertz**, which Wi-Fi and microwave ovens also use. So that the devices do not interfere with each other, Bluetooth changes frequency very often, many hundreds of times a second. This is called **frequency hopping**. The newer version **Bluetooth LE** (Low Energy) uses especially little power. That is why a fitness watch or a small sensor lasts a long time on a button cell.

The name recalls the Danish king **Harald Bluetooth**, who lived in the 10th century. He is said to have united parts of Denmark and Norway, just as Bluetooth connects different devices. The **logo** consists of the two **runes** for H and B, the initials of his name. The runes were merged into one sign.

The Swedish company **Ericsson** began development in 1994. In 1998 several large companies founded a joint group, the **Bluetooth SIG**, which still develops the standard further today. Around the year 2000 the first mobile phones with Bluetooth came onto the market. Today billions of Bluetooth devices are in use every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: Shared rules so that devices from different companies can understand each other by radio.
Connecting two Bluetooth devices for the first time.
A unit of frequency; 2.4 gigahertz is 2.4 billion oscillations per second.
An old written character of the Germanic peoples and the Vikings.

gewusst: Bluetooth changes its radio frequency hundreds of times every second.
The name Bluetooth was originally only meant as a working title and then simply stuck.
King Harald is mentioned on old rune stones at Jelling in Denmark.

teile.einleitung: Printing with movable type is one of the most important inventions in history. Johannes Gutenberg developed it around 1450 in Mainz, and with it books could for the first time be produced quickly and in large numbers.
wichtigste: In printing, the letters were put onto the paper with ink and a press.
The individual metal letters are called type.
The type is a mirror image so that the print comes out the right way round.
The type could be put together again and again and reused.
The printing press pressed the paper onto the inked type.
Typesetters put the type together into words and lines.
Basel became an important printing town early on.
Thanks to printing, books could be produced much faster.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages books were mostly copied by hand, often by monks in monasteries. A scribe sometimes needed years for a single Bible. Books were therefore very expensive and rare, and only a few people could read. Printing methods had been known earlier in China and Korea, but in Europe printing with **movable type** only spread thanks to Gutenberg.

Around 1450 Johannes Gutenberg from **Mainz** cast individual letters from a metal alloy, the **type**. With a special hand mould he could quickly make a great many identical letters. The type is a mirror image so that the print on the paper comes out the right way round. After printing, the page was taken apart again and the type was put together for a new page.

The **typesetter** put the type together letter by letter into lines and whole pages. Then the type was inked with a sticky printing ink. With the **printing press**, which looked like a wine press, the paper was pressed firmly onto the type. Gutenberg’s most famous work is the Gutenberg Bible, which was finished around 1454.

Printing spread rapidly throughout Europe and also came to Switzerland. **Basel**, with its university, became an important printing town early on. The printer Johann Froben, for example, worked there and published works by the scholar Erasmus of Rotterdam. Important printing works also grew up in Zurich, such as that of Christoph Froschauer, who printed Bibles.

Thanks to printing, books became much cheaper and more numerous. Knowledge, news and new ideas spread faster than ever before, for example during the Reformation. More and more people learnt to read and write. Many experts therefore see printing as the beginning of a new age, much like the **internet** today.

begriffe.erklaerung: Individual metal letters for printing.
A job: puts type together into words, lines and pages.
A machine that presses paper onto the inked type.
Reversed left to right, as you see it in a mirror.
A movement in the 16th century that led to the creation of the Reformed churches.

gewusst: Only just under 50 copies of the Gutenberg Bible survive today, complete or in part.
Until the 20th century almost every book and newspaper was set with type that basically worked on Gutenberg’s principle.
A skilled typesetter had to be able to find the letters in the type case without looking.

teile.einleitung: Digital Audio Broadcasting, DAB for short, is digital radio broadcast via aerials. The improved version used today is called DAB+. In Switzerland DAB+ has largely replaced the old FM radio.
wichtigste: DAB+ is digital radio that is received over the air.
In Switzerland DAB+ is replacing analogue FM radio.
The SRG switched off its FM transmitters at the end of 2024.
In 2017 Norway became the first country to switch off most of its national FM radio.
DAB+ offers more stations and reception without hiss.
Several programmes are bundled together as a multiplex, also called an ensemble, and broadcast on one frequency.
DAB+ uses a more efficient audio format than the older DAB.

abschnitte.text: In conventional **FM radio** the sound is stamped directly onto the radio signal as a wave; this is analogue. In DAB+ the sound is first turned into numbers, that is **digital data**, and then broadcast. The radio turns the data back into music and speech. That is why DAB+ sounds clear and without hiss, as long as the reception is good enough.

With FM, every programme needs its own frequency. With DAB+, several programmes are bundled into one package, the **multiplex** or ensemble. In this way often more than ten radio programmes fit on a single frequency. That is why there are many more stations with DAB+ than before.

The first DAB was developed from the end of the 1980s in a European research project. Later came DAB+, which uses a more efficient **audio format**. As a result each programme needs less data with equally good sound quality. Older devices that only know DAB often cannot receive DAB+.

The Swiss radio industry decided together to switch from FM to DAB+. The **SRG**, which includes Radio SRF, RTS and RSI, switched off its FM transmitters at the end of 2024. Since then its programmes can be heard via DAB+ or over the internet. The model was **Norway**, which already in 2017 became the first country to switch off most of its national FM radio.

As well as the music, a DAB+ radio often shows the **station name** and the song title. Some stations also send pictures, weather or traffic information. In the car you need a DAB+ car radio or an adapter. Many people today also listen to the radio via an app or the internet, but DAB+ works without a data connection and costs nothing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Frequency modulation on very high frequency (in German “UKW”), the old analogue way of broadcasting radio.
Turned into numbers, like data in a computer.
A bundle of several radio programmes on a shared frequency.
The number of vibrations per second on which a station broadcasts.

gewusst: More than ten radio programmes can run at the same time on a single DAB+ frequency.
In 2017 Norway was the first country to switch off most of its national FM radio.
With DAB+ you hear no hiss when reception is poor; instead the sound tends to drop out briefly.

teile.einleitung: Frequency modulation, FM for short, is a method of transmitting sounds or data with radio waves. The frequency of a carrier wave is changed in time with the signal. FM is best known from VHF radio, which for decades was the most important way to listen to the radio.
wichtigste: In frequency modulation, the instantaneous frequency of the carrier wave changes.
In the 1930s Edwin Howard Armstrong developed VHF broadcasting with FM.
In Europe VHF broadcasting lies between 87.5 and 108 MHz.
The greatest deviation from the carrier frequency is called the frequency deviation.
According to Carson's rule, a VHF signal with 75 kHz deviation and 15 kHz audio frequency needs a bandwidth of 180 kHz.
A pilot tone of 19 kHz marks a stereo signal.
FM is less prone to interference than AM, because a limiter cuts off amplitude disturbances.
With the capture effect, a receiver picking up two stations hears almost only the stronger one.

abschnitte.text: A radio station sends out an even radio wave, the **carrier wave**. For it to carry music or speech, it has to be changed; this is called **modulation**. In amplitude modulation, AM for short, the strength of the wave changes. In frequency modulation the strength stays the same, but the frequency varies in time with the sound. The receiver in the radio turns these variations back into sounds.

The greatest deviation of the frequency from the carrier frequency is called the **frequency deviation**. In VHF radio it is 75 kilohertz. An FM signal needs more room in the frequency range than an AM signal; this is called **bandwidth**. According to Carson's rule, you take twice the sum of the frequency deviation and the highest audio frequency. With 75 kHz and 15 kHz, that gives 180 kilohertz.

In the 1930s the American engineer **Edwin Howard Armstrong** developed broadcasting with frequency modulation. He showed that FM has much less noise than the AM radio usual at the time. After the Second World War, FM stations on **very high frequency**, VHF for short, spread in many countries. In Europe VHF broadcasting lies between 87.5 and 108 megahertz.

Interference such as lightning or electrical appliances usually changes the strength of a radio wave. Because with FM the information is in the frequency, a **limiter** in the receiver can simply cut off these changes in strength. That is why VHF radio sounds clearer than medium wave. If two stations transmit on the same frequency, an FM receiver hears almost only the stronger one. This is called the **capture effect**.

For stereo radio, an additional signal is sent along that contains the difference between the left and right channels. A **pilot tone** of 19 kilohertz shows the receiver that it is a stereo broadcast. The Radio Data System, **RDS** for short, also shows the station name on the display. Traffic announcements can also be marked this way.

Frequency modulation is used not only for radio but also for walkie-talkies and, in the past, for the sound of analogue television. In Switzerland VHF is being replaced step by step by digital radio, **DAB+**. The SRG switched off its VHF transmitters at the end of 2024. But many car radios and old kitchen radios still receive VHF.

begriffe.erklaerung: Even radio wave that carries information through modulation.
Changing a wave so that it transmits a signal.
Greatest deviation of the frequency from the carrier frequency.
Very high frequency, the frequency range of classic FM radio.
How much room a signal needs in the frequency range.

gewusst: The number on the radio dial, such as 101.7, is the carrier frequency in megahertz.
The 19 kHz pilot tone is so high that most people can hardly hear it.
The sound in old analogue television was also transmitted with frequency modulation.

teile.einleitung: A pressurised water reactor is the most common type of nuclear reactor in nuclear power stations worldwide. In it, the splitting of uranium heats water that is under such high pressure that it does not boil. In Switzerland the Beznau and Gösgen nuclear power stations work with pressurised water reactors.
wichtigste: In the primary circuit the water is under about 150 bar, so that it does not boil despite being at about 300 °C.
The steam for the turbine is produced in the steam generator of a separate secondary circuit.
The water in the core is coolant and moderator at the same time.
The pressuriser keeps the pressure in the primary circuit constant.
Boric acid in the cooling water captures neutrons and helps to control the reactivity.
The fuel typically contains about 3 to 5 per cent uranium-235.
The Swiss nuclear power station Leibstadt, by contrast, has a boiling water reactor.

abschnitte.text: In a nuclear reactor the nuclei of **uranium** atoms are split, releasing a great deal of heat. In a pressurised water reactor this heat is used to heat water. The water is under about 150 bar, which is about 150 times air pressure. That is why it does not boil even at about 300 degrees Celsius.

The hot water from the reactor flows in the **primary circuit** to the steam generator. There it gives off its heat through thousands of thin tubes to the water of a second circuit. In this **secondary circuit** steam is produced, which drives the turbine and the generator. Because the circuits are separate, no radioactive water reaches the turbine.

The water in the core is coolant and **moderator** at the same time: it slows the neutrons down so that they can split more uranium nuclei. If the water gets too hot and less dense, the moderation decreases and the power drops by itself. In addition, **boric acid** is mixed into the water, because boron captures neutrons. Control rods can shut the reactor down very quickly, and a **pressuriser** keeps the pressure even.

The fuel consists of small pellets of uranium dioxide, which are filled into long metal tubes. Natural uranium contains only a little of the fissile **uranium-235**. For pressurised water reactors it is enriched to about 3 to 5 per cent. Many such fuel rods together form a fuel assembly.

The nuclear power stations **Beznau** in the canton of Aargau and **Gösgen** in the canton of Solothurn work with pressurised water reactors. Leibstadt in Aargau, on the other hand, uses a **boiling water reactor**, in which the water turns to steam directly in the reactor. The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was also a boiling water reactor and was shut down at the end of 2019. Under the Energy Act, no new nuclear power stations may currently be approved in Switzerland.

Nuclear power stations give off hardly any CO2 while operating and supply electricity around the clock. At the same time they produce **radioactive waste**, which has to be stored safely for a very long time. The risk of serious accidents, as in Fukushima in 2011, is also debated in society. People therefore have different opinions about the future of nuclear energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that slows neutrons down so that they can split atomic nuclei.
The water circuit that flows directly through the reactor core.
A large heat exchanger in which the water of the second circuit turns into steam.
Increasing the share of fissile uranium-235 in the fuel.

gewusst: In the reactor the water is about 300 degrees hot and still does not boil, because the pressure is so high.
About two thirds of all nuclear reactors worldwide are pressurised water reactors.
Even small amounts of boron in the water can noticeably change the power of a reactor.

teile.einleitung: A brake is a device that slows down or stops a vehicle or a machine. Without good brakes no bike, car or train could travel safely.
wichtigste: A friction brake turns kinetic energy mainly into heat.
In a disc brake, brake pads press on a brake disc on the wheel.
In a drum brake, brake shoes press from the inside against a drum.
In a car, brake fluid passes the force from the brake pedal to the wheels.
The anti-lock braking system (ABS) makes sure that the vehicle can still be steered when braking.
When braking electrically, SBB electric locomotives feed electricity back into the grid.
On long descents you should select a lower gear so that the brakes do not overheat.
A back-pedal brake on a bike is operated by pedalling backwards.

abschnitte.text: A moving vehicle has **kinetic energy**. To stop it, this energy has to be turned into another form. A **friction brake** rubs two parts against each other and so turns the energy mainly into heat. You can feel this if, after a long descent on your bike, you carefully touch the rim or the brake disc.

In a **disc brake** a metal disc turns with the wheel, and brake pads press on it from both sides. In a **drum brake** brake shoes press from the inside against a round drum. Disc brakes are cooled better and are usual on cars and motorbikes today. In a car, **brake fluid** in thin pipes passes the force from the pedal to all the wheels at the same time.

If you brake too hard, the wheels can lock and skid, and then the car can no longer be steered. The **anti-lock braking system** (ABS) measures how the wheels turn and releases the brake a little, again and again, in a flash. In this way the vehicle can still be steered even in an emergency stop. ABS was introduced in production cars at the end of the 1970s and is standard today.

SBB electric locomotives can use their motors as generators when braking. The kinetic energy is turned into electricity and fed back into the grid; this is called **regenerative braking**. Especially on the steep lines in the Alps this saves a lot of energy. Electric cars also recharge their batteries when braking.

abschnitte.titel: Brakes on bikes and in the mountains
abschnitte.text: On bikes there are rim brakes, disc brakes and the **back-pedal brake**, which you use by pedalling backwards. On long descents in a car you should select a lower gear and let the engine help with braking. Otherwise the brakes get so hot that they hardly work any more. Lorries and coaches have extra continuous brakes for this, which work without wear.

begriffe.erklaerung: Resistance when two surfaces rub against each other.
A part that presses against the brake disc and wears down in the process.
Anti-lock braking system, which stops the wheels from locking.
Recovering energy when braking.
A liquid that transmits the braking force in a car.

gewusst: The brake discs of Formula 1 cars can get hotter than 1000 degrees Celsius when braking and glow.
After landing, planes also brake by redirecting the thrust of their engines.
Brake fluid absorbs water from the air over time and therefore has to be changed regularly.

teile.einleitung: Saving energy means using less electricity, heat or fuel without going without the important things. This protects the environment, the climate and your wallet. Even small everyday habits make a difference.
wichtigste: When you leave a room, you should switch off the light.
Switching televisions and other devices off completely instead of leaving them on standby saves electricity.
If the fridge door stays open for a long time, the fridge uses more electricity.
A short shower usually uses less hot water than a bath.
In winter the most economical way to air a room is briefly with the window wide open.
The energy label shows how economical a device is.
On a washing line, laundry dries with no electricity at all.
When the phone is fully charged, you unplug the charger from the socket.

abschnitte.text: Electricity, heating and fuel first have to be produced, and this often harms the environment. Burning oil, gas or petrol produces **CO2**, which contributes to climate change. Even renewable energy from water, sun and wind is not available without limit. The energy you do not need at all is therefore the cleanest and cheapest.

When you leave a room, you switch off the light. **LED bulbs** use much less electricity than old light bulbs. Televisions, games consoles and computers should be switched off completely, because they use electricity even on **standby**. A power strip with a switch helps to disconnect several devices at once.

A large share of the energy in Swiss households goes into heating and hot water. In winter it is best to air a room briefly with the window wide open; this is called **burst airing**. A window left tilted open all the time, on the other hand, cools down the walls. Taking a short shower instead of a bath saves a lot of hot water. Even one degree less room temperature saves a noticeable amount of heating energy.

Fridges, washing machines, lamps and many other devices carry a coloured **energy label**. It uses letters and colours from green to red to show how economical a device is. Green and the letter A mean very economical. When buying a new device, you can compare easily this way.

Laundry dries on a **washing line** with no electricity at all. You should open the fridge door only briefly, otherwise the appliance has to do a lot of cooling again. When the phone is fully charged, you unplug the charger from the socket. For short journeys, bikes and feet are the most economical ways to travel, and for longer distances public transport is.

begriffe.erklaerung: Ready mode in which a device seems to be off but still uses electricity.
Coloured label that shows how much energy a device uses.
Airing a room briefly and thoroughly with the window wide open.
Energy from sources that keep renewing themselves, such as sun, wind and water.

gewusst: An LED bulb needs only a fraction of the electricity of an old light bulb for the same brightness.
A window left tilted open all the time in winter wastes more heat than brief burst airing.
Even a charger with no phone attached can use a little electricity.

teile.einleitung: Torque describes how strongly a force makes something turn. It explains why you can undo a screw more easily with a long spanner and why door handles are placed far away from the hinges.
wichtigste: Torque is calculated as force times lever arm when the force acts at right angles.
It is measured in newton metres (Nm).
50 newtons on a spanner 0.4 metres long give 20 Nm.
With a spanner twice as long, the torque doubles for the same force.
Torque is greatest when the force acts at right angles to the lever.
A torque wrench tightens screws exactly the right amount.
Electric motors have a high torque even from a standstill.

abschnitte.text: When a **force** pulls or pushes on a lever, it can turn something about an **axis of rotation**. How strong this turning effect is is given by the **torque**. It depends on the size of the force and on the distance from the axis, the **lever arm**. If the force acts at right angles to the lever: torque equals force times lever arm. It is measured in **newton metres**, Nm for short.

If you press with 50 newtons at right angles on the end of a spanner 0.4 metres long, this gives 50 × 0.4 = 20 Nm. If a screw needs 30 Nm and the spanner is 0.2 metres long, you have to apply 30 ÷ 0.2 = 150 newtons. If you take a spanner twice as long, the torque doubles for the same force. If you press at an angle instead of at right angles, only part of the force has a turning effect. That is why torque is greatest when the force is at right angles.

A heavy door is easiest to open far away from the **hinges**, because that is where the lever arm is greatest. On a **seesaw** a light child can balance a heavy one by sitting further out. On a bike your foot presses on the pedals, and the crank produces a torque. A screwdriver with a thick handle also turns more easily than one with a thin handle.

Some screws must be neither too loose nor too tight. With a **torque wrench** you set the torque you want. When it is reached, the wrench clicks or gives way. This is how, for example, car wheels are fitted, or parts on a carbon racing bike, which could break if too much force were used.

For engines, torque says how powerfully they can drive the wheels. An **electric motor** has a high torque even from a standstill. That is why electric cars often accelerate very powerfully from a standstill. Petrol engines only reach their greatest torque at higher engine speeds. A **gearbox** helps to adapt the torque to the driving situation, for example when pulling away on a hill.

More than 2000 years ago the Greek scholar **Archimedes** studied the **law of the lever**. It says that a lever is in balance when the torques on both sides are equally large. Archimedes is said to have claimed that with a fixed point and a long lever he could move the Earth. Since ancient times people have used levers, for example in scales, crowbars and oars.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the axis of rotation and the point where the force acts.
The unit of torque: force in newtons times length in metres.
The imaginary line about which something turns.
The rule that a lever is in balance when both torques are equal.

gewusst: With a long pipe over the spanner you can undo even very tight screws.
Door handles are always on the side opposite the hinges, so that you need little force.
One newton metre is roughly the torque produced when a bar of chocolate hangs from the end of a metre rule.

teile.einleitung: An electric toothbrush is a toothbrush with a built-in motor whose head rotates or vibrates by itself. As a result it removes plaque thoroughly, even if you move your hand only slowly. The first electric toothbrush was invented in Switzerland.
wichtigste: The head of an electric toothbrush rotates or vibrates.
The handle contains a rechargeable battery and a motor.
It is usually charged in a charging stand.
You should brush your teeth for about two minutes.
You should brush at least twice a day.
You brush the outer, inner and top surfaces of the teeth.
You do not need to press hard, because the brush moves by itself.
You change the brush head about every three months.

abschnitte.text: An electric toothbrush looks similar to a normal one but has a thicker handle. Inside it are a small **electric motor** and a **rechargeable battery**. The motor moves the brush head many thousands of times a minute. In this way the brush does a large part of the cleaning work.

On **oscillating-rotating** toothbrushes the head is round and turns quickly back and forth. **Sonic toothbrushes** have a long head that vibrates very fast. Both kinds remove plaque well if they are used correctly. Many models have a pressure sensor that warns you if you press too hard.

Most electric toothbrushes are charged in a **charging stand**. Often there are no metal contacts; the electricity is transferred through a magnetic field. This technology is called **inductive charging**. It is practical in the bathroom, because no water can get into plug contacts.

You should brush at least twice a day for about two minutes. Many brushes have a **timer** that buzzes briefly every 30 seconds so that you move on to the next quarter of your mouth. You guide the brush slowly from tooth to tooth and clean the outer, inner and top surfaces. It is important to use a toothpaste with **fluoride**, which strengthens tooth enamel.

The first electric toothbrush was developed in Switzerland in 1954 by Philippe-Guy Woog. It was called the **Broxodent** and was first intended for people who cannot move their hands well. Later it was also sold in other countries. Today electric toothbrushes are a matter of course in many households.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft, sticky film of bacteria on the teeth.
A battery that can be charged again.
Charging without cable contact, in which the energy is transferred through a magnetic field.
A substance in toothpaste that makes teeth more resistant to tooth decay.

gewusst: The first electric toothbrush comes from Switzerland and went on sale in the 1950s.
A sonic toothbrush vibrates so fast that you cannot see the individual movements.
You can recognise worn-out bristles because they splay apart.

teile.einleitung: A fibre-optic cable carries data not with electricity but with light. In hair-thin fibres of glass, pulses of light race over huge distances. Without optical fibres there would be no fast internet and no video calls across continents.
wichtigste: Fibre-optic cables carry data as pulses of light.
The light is held inside the fibre by total internal reflection.
The light travels in the innermost part of the fibre, the core.
Optical fibres are made mainly of quartz glass, that is, silicon dioxide.
Electrical interference does not affect fibre-optic cables.
Submarine cables on the sea floor connect the continents.
In 2009 Charles Kao received the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on transmitting light in optical fibres.

abschnitte.text: In a copper cable, electrical signals flow. In a **fibre-optic cable**, on the other hand, the data is encoded in rapid flashes of light. Light on means, for example, a one, light off a zero. Usually invisible **infrared light** is used, because it is weakened especially little in glass. A laser at one end sends, and a light sensor at the other end receives.

An optical fibre has a **core** surrounded by a cladding of slightly different glass. If the light hits the boundary with the cladding at a slant, it is reflected back completely. This effect is called **total internal reflection**. In this way the light zigzags through the fibre and stays inside, even when the cable goes round bends. A single fibre is about as thin as a hair.

Optical fibres can carry much more data at the same time than copper cables. The signal weakens only a little over long distances, so amplifiers are needed less often. Because no electricity flows, **electrical fields**, for example from motors or lightning, do not disturb the transmission. Optical fibres are also light and thin. However, they are more delicate to lay and join, because the fibres have to be lined up precisely.

Almost all internet traffic between continents runs through **submarine cables**. These fibre-optic cables lie on the sea floor, in places several kilometres deep. Special cable ships lay them over thousands of kilometres. Near the coast they are buried in the ground so that anchors and fishing nets do not damage them. Satellites carry only a small part of the data.

The abbreviation **FTTH** stands for “fibre to the home”, that is, optical fibre right into the flat. In Switzerland, Swisscom and many city electricity companies have been expanding fibre networks for years. This makes very fast internet connections possible. The idea of optical fibre for data was developed in the 1960s by **Charles Kao**. Around 1970 it first became possible to make glass so pure that light could travel long distances in it.

begriffe.erklaerung: The complete reflection of light at a boundary.
The innermost part of the optical fibre, in which the light travels.
A cable laid on the sea floor.
Optical fibre right into the flat, “fibre to the home”.
Light that is invisible to our eyes.

gewusst: The glass for optical fibres is so clear that you could still see through a block of glass many kilometres thick.
Many colours of light can travel in a single fibre at the same time, each with its own data.
Sharks have bitten submarine cables, so some cables were given a special protective sheath.

teile.einleitung: The European Train Control System, ETCS for short, is a single European system that monitors trains and guides them safely. It makes sure that no train goes too fast or passes a red signal. In Switzerland, for example, the trains through the Lötschberg and Gotthard base tunnels run with ETCS.
wichtigste: ETCS is a single European train protection system.
It is part of the wider European system ERTMS.
Eurobalises in the track send information to the train passing over them.
With ETCS Level 2 the train receives its movement authority continuously by radio.
Movement authorities are issued by a control centre for the line, the Radio Block Centre.
The driver sees the information on a screen in the cab instead of on lineside signals.
The Lötschberg Base Tunnel opened in 2007 with ETCS Level 2.

abschnitte.text: In the past almost every country in Europe had its own **train protection system**. A train travelling from Switzerland to Germany or Italy therefore needed several devices on board. ETCS is meant to standardise this so that trains can cross borders without obstacles. It is part of **ERTMS**, the European Rail Traffic Management System. This also includes the railway radio network GSM-R.

Between the rails lie flat yellow boxes, the **Eurobalises**. When a train passes over one, it briefly supplies the balise with energy, and the balise sends data back to it. In this way the train learns, for example, exactly where it is and how fast it may go. The balises need no power supply of their own for this. With ETCS Level 1, the most important information comes via these balises.

With **ETCS Level 2** there are no longer any signals beside the track. Instead, the train is constantly in radio contact with a control centre for the line, the **Radio Block Centre**. This calculates how far the train may safely travel and sends it the movement authority. So far the radio runs over the GSM-R network; a successor called FRMCS is planned. The balises then serve mainly to determine the exact position of the train.

In the cab, a **screen** shows the driver the permitted speed and the distance he may still travel. Outside, he no longer has to spot signals at high speed. This is especially important at 200 km/h and more, where you would hardly see signals in time. If the train goes too fast, ETCS first gives a warning. If the driver does not react, the system brakes the train automatically.

Switzerland is one of the pioneers of ETCS. Level 2 was used early on the new **Mattstetten-Rothrist** line between Bern and Olten and in the **Lötschberg Base Tunnel** (2007). The Gotthard Base Tunnel, which opened in 2016, also runs with ETCS Level 2. According to SBB planning, the standard-gauge network was to be fully equipped with ETCS by the end of 2017, on many lines at first in a simple form of Level 1. In the long term, Level 2 is to replace the signals on more and more lines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Technology that monitors a train and brakes it automatically if necessary.
A data point in the track that sends information to the train.
A control centre for the line that gives trains movement authorities by radio.
A mobile network just for the railway.
The place at the front of the train where the driver sits.

gewusst: With ETCS Level 2, there are no normal light signals for train traffic in the Lötschberg and Gotthard base tunnels.
A Eurobalise needs no battery, because the train supplies it with energy as it passes over.
ETCS allows trains to run closer behind one another, because the distances are calculated precisely.

teile.einleitung: A pedestrian crossing is a marking on the road where people on foot can cross safely. In Germany and Austria it is called a “Zebrastreifen” (zebra crossing), in Switzerland a “Fussgängerstreifen”. It is one of the most important rules that children learn in road safety lessons.
wichtigste: In Switzerland people say “Fussgängerstreifen” instead of “Zebrastreifen”.
Swiss pedestrian crossings are yellow.
The first yellow pedestrian crossing in Switzerland was painted in Basel in 1948.
At a pedestrian crossing, pedestrians have priority over cars.
Until 1994 pedestrians in Switzerland had to give a hand signal.
Before crossing, you look for eye contact with the driver.
You cross the road briskly, but without running.

abschnitte.text: A pedestrian crossing consists of wide stripes painted across the road. It shows everyone that people on foot may cross the road here. At a pedestrian crossing, pedestrians have **priority**. Cars, buses and bicycles must stop if someone wants to cross the road. A blue road sign showing a pedestrian also points out the crossing.

In most countries zebra crossings are white, but in Switzerland they are **yellow**. Here yellow is the colour for markings that concern pedestrians, or for parking bans. The first yellow pedestrian crossing in Switzerland was painted in **Basel** in 1948. So that the crossing stays easy to see, the paint is renewed regularly. Often the road around it is also well lit.

In the past pedestrians in Switzerland had to show with a **hand signal** that they wanted to cross the road. Since 1994 this has no longer been necessary; cars must stop even without a hand signal. But a pedestrian must not suddenly jump into the road when a vehicle is already too close. If there is a pedestrian crossing nearby, you should use it. Where there are traffic lights, the light signals also apply.

In Switzerland children learn the Swiss German rule “**Warte, luege, lose, laufe**”, which means “wait, look, listen, walk”. You stop at the roadside, look left and right and listen for vehicles. It is best to make **eye contact** with the driver to be sure you have been seen. Only when the vehicles have stopped do you set off. You cross the road briskly but do not run, so that you do not trip.

The pedestrian crossing is the safest place to cross a road, but accidents happen there too. It is especially dangerous at dusk and in rain and fog, when pedestrians are hard to see. Light-coloured clothes and **reflectors** help you to be seen earlier. Many pedestrian crossings have a **traffic island** in the middle where you can wait. On the way to school, crossing patrols sometimes help children cross.

begriffe.erklaerung: The right to go first.
Name for the pedestrian crossing in Germany and Austria (Zebrastreifen).
Raised island in the middle of the road where pedestrians can wait.
Item that throws light back and makes you visible in the dark.

gewusst: Switzerland is one of the few countries with yellow pedestrian crossings.
Until 1994 you had to raise your hand at a pedestrian crossing in Switzerland to get priority.
At night drivers see a person in dark clothes much later than one with reflectors.

teile.einleitung: Glasses are a frame with two ground lenses that you wear in front of your eyes to see better. They were invented in Italy more than 700 years ago and today help millions of people in everyday life.
wichtigste: Glasses help you to see better.
The parts that go over the ears are called arms.
Glasses were invented in Italy more than 700 years ago.
Short-sighted people cannot see clearly into the distance.
In Switzerland people usually buy glasses from an optician.
Sunglasses protect against strong sun, swimming goggles help under water.
Instead of glasses, many people wear contact lenses directly on the eye.

abschnitte.text: A pair of glasses consists of the **frame** and two **lenses**. The frame has a bridge that sits on the nose and two **arms** that rest over the ears. There are frames made of metal, plastic or even wood. Today the lenses are mostly made of light plastic instead of real glass. They are best cleaned with a soft glasses cloth.

In the eye the **lens** focuses light onto the retina. In **short-sighted** people the image from far away lands in front of the retina, so they see distant things blurred. They are helped by diverging lenses, which are thinner in the middle. **Long-sighted** people see badly close up and need converging lenses, which are thicker in the middle. The strength of a lens is measured in **dioptres**.

As early as the Middle Ages monks used polished stones as reading aids, which they laid on the writing. Towards the end of the 13th century the first glasses with two lenses were invented in **Italy**. These early rivet spectacles had no arms yet and were clipped onto the nose or held in the hand. Arms that go over the ears only became common in the 18th century.

**Sunglasses** protect the eyes from glaring light and harmful UV radiation, especially in the mountains and in snow. **Swimming goggles** or a diving mask keep a layer of air in front of the eyes so that you can see clearly under water. Skiers wear ski goggles, and craftspeople wear safety glasses against splinters. Many older people need **reading glasses**, because the lens of the eye becomes less flexible with age.

In Switzerland you have your eyes tested by an **optician** or an eye doctor. There you read letters on an eye chart, and the right lenses are worked out. The optician fits the lenses into the frame and adjusts the arms properly. Children should have their eyes checked regularly, because poor eyesight makes learning harder. An alternative to glasses is **contact lenses**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of the glasses that holds the lenses.
The unit for the strength of a lens.
You see near things well, but things in the distance are blurred.
You see better in the distance than close up.
A thin lens that sits directly on the eye.

gewusst: The first glasses had no arms and had to be balanced on the nose.
Almost everyone needs reading glasses at some point in old age.
In the snow in the mountains you can get painful snow blindness without sunglasses.

teile.einleitung: In mathematics the root is the inverse of raising to a power. The square root of a number is the number which, multiplied by itself, gives the original number. So the square root of 144 is 12, because 12 times 12 gives 144.
wichtigste: The square root of a is the non-negative number that, multiplied by itself, gives a.
The root sign looks like this: √.
The cube root of 125 is 5, because 5 times 5 times 5 gives 125.
Many roots such as √2 or √12 are irrational numbers.
Roots can be partly taken out, for example √72 = 6√2.
Roots can be written as powers with a fraction, for example 8^(2/3) = 4.
You cannot take a real square root of a negative number.

abschnitte.text: **Taking a root** is the opposite of squaring. 12 squared is 144, so the square root of 144 is 12 again. The number under the root sign is called the **radicand**. As well as the square root, there are also the cube root, the fourth root and so on. The cube root of 125 is 5, because 5 to the power of 3 is 125.

Numbers such as 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100 and 144 are called **square numbers**. Their roots are whole numbers. For all other natural numbers the root is neither a whole number nor a fraction. Such numbers are called **irrational**, for example √2, √3 or √12. Their decimal places go on for ever without repeating.

Roots can often be simplified by taking out a square number. Because 72 equals 36 times 2, √72 = 6√2. This is called **partly taking the root**, or simplifying a surd. If there is a root in the denominator, you rationalise it, that is make it root-free: 1/√2 becomes √2/2. In addition, the root of a product is the product of the roots.

Every root can be written as a **power** with a fraction as the exponent. The square root of a is a to the power of 1/2. 8 to the power of 2/3 means: first take the cube root of 8, which gives 2, and then square it, which gives 4. With this notation the usual **laws of indices** apply. Calculators and computers often work like this.

In an **equation with a root**, the unknown is under the root. For √(x + 5) = 4 you square both sides and get x + 5 = 16. It follows that x = 11. After squaring you must always **check** the solution by substituting it. Sometimes false solutions arise that are not correct.

The Babylonians calculated √2 astonishingly accurately around 3800 years ago, as a clay tablet shows. The Greek mathematician **Heron of Alexandria** described a method for approximating roots step by step. Today’s root sign developed in Germany in the 16th century from a small r for the Latin “radix”, which means root. In everyday life roots are needed, for example, with **Pythagoras’ theorem** to calculate diagonals and distances. The diagonal of a square with a side length of 1 m measures exactly √2 m, that is about 1.41 m.

begriffe.erklaerung: The number under the root sign.
A number made by multiplying a whole number by itself.
A number that cannot be written as a fraction and whose decimal places never end.
Another term for taking a root.

gewusst: The German word for root, Wurzel, translates the Latin “radix”, which also gave us the word radish.
The Babylonians knew √2 to about six decimal places.
The format of an A4 sheet is based on √2: its long side is about 1.41 times as long as its short side.

teile.einleitung: A number line is a straight line on which numbers are arranged in order of size at equal distances. It usually starts at 0 and has an arrowhead to show that it goes on for ever. With it you can see numbers, compare them and even calculate.
wichtigste: On a horizontal number line the larger numbers are further to the right.
Equal distances on the line mean equal differences between the numbers.
The midpoint between 0 and 10 is 5, the midpoint between 20 and 40 is 30.
Adding is a jump to the right, subtracting a jump to the left.
The number 64 lies between the tens numbers 60 and 70.
If you extend the line to the left, you get the full number line with negative numbers.
Rulers and thermometers are number lines from everyday life.

abschnitte.text: A number line is a line with a **starting point**, usually at 0. Small marks show numbers at equal distances. An arrowhead points to the right, because the numbers go on for ever. The further to the right a number is, the bigger it is.

On the number line you can see which number is bigger and how far apart numbers are. The **midpoint** between two numbers lies exactly halfway along the distance: between 100 and 200 it is 150. The number 47 is closer to 50 than, say, 43 or 56. With the help of the tens numbers you can quickly place any number; 64 lies between 60 and 70.

Calculations can be shown as **jumps**. If you are at 35 and jump 10 to the right, you land on 45. If you are at 80 and take 3 steps to the left, you land on 77. For harder sums you break big jumps into small ones, for example first up to the next ten.

Not every number line shows every single number. On a line up to 1000, perhaps only every hundred is labelled. The **scale** tells you how much one section means. One centimetre can stand for 1, for 10 or for 100, depending on the problem.

If you extend the number line beyond 0 to the left, you get the full **number line**. To the left of 0 are the negative numbers such as −1, −2 and −3. A thermometer is a number line like this: in winter in the Swiss mountains it can be −15 °C. Fractions and decimal numbers such as 0.5 also have their place between the whole numbers.

Many things in everyday life work like a number line. A **ruler** and a tape measure show centimetres at equal distances. A timeline in history puts years in order on a line, for example from the founding of the Swiss Confederation in 1291 to today. The progress bar when downloading a file is also a simple number line.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line with a starting point on which numbers are placed at equal distances.
A line without beginning or end on which negative numbers are shown too.
Tells you how much one section of the line means in numbers.
A number that is less than zero, such as −5.

gewusst: Between any two numbers on the number line there are always infinitely many more numbers, if you count fractions and decimals.
The English mathematician John Wallis is regarded as one of the first people to show numbers on a line, in the 17th century.
A thermometer is really a vertical number line on which the bigger numbers are at the top.

teile.einleitung: A bridge is a structure that lets you cross an obstacle such as a river, a valley or a road. In Switzerland, with its many mountains, gorges and lakes, there are thousands of bridges, from old wooden bridges to modern suspension bridges.
wichtigste: Bridges are built to get over an obstacle.
A suspension bridge hangs from thick cables.
Old stone bridges often have a round arch underneath.
At a castle the drawbridge can be pulled up.
The Charles Kuonen Suspension Bridge in Valais is almost 500 metres long.
The red Golden Gate Bridge is in San Francisco.
According to legend, a billy goat had to be the first to cross the Devil’s Bridge in the Schöllenen Gorge.

abschnitte.text: Bridges carry paths, roads or railway lines over **obstacles** such as rivers, gorges, valleys or other transport routes. Without bridges you would have to take long detours or cross by ferry. A bridge must carry its own weight and the load of people and vehicles. On top of that come wind, snow and changes in temperature. That is why engineers calculate every bridge very precisely.

The simplest form is the **beam bridge**, in which a beam rests on piers, as with many motorway bridges. **Arch bridges** pass the load into the ground through a round arch, as with the old stone bridges of the Romans. In a **suspension bridge** the deck hangs from thick cables stretched over towers. In a cable-stayed bridge the cables run diagonally straight from the pylon to the deck. A **drawbridge** at a castle could be pulled up to keep enemies away.

The first bridges were probably fallen tree trunks over streams. For a long time simple bridges were built of **wood**.
