On 29 January 1886 **Carl Benz** in Mannheim applied for a patent for his motor car. This three-wheeled vehicle is regarded as the first car with a petrol engine. At almost the same time Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach built a motor carriage in Cannstatt. In August 1888 **Bertha Benz**, Carl Benz’s wife, drove with her two sons from Mannheim to Pforzheim. The journey of about 100 kilometres proved that the car was fit for everyday use.

The first cars were expensive one-off vehicles for rich people. From 1913 the American **Henry Ford** had his Model T built on an **assembly line**. Each worker did only a few tasks, and the car moved from station to station. This made cars much cheaper, and more than 15 million Model Ts were built.

In a **combustion engine**, petrol or diesel burns in cylinders and moves pistons up and down. This movement is passed through the gearbox to the wheels. An **electric car**, on the other hand, has a large battery and an electric motor, so it fills up with electricity at a charging station. Electric cars give off no exhaust fumes while driving and are very quiet.

The most important lifesaver in a car is the **seat belt**. The three-point belt used today was developed by the Swede Nils Bohlin in 1959 for the company Volvo. In Switzerland everyone in the car must wear a seat belt, and small children need a suitable **child seat**. Modern cars also have airbags and electronic aids such as the anti-lock braking system ABS.

More than 4.5 million cars are registered in Switzerland (as of about 2024). There are hardly any big car factories here, but in the past, for example, the company Saurer in Arbon built well-known lorries and postbuses. Anyone who wants to drive a car needs a **driving licence**. In Switzerland you can get a learner’s permit from the age of 17.

begriffe.erklaerung: An engine in which petrol or diesel burns and so produces movement.
A moving belt on which a product travels from workplace to workplace.
A car that runs on electricity from a battery.
An official right that protects an invention for the inventor.

gewusst: On her famous journey Bertha Benz had to buy petrol at a chemist’s, because there were no petrol stations yet.
The first cars only went at about 16 kilometres per hour, hardly faster than a bike.
Electric cars existed as early as 1900 and were even more popular than petrol cars at the time.

teile.einleitung: In autonomous driving a vehicle steers, brakes and accelerates fully or partly by itself, without a person having to intervene. Cameras, radar, lidar and powerful computers replace the driver’s eyes and brain.
wichtigste: The SAE J3016 standard distinguishes 6 levels of driving automation, from level 0 to 5.
At level 3 the system drives itself, but the person must take over when asked.
Lidar scans the surroundings with laser pulses.
Sensor fusion combines the data from camera, radar and lidar into a model of the surroundings.
In Switzerland the Ordinance on Automated Driving has applied since 1 March 2025.
With an approved motorway pilot you may take your hands off the wheel but must stay ready to take over.
From 2016 the first self-driving postbuses ran in public traffic in Sion.
In 2005 the vehicle Stanley from Stanford University won the DARPA Grand Challenge.

abschnitte.text: The American standard **SAE J3016** divides automated driving into 6 levels from 0 to 5. At level 0 the person does everything themselves; at levels 1 and 2 systems such as cruise control with distance control or a lane-keeping assistant help. At **level 3** the car drives itself in certain situations, but the person must take over when asked. At levels 4 and 5 no driver is needed at all, in certain areas or even everywhere.

An autonomous vehicle has lots of sensors. Cameras recognise road signs, traffic lights and road markings. **Radar** uses radio waves to measure the distance and speed of other vehicles, even in fog. **Lidar** sends out laser pulses and uses them to create an accurate three-dimensional picture of the surroundings. In **sensor fusion** all the data is combined into a model of the surroundings, from which the computer decides how the car drives.

An important milestone was the **DARPA Grand Challenge**, a race for robot cars in the desert of the USA. In 2005 it was won by the vehicle Stanley from Stanford University, which covered more than 200 kilometres without a driver. After that, big technology companies and car makers joined the development. Today robotaxis without drivers carry passengers around in some cities in the USA and China.

From 2016 Swiss Post tested the first self-driving postbuses in public traffic in **Sion**: small electric shuttles for passengers. Since 1 March 2025 the **Ordinance on Automated Driving** has regulated, among other things, the motorway pilot and automated parking. With an approved motorway pilot you may take your hands off the steering wheel. But you must stay ready to take over and may not, for example, sleep.

Autonomous vehicles could reduce accidents, because most accidents are caused by human error. Older or visually impaired people could become more mobile. At the same time there are open questions: who is liable in an accident, and how safe is the software against **hacker attacks**? Snow, covered markings and unexpected situations are also still difficult for the technology.

begriffe.erklaerung: A sensor that measures distances with laser light and creates a 3D picture of the surroundings.
A device that uses radio waves to detect objects and their speed.
Combining the data from several sensors into a single picture.
A system that lets a car drive by itself on the motorway.
A taxi that travels without a driver.

gewusst: A lidar sensor can capture hundreds of thousands of measuring points per second.
The winning car Stanley from 2005 is now in a museum in Washington.
With automated parking, in some car parks the car can look for a free space all by itself.

teile.einleitung: Earthquake-resistant construction means designing houses, bridges and other structures so that they do not collapse in an earthquake. The main aim is to protect people and allow them to get outside in time. There are earthquakes in Switzerland too, which is why special building regulations apply here.
wichtigste: Earthquake-resistant structures should be able to bend without breaking.
Continuous walls made of reinforced concrete absorb the horizontal forces of an earthquake.
A ground floor with only a few slender columns and no walls can buckle sideways.
With base isolation, rubber bearings separate a building from the movements of the ground.
In 1356 the strongest known earthquake north of the Alps badly destroyed the city of Basel.
Valais and the Basel region have the highest earthquake risk in Switzerland.
The Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich monitors earthquakes in Switzerland.
Japan is especially known for strict earthquake regulations.

abschnitte.text: In an earthquake the ground jerks back and forth and up and down. For buildings, the **horizontal forces** are especially dangerous, because houses are normally built to carry loads from above. A building starts to sway, rather like a glass of water that you push quickly back and forth. If it collapses, the people inside are in great danger.

An earthquake-resistant building needs **reinforced concrete walls** that run continuously from the cellar to the roof. They act like strong panels and absorb the horizontal forces. A **soft storey** is dangerous, for example a ground floor with only a few slender columns and no walls, because it can buckle sideways. It is also important that the structure can deform without suddenly breaking; this is called **ductility**.

With **base isolation**, a building stands on thick bearings made of rubber and steel. These separate the house from the ground, so that the ground moves but the building stays much calmer. Some skyscrapers also have huge pendulums or dampers that slow down vibrations. A well-known example is the skyscraper **Taipei 101** in Taiwan, with an enormous steel ball in its top section.

In 1356 the strongest known earthquake north of the Alps badly destroyed the city of **Basel**, and a fire caused further damage. Today we know that the Basel region and **Valais** have the highest earthquake risk in Switzerland. In 1855 a strong earthquake shook the area around Visp. The **Swiss Seismological Service** at ETH Zurich measures hundreds of mostly small quakes every year, which people often do not feel at all.

In Switzerland the building standards of the Swiss Society of Engineers and Architects, **SIA**, set out how earthquake-resistant buildings must be. Switzerland is divided into zones with different levels of risk. The rules are especially strict in **Japan**, where strong quakes happen very often. There, new buildings are constantly being improved, and children regularly practise at school what to do in an earthquake.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rubber bearings under a building that separate it from the movements of the ground.
Concrete with steel bars set inside it that can withstand pushing and pulling.
The ability of a building part to deform a lot without breaking.
Specialist body that measures and analyses earthquakes and informs people about dangers.

gewusst: The Basel earthquake of 1356 is still considered the strongest known quake north of the Alps.
Hundreds of earthquakes are measured in Switzerland every year; nobody feels most of them.
Some skyscrapers have a ball weighing many tonnes that swings to counter swaying in wind and earthquakes.

teile.einleitung: Amplitude modulation, AM for short, is a method of transmitting sounds or other signals with radio waves. The strength of a radio wave is changed in time with the speech or music. This is how classic radio on medium wave and long wave worked.
wichtigste: In amplitude modulation the amplitude of the carrier wave changes in time with the signal being sent.
Two sidebands are created to the left and right of the carrier frequency.
A sound signal of up to 4.5 kHz needs a bandwidth of 9 kHz with AM.
A modulation depth of more than 100 per cent leads to distortion.
AM signals can be received with a simple diode circuit.
The national transmitter at Beromünster broadcast on medium wave until 2008.
Amplitude modulation is still used in aviation radio today.

abschnitte.text: A radio transmitter sends out an even radio wave, the **carrier wave**. It has a fixed frequency, for example a few hundred kilohertz. With AM the height of the wave, the **amplitude**, becomes larger and smaller in the rhythm of the sound. The outline of this wave, the **envelope**, then looks like the sound signal itself. The receiver only has to extract this envelope again.

Modulation creates two **sidebands** beside the carrier frequency, one above and one below. Both contain the same information. If the sound signal contains frequencies up to 4.5 kHz, the transmitter therefore takes up 9 kHz of **bandwidth** altogether. **Single-sideband modulation** (SSB) transmits only one sideband and so needs only half as much space. It is used mainly in amateur radio and on short wave.

The **modulation depth** tells you how strongly the amplitude varies. At 100 per cent the wave drops exactly to zero at the quietest moment. If it is modulated even more strongly, this is called **overmodulation**. Then the envelope is deformed, and ugly distortion and interference on neighbouring frequencies are produced.

AM is very easy to receive. Even the **crystal set** from the early days of radio needed only an aerial, a coil, a **diode** and headphones. The diode lets only one half of the wave through, so the envelope is left. This is called an envelope detector. Such a radio even works without a battery, because the energy from the radio wave is enough.

Medium waves and long waves reach very far, especially at night, sometimes more than a thousand kilometres. A big disadvantage is **susceptibility to interference**. Lightning and electric motors also change the amplitude and can therefore be heard as crackling. In addition, AM radio sounds duller than VHF, because the bandwidth is small. That is why people later preferred to listen to music on VHF with frequency modulation.

From 1931 the **national transmitter at Beromünster** in the canton of Lucerne was a well-known Swiss medium-wave transmitter. During the Second World War people all over Europe listened to it. At the end of 2008 broadcasting was stopped. AM is still used in **aviation radio** between about 118 and 137 MHz. There it has the advantage that you can hear two stations speaking at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The even radio wave onto which the signal is impressed.
The height or strength of a wave.
A frequency range beside the carrier frequency in which the information is contained.
Getting the sound back out of the radio wave in the receiver.
An electronic component that lets current through in only one direction.

gewusst: A crystal radio can play without any battery or socket at all.
Medium wave reaches much further at night than during the day, because a layer of the atmosphere changes.
The name Beromünster used to appear on many radio dials all over Europe.

teile.einleitung: A cylinder is a geometric solid with two round faces of the same size at the top and bottom and a curved surface in between. A tin can, a candle or a glass without a handle have this shape. The cylinder is special because it can roll and also stand flat.
wichtigste: A cylinder has two flat, circular faces and a curved lateral surface.
A tin can has the shape of a cylinder.
A cylinder can roll and can also stand flat.
A cylinder has no vertices, but two curved edges.
The volume is calculated as base area times height.
If you unroll the lateral surface, you get a rectangle.

abschnitte.text: A **cylinder** is a solid bounded at the top and bottom by two **circles** of the same size. These two circles are called the base and the top, and they lie exactly one above the other. Between them is a curved surface called the **lateral surface**. The distance between the two circles is the height of the cylinder. The word comes from Greek and means something like “roller”.

A cylinder has three faces: two flat circles and the curved lateral surface. It has two edges, namely the round rims at the top and bottom. A cylinder has not a single vertex. Because it has flat faces, it can stand without falling over. If you lay it on its curved surface, it rolls straight ahead, quite unlike a sphere, which rolls in all directions.

If you cut open a paper cylinder and spread it out flat, you get its **net**. It consists of a rectangle and two circles. The rectangle is the unrolled lateral surface. One of its sides is as long as the circumference of the circle, the other as long as the height. With a net like this you can make your own cardboard tin.

The **volume** tells you how much fits into a cylinder. You work out the area of the circle times the height; as a formula, V equals pi times r times r times h. Here r is the radius of the circle and pi is about 3.14. So a tin with a radius of 4 centimetres and a height of 10 centimetres holds about 500 cubic centimetres, which is half a litre. For the surface area you add together the two circles and the rectangle of the lateral surface.

We come across cylinders everywhere: tins, candles, pipes, batteries and tree trunks have roughly this shape. In technology the space in an engine in which the piston moves is also called a cylinder. Advertising columns in towns are large cylinders for posters. The shape is popular because it is stable and easy to make and stack. The tall hat worn by magicians and at formal occasions is called a “Zylinder” in German because of its shape.

begriffe.erklaerung: The curved surface of a cylinder between the two circles.
A solid spread out flat, from which it can be folded back up.
How much space a solid has inside.
The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.

gewusst: A cylinder and a cone with the same base and height: exactly three times as much fits into the cylinder.
Many drinks cans are shaped so that as little metal as possible is needed for as much content as possible.

teile.einleitung: An aeroplane is an aircraft that flies through the air with fixed wings. It can carry people and goods across oceans and continents in a few hours. The dream of flying is ancient, but it only came true a little over 100 years ago.
wichtigste: An aeroplane has wings on the left and right.
The wings create an upward force, lift.
From 1891 Otto Lilienthal flew with gliders he built himself.
In 1903 the Wright brothers achieved the first controlled powered flight.
A pilot steers the aeroplane.
The largest airport in Switzerland is Zurich.
The Swiss solar aeroplane Solar Impulse 2 flew around the Earth without fuel in 2015 to 2016.

abschnitte.text: The **wings** are shaped and tilted slightly so that the air flowing past is deflected downwards. This creates an upward force, **lift**. For enough lift, the aeroplane has to be fast, which is why it needs a long runway. Flaps on the wings and the tail help with steering, climbing and descending. In this way a huge passenger aircraft weighing several hundred tonnes can stay in the air.

From 1891 the German **Otto Lilienthal** flew with gliders he built himself and made about 2,000 glides. He proved that people can fly with wings. On 17 December 1903 the American **Wright brothers** made the first controlled powered flight in North Carolina. Their aeroplane was called the Flyer, and the first flight lasted only 12 seconds. Only a few decades later aeroplanes were flying across the Atlantic.

Early aeroplanes had **propellers** turned by an engine. Today large passenger aircraft usually have **jet engines**. Such an engine sucks in air, compresses it, burns kerosene in it and pushes hot gases out backwards. This pushes the aeroplane forwards. Airliners often fly at a height of about 10 to 12 kilometres at about 900 kilometres per hour.

The Swiss **Bertrand Piccard** and André Borschberg developed the solar aeroplane **Solar Impulse**. It flew only on solar energy, captured by thousands of solar cells on its wings. With Solar Impulse 2 they flew around the Earth in 2015 to 2016 without a drop of fuel. At night it flew on electricity from batteries charged during the day. The project showed what is possible with renewable energy.

The largest airport in Switzerland is **Zurich**, followed by Geneva and Basel. Basel-Mulhouse, by the way, is on French soil and is run jointly by both countries. **Swiss** is the country's best-known airline. Besides aeroplanes there are helicopters, which have a large rotor on top instead of fixed wings. In Switzerland, Rega rescues injured people in the mountains with helicopters.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of an aeroplane that creates lift.
Force that raises an aeroplane upwards.
Engine that pushes hot gases out backwards and pushes the aeroplane forwards.
The fuel for jet aircraft.
The room at the front of the aeroplane where the pilots sit.

gewusst: The Wright brothers' first powered flight was shorter than the wingspan of a modern jumbo jet.
As early as 1999, Bertrand Piccard was the first to fly non-stop around the Earth in a balloon.
At about 72 metres, the wingspan of Solar Impulse 2 was greater than that of a jumbo jet.
